Depression doesn’t shrink the brain like we thought it did

New Scientist August 20, 2026

For more than a decade, depression has been linked to a shrunken hippocampus, the main memory centre of our brain. But now, a study of more than 23,000 brain scans suggests this doesn’t stack up.

In 2015, a study of nearly 9000 people – the largest of its kind at the time – concluded that people with recurrent depression have smaller hippocampi. It also suggested that the area gets progressively smaller alongside a growing number of depression episodes, implying that the mental health condition may be responsible for this shrinkage, rather than a small hippocampus causing depression.

Alzheimer’s, stroke, depression: The preventative power of sauna

Now, Janine Bijsterbosch at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis, Missouri, and her colleagues have analysed brain scans from 23,417 participants in the US and the UK across six large-scale datasets, including the UK Biobank. The team used modern imaging techniques that weren’t available in 2015, says Bijsterbosch.

Advertisement

The researchers were surprised to find no significant link between depression – assessed via questionnaires – and hippocampal volume. “It is surprising [that] no [hippocampal] shrinkage was seen,” says John Fleming at Southern Colorado TMS Center. “This study is very important and tells us we still need to learn more about all brain regions and not take hippocampal shrinkage as a given.”

Free newsletter

The team did link depression to reduced grey matter volume or cortical surface area in the frontal cortex, the anterior cingulate and the insula. All three of these areas are involved in emotional regulation. The frontal cortex is also involved in judgement and self-control, while the anterior cingulate has been linked to decision-making and motivation, and the insula helps perceive pain.

“All of these [traits and conditions] are disrupted in depressive symptoms,” says Fleming. The reduced volumes may therefore help explain common depression symptoms, such as brain fog and pain, he says.

It is unclear why depression seems to affect these areas specifically. One possibility may be that areas like the insula have a high degree of neuroplasticity, which may make them more vulnerable to the stress of depression, says Bijsterbosch.

Bijsterbosch stresses that her team measured depression at only a single time point, while the 2015 researchers tracked the condition across multiple episodes. What’s more, most of the participants in the latest study had mild to moderate symptoms, so hippocampal shrinkage may occur in recurrent or severe cases, she says.

If the effects of depression on the brain are explored further, this could help us understand the link between the mental health condition and dementia, says Fleming. A larger brain can protect against cognitive decline – if you assume cognition diminishes at some threshold of damage, then a bigger brain is going to succumb later.

Drugs like psilocybin that induce psychedelic effects have shown promise for treating depression. Now, a review of the evidence suggests that they are effective, but no more so than traditional antidepressants

It is feasible that brain shrinkage due to depression could raise the risk of this decline, says Fleming. But dementia is an umbrella term for a range of complex conditions associated with reduced brain function. Many factors can be involved, including inflammation and sticky protein plaques and tangles in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease, he says.

If future research robustly links brain shrinkage to depression, transcranial magnetic stimulation – using magnetic fields to stimulate specific areas of the brain – has been linked to modest increases in volume, so it could be explored as a treatment, says Bijsterbosch.

“We hope that getting a clearer picture of the brain basis of depression will inform future work to understand individual differences and ultimately guide improvements in personalised treatment,” she says.

Nature Mental Health DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00680-y

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is doomed to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in the coming months, after a high-risk effort to save it failed.

SpaceX crash site on moon revealed by South Korean orbiter

“The El Niño has blossomed. It is off the charts. Usual measures of El Niño have blown past prior record levels in the period with good data, even though maximum effects are still several months in the future.”

So writes renowned climate scientist James Hansen at Columbia University in New York in a newsletter sent today.

There are different ways of measuring El Niños, which occur when warm surface waters spread eastwards along the equator across the surface of the tropical Pacific Ocean. Hansen thinks the best measure is how much warmer than usual the upper 300 metres of the eastern tropical Pacific becomes.

Advertisement

This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

“Our preferred metric, the heat anomaly in the upper 300 meters of the Equatorial Pacific Ocean… already exceeds the 1997-98 super El Niño,” he writes.

A more common measure, called the Niño3.4 index, is based on how much warmer than usual the sea surface temperature is in the Pacific in the long rectangle between 5 degrees north and south of the equator, and between 120 and 170 degrees west.

“The more common Niño3.4 metric, sea surface temperature… in the equatorial Pacific, also far exceeds prior values,” Hansen writes.

But Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s national weather service, says the Niño3.4 index has not yet exceeded previous super El Niños. “The anomaly in Niño3.4 is currently about 2 degrees above the norm which is very high for this time of year but not quite as high as the anomaly at the peak of the 1997/1998 El Niño which was around 2.5 degrees,” Scaife told New Scientist.

Free newsletter

The disagreement on the Niño3.4 index might partly be because this index is usually expressed as a three or five-month running mean. By contrast, the daily Niño3.4 value hit 2.75°C earlier this month before dropping back slightly.

“In this case, I would agree with Jim,” says Daniel Swain at the California Institute for Water Resources. “Niño3.4 values are clearly now the highest on record for the time of year, and are expected to remain so for the rest of the calendar year.”

Using a running mean with a long lag is misleading in a rapidly evolving situation like this, says Swain.

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

However, during November 2015 the daily Niño3.4 reached nearly 3.1°C, so the current event is not yet as strong as the 2015 one on this measure, either. It appears Hansen meant to say the Niño3.4 index exceeds values for this time of year, as Swain says. New Scientist has asked Hansen for clarification, but had no response at the time of publication.

“Under the standard El Niño metric region it’s still currently the third strongest event on record,” says Zeke Hausfather at Berkeley Earth. “But upper 300m heat is generally a leading indicator of what we will see at the surface.”

“I agree that this El Nino is the biggest on record,” says Kevin Trenberth at the National Center of Atmospheric Research.

What’s clear is that this developing super El Niño will soon exceed previous events on all measures. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts,” Scaife said in a statement released today. “If the forecast is accurate… then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”

While Hansen is comparing the developing super El Niño to other modern events for which we have direct temperature records, Hayley Fowler at Newcastle University in the UK thinks it could also exceed historical events suspected to be even larger.

“The super El Niño evolving in the Pacific will likely be the biggest ever recorded, reaching or exceeding the levels of the 1877-1878 El Niño which caused widespread impacts, including famines and around 50 million deaths (3-4 percent of the global population at the time), mostly across Asia and South America,” Fowler said in a statement.

New Scientist August 21, 2026

The melting of the Greenland ice sheet is causing more extreme heat in Europe, contributing to the major heatwaves experienced there so far this year.

The surge of cold meltwater into the North Atlantic is altering ocean temperatures and shifting the jet stream to favour heatwaves in western Europe and the Mediterranean, a study undergoing peer review has found. As Greenland ice loss accelerates, Europe may suffer more frequent and intense heatwaves than climate models currently predict.

This newly discovered “atmospheric bridge” played a major role in the unprecedented heatwaves this summer, according to Marilena Oltmanns at the UK’s National Oceanography Centre, who is one of the study’s authors.

Advertisement

Drought and heat push Europe’s power grid to breaking point

“Europe heats up faster. This is because of the jet stream shift,” she says. “In future years… it will be even more extreme. In the future we will think this [year’s heatwave] was not a heatwave; this was nice.”

The steady rise in global temperature has increased heatwaves. But it’s still debated whether changes in prevailing weather patterns are also contributing.

In the past 30 years, high-pressure ridges – large areas of elevated air pressure that look like a ridge or upside-down U on weather maps – have been forming more frequently over Europe, the study finds, leading to sunny skies and extreme heat. These ridges are caused by waviness in the jet stream, the band of strong winds that circles the northern hemisphere. When the more or less straight-flowing jet stream meanders northward around western Europe, it allows warm air from the central Atlantic and Sahara desert to pour into the ridge that’s been created.

Years with extensive high-pressure ridges over Europe have resulted in heatwaves like the one that killed 70,000 people in 2003.

Free newsletter

The researchers say the formation of the ridges can be traced back to Greenland through a cascade of climate events. In the summer before years of extensive ridging, an average of 81 billion tonnes more meltwater rushes off the ice sheet, they found. The cold meltwater lowers sea surface temperatures as it spreads through the North Atlantic in the autumn and winter. Its freshness inhibits mixing with saltier, warmer deep layers, further cooling the surface.

These pulses of meltwater cooling come on top of the “cold blob,” a long-term decline in ocean temperatures in the North Atlantic that some scientists blame on the weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) system of currents. Together, they create a sharp temperature front between the cold waters and the warmer surface waters further south in the Atlantic.

As warm air masses rise to the south of the front and cold masses descend to the north of it, they begin to swirl and generate cyclones. This makes the jet stream wavier. It tends to meander southward of these cyclones, then back northward over western Europe, creating the persistent, high-pressure ridges and heatwaves there.

The critical current could remain stable beyond 5°C of warming, but only if the warming happens very slowly

Most worryingly, climate models don’t fully capture this process, according to Oltmanns.

“This is a big problem,” she says. “It’s going to be even more intense in terms of heatwaves and droughts, in particular in the Mediterranean region, so the weather extremes are likely underestimated.”

A study in July found that the jet stream has shifted southward in the Atlantic in recent decades, similar to the pattern shown in the study. But it concluded that this was due to natural fluctuations in the climate and would eventually reverse.

Meltwater from Greenland could be forcing the jet stream to meander, according to John Methven at the University of Reading, UK, who was one of the authors of the July study. But the weakening of the AMOC or changes in atmospheric circulation over the North Atlantic could also be causing this shift.

“That’s the weak link as far as I’m concerned, the link between the cold blob and whatever’s melting in Greenland is not established, and there might be other things going on,” he says.

If North Atlantic cooling continues to affect the jet stream, it could cause not just heatwaves but also other extreme weather, according to Oltmanns. The research linked it to an unprecedented derecho, a stream of thunderstorms and strong winds, in the Mediterranean in 2022. Winds reached more than 60 metres per second, and fist-sized hail killed 12 people.

“We [will] have more droughts at some locations, flooding events at others, and the variability on top of this increases,” she says.

Burns improve more rapidly after treatment with fish skin

New Scientist August 21, 2026

Fish skin may be the safest and most effective way of treating severe burns. Exposing burns to the skin of Atlantic cod seems to result in patients spending less time in hospital and experiencing fewer complications compared with other treatments. This may be due to cod skin containing omega-3 fatty acids that trigger just the right amount of inflammation to assist the healing process.

“Fish skin actually looks a lot like human skin when you look at it with a microscope, so maybe it works like [our] skin,” says John Lantis at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York. “[It] offers a faster, possibly slightly cleaner way of rebuilding your skin than some other options.”

Every day, more than 30,000 people worldwide develop burns that require medical attention. Severe cases are often treated with grafts, where healthy skin is taken from one part of the body and moved to cover or replace skin that is damaged or missing.

Advertisement

Humans evolved to survive mild burns at the expense of severe ones

Prior to graft surgery, many patients undergo temporary wound coverage to prepare the area and manage infection risk. This can involve applying synthetic or biosynthetic scaffolds made up of collagen, the most abundant protein in skin. But an Icelandic company called Kerecis manufactures products made from wild Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), which are approved to treat burns and other wounds in the US and the UK.

To compare these approaches, Lantis and his colleagues used data from 465 adults who attended 49 burn centres between 2019 and 2025.

All the adults had moderately sized burns affecting 13 per cent of their body, on average. Most of the burns were either mixed – affecting multiple layers of the skin – or third-degree, in which the outer and middle layers of the skin are destroyed, with no sensation in the area. The underlying bones, muscles and tendons are sometimes also affected.

Free newsletter

Prior to undergoing a skin graft, 93 of these patients were treated with GraftGuide, a minimally processed intact fish skin from Kerecis, which funded the study but didn’t analyse the data. The remaining patients received approved synthetic substitutes. The two groups were matched for factors like age, sex, burn severity and size, and any other complications from the injury.

The researchers found that the individuals treated with GraftGuide spent 12 fewer days in hospital, on average, than those who got synthetic substitutes, with the former group being discharged after an average of 23 days and the latter after an average of 35.

What’s more, rates of complications were twice as high in the synthetic-substitute group, with 16 per cent experiencing issues like sepsis, compared with 8 per cent who received GraftGuide.

How much sunscreen should you be using, when should you apply it, and are there any downsides to doing so? Skin cancer expert Rachel Neale is here to answer all of these questions and more

Atlantic cod naturally contains collagen and omega-3 fatty acids. Unpublished data suggests that putting omega-3 on burns causes an initial spike in inflammation, which helps stop any bleeding, says Lantis. This inflammation then quickly fades, assisting healing, he says. “If you had a wish list, you’d say, we want a lot of inflammation [initially], but you don’t want to keep inflammation going.”

Very few fish viruses are thought to affect people, which means the skin doesn’t have to be treated with harsh detergents that could wash away the omega-3, says Lantis. An advantage of Atlantic cod over other fishes is that it has a relatively large body size, so you can get a lot of skin from each fish, he says.

Comparing equivalent patients who received different treatments is always difficult, says Fiona Wood at the University of Western Australia. Formal head-to-head trials directly comparing the approaches are needed, she says.

One such ongoing trial is assessing whether Kerecis’s fish-skin product reduces the need for grafts in second-degree burns, which affect just the outer and middle layers of the skin. Each participant will receive fish skin to part of their burn, while the rest of it will be treated with a graft. “Every patient’s their own control,” says Lantis. This should eliminate the risk of discrepancies between participants affecting the results, he says.

Super El Niño could lead to mega CO2 emissions from fires in Indonesia

New Scientist August 21, 2026

Intense wildfires burning in Indonesia have likely been ramped up by the building Super El Niño – and could get much worse if this El Niño event continues to intensify to the record-smashing levels currently forecast.

“The fire emissions that we’re estimating are, for the time of year, comparable to previous really big El Niño years,” says Mark Parrington at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, who tracks wildfire emissions as part of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.

Wildfires do normally occur in the region between August to October, but are more intense in El Niño years. “Fire has certainly been greatly enhanced in those previous El Niño years,” says Parrington.

Advertisement

This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

During the strong El Niño in 1997 and 1998, wildfires in Indonesia emitted as much as 2.5 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, equivalent to around a third of annual fossil fuel emissions at the time.

That led to a big jump in global CO2 levels – the key driver of global heating – as well as being disastrous for people and wildlife in the region. During another strong El Niño in 2015, wildfires in Indonesia emitted an estimated 1.5 gigatonnes of CO2.

The 2015 and 1997 El Niño are the strongest on record, but the developing Super El Niño could far exceed them.

Free newsletter

“This is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts,” said Adam Scaife at the UK Met Office in a statement released today. “If the forecast is accurate… then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”

Definitions vary, but El Niños are generally defined as a sea surface temperature 0.5°C above normal in part of the Pacific. During 1997 and 2015, temperatures in this region were more than 2°C above normal, and the Met Office is forecasting the temperature there could exceed 3°C higher than normal around October.

If the El Niño is as extreme as the Met Office is suggesting, it wouldn’t be a surprise if the wildfires produced emissions totals similar to those that occurred in previous strong El Niños, says Parrington.

Seeding clouds with seawater could prevent a super El Niño

In Indonesia, there have been wildfires on the island of Borneo and in the provinces of West and Central Kalimantan. Smoke pollution has led to school closures and is affecting other countries such as Singapore and Malaysia.

Ground-based sensors in the region are measuring levels of smoke that have previously been detected only in El Niño years, says Parrington. “And we’re still at the start of the season.”

In much of the region, thick layers of peat have built up beneath rainforests over millennia, storing vast amounts of carbon. The clearing of forests leads to peat drying out, making it more likely to catch fire during hot, dry conditions. Peat fires are very difficult to put out, as they can burn underground.

A planet-warming El Niño climate phase has begun, but while the phenomenon can influence Europe’s weather through long-distance atmospheric teleconnections, the effects are often uncertain

Next year, there could be particularly intense fires in the Amazon and parts of North America, says Parrington.

The developing Super El Niño will also have many other impacts on weather around the world, bringing heat and drought to areas such as Australia, and more rainfall and flooding to others. Its impact on Europe is uncertain, but Scaife said there could be increased rainfall and storminess during the autumn in the UK.

It isn’t clear if global heating is making stronger El Niños more likely, but what is clear is that when El Niños occur in a hotter world, their impacts are amplified.

How long could we possibly live? A new estimate is mind-boggling

New Scientist August 21, 2026

A few years ago, I wrote a memorable and quite controversial story about Jeanne Calment, who was then – and remains now – the official holder of the world longevity record. She was born in 1875 and died in 1997, aged 122 years and 164 days. At least that’s the official version of events. According to some doubters, the woman who died as Jeanne Calment was actually her daughter Yvonne, who fraudulently assumed her mother’s identity when Jeanne died in 1934. Yvonne was 23 years Jeanne’s junior. Still a good innings, but not a record-breaking one.

The matter remains unresolved, and so, for now, Calment remains one of the most important data points in biogerontology. When we ask, “how long can a person live?”, the answer is “at least 122 years and 164 days” – assuming Jeanne Calment really did live that long.

Whether a person could live longer has long troubled scientists. It’s an important question in biogerontology because, if we want to achieve life extension, we need to know what we’re aiming for. But it’s surprisingly hard to answer. Calment is an outlier: nobody else has reached 120, which is one reason for the suspicion. The second-longest-lived person was Kane Tanaka, who racked up 119 years and 107 days, and the oldest person today has just turned 117. Aside from a few mavericks, however, everyone agrees that there is a natural limit.

Advertisement

But where is it? There are two main ways of tackling this question. One is by studying demographic data on verified supercentenarians. One such frequently cited analysis produced an estimate of roughly 115, but did not rule out somebody living to 125. Another concluded that Calment’s record is likely to be broken fairly soon.

Another approach is by computer modelling. One such model analysed short-term fluctuations in red and white blood cell counts in adults aged 85 and over, which the researchers converted into a measure of their resilience to terminal age-related disease. At some point, resilience breaks down completely, marking the point of no return. The researchers concluded that this varies from person to person, usually kicking in at about 120. But even for the most resilient individuals there is a hard upper limit of 150.

There’s a big difference between 125 and 150, and we’ll get onto this. But one thing these studies don’t take into account is future advances in medicine. In the 1920s, scientists believed that it was impossible to live past 105, according to biogerontologist Richard Faragher at the University of Brighton, UK. But over the following century, medical breakthroughs steadily added years to people’s life expectancies, helping (along with better nutrition and sanitation) to nudge the longevity record upwards.

What happens if that trend continues? To find out, a team at the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology and the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, both in Moscow, Russia, ran a thought experiment. Imagine, they said, that we manage to cure all the theoretically curable causes of ageing. The only unfixable one is damage to the DNA in our cells, which accumulates remorselessly as we age. In that scenario, the upper limit of a human life soars to 194 years.

I’ll stick my neck out and say it ain’t going to happen in my lifetime, and also point out that the causes of ageing are not yet fully understood. Even so, it suggests there’s quite a lot of room for improvement.

But back to the real world. Why do upper age estimates vary so much? Re-enter Jeanne Calment. When I was reporting that story, I spoke to a longevity researcher called Saul Newman, then at the Australian National University in Canberra. He had just published a paper showing that a small number of errors or fraudulent entries in paper records such as birth certificates can significantly distort longevity data. He told me he suspected the Calments’ alleged identity fraud was just the tip of the iceberg.

Newman, now at the University of Oxford, has just published a book, Morbid: Debunking modern longevity science, revealing the shocking extent of those errors and frauds. In Greece, for example, around 70 per cent of centenarians were found to be dead, kept alive on paper so their relatives could keep on drawing their pensions. Even higher levels of pension fraud were discovered in Japan. People have historically inflated their age for many other reasons, to join (or dodge) military service, get married or get a job. Clerical errors are rife too, especially from the time when today’s centenarians and supercentenarians were born.

Free newsletter

These errors inevitably feed into estimates of the upper limit of human longevity. If the demographic data used as an input is riddled with inflated ages, the output is probably also inflated. Garbage in, garbage out. People used in modelling studies are also tagged with an age, which could well be wrong. When the journal Nature asked Newman where this leaves the debate about a maximum human lifespan, he answered: “in an absolute shambles.”

When I was researching the Calment story, I also came across a 2011 paper that found that, across the whole world, 98 per cent of claims of lifespans over 115 could not be verified. The same paper also found that, in countries with rigorous birth records going back more than 150 years, not one person has been proved to have lived past 115. That, I think, is the best estimate we’ve got. Five score years and fifteen. I’m halfway there.

Tupperware returns: Homeware brand to be sold online and in store in NZ

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Auckland Tupperware addict Tina Hunter with some of the more than 500 pieces of Tupperware she's amassed over almost 50 years of buying the ubiquitous plastic homeware.

She’s a self-described Tupperware addict with “hundreds and hundreds” of pieces of the ubiquitous plastic homeware spread across every room of her rural South Auckland home.

Twenty are in Tina Hunter’s fridge, a further 10 occupy her freezer, and more than 50 Modular Mates are in constant use throughout the rest of her kitchen – which now risks getting even more organised with Tupperware’s return to New Zealand four years after the business shut the lid on sales here.

“My house is like a Tupperware explosion … every room in the house has Tupperware”, the 59-year-old said, admitting to a “seriously bad addiction” to the kitchenware brand.

“But I was thinking, what is it? And I came to the conclusion that it’s actually its usefulness … have you noticed people never throw away Tupperware?”

The homeware that helped generations store leftovers and organise pantries is back on sale in New Zealand from tomorrow after a four-year absence sparked by the disruption of its traditional party-plan model during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Although famously sold for decades through home-based gatherings hosted by independent salespeople, under new Australian distributor H. A. G. Tupperware will be sold online, as well as in-store at yet-to-be-publicised retailers, H. A. G. imports head of sales Daniel Grundmann said.

Tupperware was a trusted heritage brand that had “missed the boat” in changing its business model away from house parties, so they were thrilled with the chance to launch it back into the market, Grundmann said.

“We expect some beautiful, very fresh, exciting colours, and the nostalgic ranges that were there in the past … and [we’re] looking forward to new shapes and moulds coming forward in the future.”

Tupperware’s Australian launch three months ago had already seen “huge” sales, and he expected no less on this side of the Tasman given the 80-year-old brand was “very much a household name” in New Zealand.

New products ranged from stackable containers and multi-compartment containers to water bottles and bowls, all free of the chemicals BPA, PFAS, PFOA and PTFE and including replicas of heritage designs such as the sunburst lid.

As for Hunter, she’s excited to see the new collection, even if she’s not sure she needs any more Tupperware.

While the mother-of-one’s Tupperware treasure trove is estimated at somewhere beyond 500 pieces, she’s quick to describe herself as “an accumulator, rather than a collector”.

“I’m sometimes called Tupperware Queen, but I don’t sort of go about flaunting the fact that I’ve got lots of Tupperware. It’s just that I have lots of Tupperware.”

Her favourite in the five decades since her first purchase – a wheaten-coloured baking storage container – is a can opener she’s owned more than 20 years.

It’s still the easiest to use despite arthritis in her hands, said Hunter, who is also a former Tupperware consultant and party host.

Also prized are a vintage vegetable keeper gifted by her grandfather-in-law, a highly sought-after cheese keeper from the 1990s and a rare Shape-O keyring, believed to be scarce after the original manufacturing mould for the tiny replica blue and red kids’ shape sorting ball was broken.

But aesthetic still sometimes trumped practicality.

A white double colander had joined her collection despite the married mum already owning two more.

She couldn’t resist the all-white version because it resembled a fictional spacecraft famous for its warp-speed adventures across the cosmos.

“I’m a Trekkie ... and to me it looks like the [Star Trek TV show spaceship] USS Enterprise”.

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Gold mines are part of Central Otago's past, and Santana Minerals wants to make them part of its future. Photo / Supplied

Supporters of Central Otago’s proposed Bendigo-Ophir gold mine say local backing is becoming louder – but not necessarily larger.

Santana Minerals has pointed to a growing number of vineyards, suppliers and contractors publicly associating themselves with the project after years of heated debate.

The company recently backed a supporters’ initiative selling Santana caps to raise money for the Cromwell and Tarras volunteer fire brigades, while mine supporter stickers have appeared on vehicles around the country.

Supporters spoken to by the Herald said backing for the project had been present for some time.

Shane Norton, who runs Radio Central and is reopening the Omakau pub after it had been closed for nearly three years, said he believed the mine represented an opportunity for the region.

“It’s the future of Central, really.”

Norton, who previously lived in the Thames Valley, pointed to the history of gold mining in Waihi and Otago and the development it had helped fund.

“I think the gold from Santana and the other mines that will happen will help Central Lakes, which we desperately need if you look at all the infrastructure issues around Queenstown.”

Through his work, Norton said he spoke to people from a broad cross-section of the community and had not personally encountered anyone opposed to the mine.

“A lot of people sort of like to keep to themselves because they open up and they get shot down, but if you look at the Santana Mine supporters page, nearly 15,000 people now, people have had enough of the naysayers and they just want to get on with it.”

He did not believe the increased visibility of supporters necessarily represented people changing their minds.

“I think the support’s always been there.”

Elevate Central business group chairman Dewald de Beer said he was seeing more businesses publicly support Bendigo-Ophir, but similarly believed much of the underlying support was not new.

He said he had not often encountered business leaders opposed to the project and believed some had previously been reluctant to express their views.

“I think it’s probably just the fact that people can now actually – they don’t feel victimised almost by showing support.”

De Beer said businesses saw economic growth as important for creating opportunities in the region, but that did not mean development should occur regardless of its consequences.

He said Santana still needed to listen closely to those living near the proposed mine, who would potentially experience its effects most directly.

His own support was conditional on the project being developed responsibly.

“We need to hold them accountable to that; that’s the thing.”

Cromwell contractor Ruben Connelly said the potential benefits were more immediate.

Connelly’s company Precise Fencing employs six people and has previously carried out work connected with exploration at the site.

“It’s a big one for us, that long-term steady flow of work for our company.

“It’s not guaranteed work, but it gives you that security that you can look to grow and invest in your business knowing that you’ve got that potential workflow coming in.”

Connelly said Precise Fencing had been involved at the site since 2018, initially working with Matakanui Gold before Santana took over the project.

The company’s work included removing and replacing boundary fences to allow drill rigs through, and it had completed more recent projects for Santana.

However, Connelly said Precise Fencing would still have to compete for any future work.

He said he had supported the project from early on: “I just feel that the positives far outweigh the negatives.”

Custom Fabricators Ltd owner Scott Canham was similarly enthusiastic about the potential flow-on effects for Cromwell businesses.

Canham expected an “absolute abundance” of opportunity in Cromwell if the mine went ahead, and a benefit for businesses beyond those directly supplying the project.

“It’s going to get a lot more foot traffic coming through.”

Contact our South Island newsroom

Like Connelly, Canham already had links to Santana. He said he had been involved with the company since it arrived in Cromwell, initially through another company that worked alongside it.

“I want to be a part of the growth, I want to be a part of the support, I want to be a part of everything moving forward – and them moving forward will help my business move forward as well.”

Canham said he had always supported the project and, like Norton, said he had not personally encountered local opposition.

“I haven’t met someone so far that has had a bad thing to say about Santana.”

He has also been distributing “Dig Baby Dig” supporter stickers, including around New Zealand and overseas.

Santana has described the increasing willingness of businesses to publicly associate themselves with Bendigo-Ophir as an important change in the debate surrounding the project.

Chief executive Damian Spring said more businesses were becoming comfortable publicly expressing views they had previously held privately.

The company says the proposed mine would produce about 120,000 ounces of gold annually at peak production over a 14-year mine life and create hundreds of jobs.

The project remains one of the highest-profile proposals being considered under the Government’s Fast-track Approvals process.

Santana plans four open pits, including one up to 1km long, 800m wide and 200m deep, alongside a processing plant and tailings storage facility.

An economic impact report commissioned for the fast-track process projected the mine would contribute about $360 million to GDP annually on average and employ about 350 workers directly.

The proposal has faced significant opposition over its potential effects on water, landscapes, the environment and nearby communities.

Sustainable Tarras, which has been campaigning against the project, has previously warned that the mine could create long-term risks for Central Otago despite its potential short-term employment benefits.

The group’s Stop Central Otago Gold Mine campaign has raised more than $53,000 from more than 400 donors, with donations surging following the death of prominent mine opponent Sir Sam Neill in July.

Santana has spent about $17.7m pursuing Fast-track approval for the project.

Processing of its application was due to resume on August 17 after a pause, with the company expected to provide final workshopped consent conditions to the expert panel later this month.

Sustainable Tarras did not respond when approached for comment.

Ben Tomsett is a multimedia journalist based in Dunedin. He Joined the Herald in 2023.

Jade Richards’ death: Coroner urges music festivals to help prevent fatigued driving

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Jade Richards died in a crash on her way home from Rhythm & Vines. Photo / Supplied

A coroner is urging music festivals to take greater responsibility to prevent fatigued drivers from leaving events.

The comments were made in a finding relating to the death of Rotorua teenager Jade Richards.

Richards, 18, was killed in a crash on her way home from the Rhythm & Vines music festival on New Year’s Day 2024 after the vehicle she was in rolled on SH30 near Rotorua.

The driver, her friend Jasmine Donaldson, was last year found guilty of careless driving causing death after a judge-alone trial.

Donaldson was found to have had a shortage of sleep over the four-day festival before making a “flawed decision” to drive home on what Judge John Bergseng described as some of the country’s “worst” roads.

Richards was asleep in the back seat when the car crashed. Donaldson and a front-seat passenger suffered minor injuries.

Donaldson had no drugs or alcohol in her system. She shared the drive home with the front-seat passenger, who drove from Gisborne to Ōpōtiki, before Donaldson took over.

Coroner Louella Dunn said in her decision, released this week, that Donaldson’s lack of responses just before the crash had “all the hallmarks” of someone who was fatigued.

Dunn said Judge Bergseng found Donaldson had between 22 and a half hours and 25 hours of sleep during the four-night festival.

“This may well be normal at a four-day music festival for younger people, however the alarming factor is that the majority of the festival attendees leave the festival either driving or being driven.”

Dunn said the coroner’s role was to make comments or recommendations that, if made public, could reduce chances of further deaths.

She said it was clear Donaldson’s fatigued state caused her to veer off the road and into a rock wall. She said Richards’ death was preventable.

Dunn said attendees of music festivals were generally young and often drove long distances to attend.

“Sleep is frequently deprived while at the festival and this means that special care should be taken when driving home. Event promoters and organisers should ensure that attendees are made aware of the dangers of driving after attending a music festival due to the risk that fatigued driving can have dangerous and, as here, fatal outcomes.”

Dunn said fatigue could not be tested but it was apparent attendees would be tired at the end of a four-day festival.

“The conditions of a music festival [do] not promote restful sleep. A decision to drive home after the festival finishes is made by young people who are no doubt keen to return home and may not fully appreciate the risk of driving while sleep deprived and fatigued.”

She said event organisers and promoters should ensure festival-goers were aware of the risk and other options were available. One suggestion was providing an opportunity to stay another day so attendees could rest and sleep before driving home.

She said attendees also needed to plan ahead and ensure their nominated drivers were alert and attentive.

“I encourage music festival promoters and organisers to not only consider the effects of alcohol and drugs consumption on driving but to also alert festival attendees that driving while fatigued can have dangerous and potentially fatal consequences.”

She said it was hoped such messaging might encourage festival attendees to ensure their drivers were alert and vigilant travelling home.

The Rotorua Daily Post asked Rhythm & Vines questions after the release of the coroner’s decision, including whether it would make changes at future festivals.

A Rhythm & Vines spokesperson said their thoughts remained with Richards’ family and loved ones.

“Safety is a top priority for Rhythm & Vines and we will consider the coroner’s comments and recommendations as part of our standard and ongoing review of festival operations.”

Rhythm & Vines announced last month that this year would be the last festival held at Waiohika Estate in Gisborne after 24 years.

The 2027-28 event will be at an as-yet-undisclosed location.

Rhythm & Vines Festival chief executive Kieran Spillane said last month that accessibility and Gisborne’s remote location had been factors.

The Rotorua Daily Post asked whether Richards’ death had been a factor in the decision to move away from Gisborne.

The spokesperson said the decision to relocate Rhythm & Vines was made as “part of the festival’s long-term future planning”.

This week, singer Benee hinted in an interview with Ryan Bridge TODAY the festival might move to Hamilton.

Asked whether she’d heard anything about R&V’s future plans, Benee responded: “What have you heard?”

“I don’t know. Well, I guess I can say, because someone - I don’t even remember who told me. Maybe Hamilton?”

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Disabled Tauranga residents protest Disability Support Services Bill

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Mount Maunganui resident and former Paralympian Stacey Roche opposes the Disability Support Services Bill.

Mount Maunganui’s Stacey Roche says she is “dependent on people to be independent”.

The former Paralympian, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, receives funding from the Government’s Disability Support Services (DSS) and employs support workers for three to four hours a day.

Roche believes the proposed DSS Bill, introduced by Minister for Disability Issues Louise Upston in May, threatens that.

She believes the bill would “compromise my ability to hire who I want to hire” and may “force” her to rely on family members.

“My mum and dad have given me so much … they can’t help me and I wouldn’t want them to help me.”

Upston says the bill represents the “current state” of DSS and that no additional expectations will be placed on families of disabled people.

She says “improvements” to the bill were made after the Social Services and Community Select Committee’s recommendations, reported on August 13.

The bill’s second reading was in the House on Tuesday.

The bill proposed to clarify the purpose of DSS, including how funding is used and clarifying that the Crown is not the employer of family carers after a Supreme Court landmark ruling in December.

It said the purpose of DSS-funded services was to help those eligible “live their everyday life”, accounting for their needs and circumstances.

Roche, 48, told the Bay of Plenty Times she felt the bill was trying to “make my life smaller”.

In 2000, she captained New Zealand’s boccia team at the Sydney Paralympic Games. She worked as an advocate for people with disabilities for the Halberg Foundation for many years.

She is on the Parafed Bay of Plenty board and played wheelchair rugby in this year’s Healthvision Festival of Disability Sport.

“I have a really big and fulfilled life.”

If the bill went through, she said, she would have to go back to her family, although ”I haven’t been supported by them for about 30-odd years”.

Roche attended a demonstration opposing the bill on August 15 in Mount Maunganui.

“Kill the Bill,” was her message.

Tauranga disability advocate Juliana Carvalho helped organise the demonstration — one of eight nationally — “to stop the DSS Bill”.

Carvalho became disabled in May 2001 after becoming severely unwell. She has used a wheelchair since.

She receives funding from DSS to employ workers for home help, personal care and “access to community”.

Carvalho said the minister said the Bill would not put more expectations on families.

“But the Bill still says they have ‘a responsibility to contribute’ without defining what that actually means.”

Carvalho said decision-makers could still consider family and whānau support when deciding what funded support someone gets.

“That creates a real risk: the more your family helps, the more that help could be used to justify providing you less support.”

After Carvalho became paralysed, her family fed, showered and dressed her. She knew they would always support her.

“So please don’t tell disabled people that we need legislation to say our families should contribute to our wellbeing and care.”

Upston said she appreciated some people felt worried about the Bill and that improvements were made after the select committee’s feedback, informed by more than 3000 submitters.

They included:

Upston said the bill provided a legislative framework for the operation of DSS. It did not currently have one, which was a community concern.

She said the Bill’s aim was to ensure the system’s operation was formalised in law, “better enabling disabled New Zealanders to live a good, fulfilled and dignified life”.

During the Bill’s second reading, Upston said it would provide better consistency, fairness and transparency about how decisions were made.

The Bill would not change current eligibility, entitlements or support, she said.

Upston said the Bill had been amended to clarify a disabled person was “not expected to exhaust family support before support from DSS is provided”.

“The Bill does not establish new or unbounded obligations on family. It does not require family to be a disabled person’s primary source of support.”

Labour List MP and former Minister for Disability Issues Priyanca Radhakrishnan said Labour would not support the bill at the second reading.

She said several submitters shared concerns about an original clause that said family members had “responsibility in the first instance” for disabled people’s wellbeing.

The clause was changed to “families have a responsibility to contribute” after a select committee recommendation.

“That is a meaningful improvement … however, the bill still does not contain a clear guarantee that family care will always be complementary rather than a substitute for funded support and we are deeply opposed to that lack of clarification in this bill.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Flaxmere resident calls for action after car crashes through three properties: ‘Somebody is going to get killed’

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

A late-night crash involving a car that crossed three Flaxmere properties jolted a family awake at their Dundee Drive home.

The car ripped out resident Addie Wainohu’s letterbox, Australia-made business sign, garden beds and a 40-year-old tree before coming to rest in the driveway next door, where two vehicles were also damaged.

But Wainohu was most concerned that the car came within about 2m of the bedroom where her 17-year-old granddaughter was sleeping.

“She’s still in shock because she had the full impact,” Wainohu said of last Saturday’s crash.

“Had any one of us been standing outside our homes, we would have been killed.”

Wainohu, who has lived on Dundee Drive since she was a teenager, estimated the damage to her property alone could cost about $5000 to fix.

Fibre-optic cables along her fence line were also severed and later repaired by Chorus.

Police said they were called about the crash at 12.20am on August 15.

“No injuries were reported and there was some damage to property,” a spokeswoman said.

“Police are making inquiries.”

That crash was not the first Wainohu had experienced.

About 10 years ago, another vehicle left the road in what Wainohu described as an almost identical crash and damaged her property.

She said Hastings District Council (HDC) assessed the road after that crash but the only change she saw was faded white road markings being repainted.

Wainohu said she was told at the time the street would be put on a waiting list for further work.

Several other crashes and near-misses over the years, she said, had never been formally reported.

Wainohu said a nearby property fence was hit three times, while a visitor’s parked vehicle outside another neighbouring house had recently been struck from behind.

Wainohu said she believed the shape of Dundee Drive was part of the problem.

“It’s probably one of the most unusual shapes you can have in a road. It’s shaped like a horseshoe,” she said.

“When you’re coming around the bend, you don’t know you’re going to be turning around a bend. There’s nothing to tell you.”

Although the speed limit is 50km/h, she said even drivers travelling within the limit could underestimate the turn if they were unfamiliar with the road.

“You think you can see a road running straight through, but when you get down, coming further, you realise there’s no road, and so that’s why they end up hitting the neighbour straight on his fence line.”

She said residents could often hear vehicles accelerating before reaching the bend.

“When I hear the vehicles speeding, my heart just goes, ‘Oh my God, it’s going to happen again’.”

Wainohu this week formally asked the council for a new road safety assessment and consideration of warning signs, advisory speed signs, traffic-calming measures and barriers.

“Realistically, all they need to do is something with that funny road that’s down there, or put arrow signs around the bend so you even know that there’s a bend.”

After watching crashes and near-misses for years, Wainohu said she no longer wanted to wait.

“Somebody is going to be killed. It’s going to happen,” she said.

An HDC spokesperson said Wainohu’s request had been referred for further investigation.

Council records showed nine reported crashes on Dundee Dr between 2016 and 2025, including two injury crashes.

The council said the only other police-attended crash recorded near Wainohu’s property was in June 2014.

It had no record confirming whether a road safety assessment was carried out after that crash, although a review of the following five years did not identify concerns requiring an assessment, the spokesperson said.

The site did not meet the criteria for traffic-calming measures.

“On the basis of the reported crash history over the last five years, with the crashes being dispersed along Dundee Drive, the criteria for traffic calming is not able to be met in terms of both the crash history and the surveyed speeds at this time.”

Residents were encouraged to report incidents and near-misses to help the council identify patterns and determine whether further investigation or intervention was needed.

Lincoln student Cameron Beck wins John Perrin Scholarship after choosing agriculture over law

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Lincoln University student Cameron Beck has earned the 2026 John Perrin Scholarship, which will support his study and ambitions in farm management and hill country development.

Cameron Beck’s path into agriculture became clear while working alongside Hawke’s Bay farmers repairing fences and infrastructure damaged by Cyclone Gabrielle.

The Lincoln University student is completing a Bachelor of Agriculture and is the recipient of Perrin Ag’s 2026 John Perrin Scholarship, receiving $6000 toward his studies.

Beck grew up on a lifestyle block south of Rotorua.

Although agriculture was part of his upbringing, he said he did not initially appreciate the breadth of career opportunities available within the sector.

“Throughout high school, the law and business pathway was heavily encouraged, and there wasn’t a lot of information about the opportunities available in agriculture,” he said.

After spending several years travelling, Beck returned to New Zealand and began reconsidering his future.

He had nearly committed to studying law when he received a phone call offering him an opportunity to work on a Hawke’s Bay farm after Cyclone Gabrielle.

His work included repairing fencing and other farm infrastructure, as well as the farm’s usual summer stock work.

“With limited practical experience in the sector, it had been difficult to get my foot in the door,” Beck said.

“Having someone recognise my drive and willingness to learn, and then give me the opportunity to do so, was exactly what I needed.”

The experience confirmed Beck’s interest in agriculture and prompted him to reconsider the career path he had previously thought he might follow.

“Coming home after travelling gave me the chance to think again about my values and what I was genuinely passionate about,” he said.

“I realised law wasn’t something I could see myself pursuing with the same passion, and that led me back to agriculture.”

Since enrolling at Lincoln University, Beck has embraced his studies and the wider opportunities available within the sector.

He was appointed chairman of Lincoln Young Farmers for 2026 and has received several academic awards, including the Sir James Wilson Prize and the Luisetti Seeds Award.

Beck described his involvement with Young Farmers as one of the most rewarding parts of his time at Lincoln.

“There have already been countless moments this year that have made the work worthwhile.

“I get a real kick out of seeing people enjoy and make the most of the opportunities the club provides.”

In his view, maintaining public confidence in farming and protecting New Zealand’s access to international markets will be two important challenges for the sector.

“Negative perceptions of animal welfare could lead to customers or markets rejecting our products.

“That risk is greater than ever because of the reach of social media and the increasing influence of personal values on food choices.”

Any loss of market access could have similarly serious consequences for farmers and the wider New Zealand economy.

Looking ahead, Beck hopes to pursue a career in farm management and has a particular interest in hill country development.

“I’m interested in the opportunity to improve both the physical and financial performance of hill country farms and contribute to food production as the global population continues to grow.

“For me, successful development means lifting production in a way that strengthens the viability of the farm business while also supporting environmental performance and staff wellbeing.”

Beck plans to continue his studies with a Master of Management in Agribusiness at Lincoln University.

The scholarship will give him more time to focus on new projects and areas he wants to become involved in and learn more about.

Applying for the scholarship was also a valuable opportunity to clarify his ambitions and consider how he will achieve them.

“The interview challenged my thinking about the direction I want to take and how my plans will help me achieve my goals in the future.”

The scholarship selection and interview process was led by Perrin Ag directors John Perrin and Carla Muller.

They were impressed by Beck’s academic achievements, leadership and commitment to building a career within New Zealand’s primary sector.

“Cameron has demonstrated a genuine willingness to learn, take on new challenges and contribute to the wider agricultural community,” Perrin said.

“His academic achievements, leadership within Young Farmers and clear sense of purpose make him a deserving recipient of this year’s scholarship.

“With his drive, passion and introspection, we see him having a significant contribution to New Zealand agriculture.”

Perrin Ag awards the John Perrin Scholarship each year to support a promising student continuing their agriculture or horticulture studies at Lincoln, Massey or Waikato universities.

Named after Perrin Ag founder John Perrin, the scholarship recognises the qualities he has brought to his clients and colleagues over many years: passion, dedication, the pursuit of excellence and a desire to make a positive impact on our communities.

Perrin Ag is also a foundation sponsor of the Tupu Rangatahi and Tupu Ahuwhenua Scholarships, part of the University of Waikato Māori Agribusiness Programme.

Delivered in partnership with the New Zealand Institute of Primary Industry Management, the programme supports rangatahi to develop the skills, knowledge and networks needed to become future leaders in Māori agribusiness.

Has modern design become too safe? Why we miss products with personality – Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

They don't make 'em like this anymore: Glenn Dwight's beloved GEC Weltron 2001. Photo / Glenn Dwight

Every house has that one thing guests point at and ask, “What’s that?”

Mine is a GEC Weltron 2001.

If you’ve never seen one, it looks like someone in the early 1970s was asked to design a stereo for the year 2001 and decided the future would be made entirely from spheres.

There’s a large central globe flanked by two matching speakers, looking less like a piece of home audio equipment and more like something that had escaped from a science fiction movie.

Something between a moon landing, a Bond villain’s living room and Newton’s cradle.

It’s gloriously impractical, takes up far too much room and weighs an absolute ton, but I love it anyway.

In fact, I think I love it because of all those things.

It’s bold, unapologetic and completely unlike anything you’d find in a shop today, which got me thinking: Has design got boring?

Not bad design. Not ugly design. Just ... safe and boring.

Somewhere along the way, it feels as though we stopped trying to surprise people and started trying not to offend anyone.

Walk into an appliance store today, and you’ll find rows of black, white and grey.

If a company is feeling particularly adventurous, they might release something in charcoal, because apparently that’s completely different to black.

The future, it seems, is 50 shades of sensible.

Cars used to have fins, giant chrome bumpers and colours with names like Burnt Orange and Avocado Green.

The dashboards were a glorious collection of dials, gauges, switches and knobs, and if you were really lucky there was a cassette deck with enough buttons that made playing a tape feel like you were about to launch a space shuttle.

Every car felt different.

Today, eight out of 10 cars are white, silver or black, and the dashboard is little more than a giant flat screen.

Apparently, the future isn’t flying cars. It’s driving around with an iPad glued to the dashboard.

Even kitchen appliances seem to have lost their sense of humour.

Toasters, kettles and coffee machines all arrive in the same handful of colours and all seem to be chasing the same look.

Minimalist. Clean. Scandinavian.

I still don’t really know what Scandinavian design means, but apparently it’s the answer to every design brief.

There was a time when designers seemed to wake up each morning and ask themselves, “What if we made it look like the future?”

Today the question seems to be, “How invisible can we make it?” No one saw that coming!

Maybe that’s why old Kiwi designs have become so memorable.

Take the Crown Lynn swan vase.

At the end of the day, it does exactly the same job as every other vase on Earth. It holds flowers. That’s it.

But somewhere in a design meeting, someone looked at a lump of clay and thought, “You know what this needs? A swan.”

Fifty or 60 years later, people are still hunting them down in antique shops and on Trade Me, not because they were the most practical vase ever made, but because they had a bit of personality.

Or those brightly coloured Formica kitchen tables that somehow survived generations of kids colouring in, doing homework and banging Hot Wheels together.

They weren’t trying to blend into the kitchen. They were the kitchen.

And perhaps that’s what good design used to do. It didn’t just solve a problem. It sparked your imagination.

Remember those old playground rocket ships? Every primary school seemed to have one.

Health and safety would probably have a collective panic attack if someone suggested building one today, but as kids we weren’t climbing on a few bits of painted steel.

We were astronauts. We were blasting off to the moon every lunchtime, discovering new planets before the bell rang for maths.

Today’s playgrounds are undoubtedly safer, and that’s a good thing, but they all seem to come from the same catalogue.

Everything is carefully rounded, thoughtfully engineered and almost impossible to fall off. They work perfectly.

They just don’t seem to ask quite as much of a child’s imagination.

Even fast-food restaurants seem to have had the colour turned down.

McDonald’s used to have bright red roofs, giant characters and enough primary colours to make a rainbow jealous.

Now many of them look more like modern apartments than burger restaurants.

Maybe that’s just the way the world works.

When you’re designing something for millions of people, in hundreds of countries, you probably can’t afford to be too weird. You have to appeal to almost everyone.

The trouble is, when you try to appeal to everyone, you rarely become unforgettable.

Which brings me back to the Weltron.

It wasn’t sensible. It wasn’t practical. It certainly wasn’t trying to blend into the background.

It was a designer being brave enough to ask, “What if a stereo looked like this?”

Someone could have designed a perfectly square stereo that stacked neatly on a shelf, cost less to build, and probably sold just as well.

Instead, someone decided music should come out of what looks like three giant white space helmets.

Fifty years later, complete strangers are still stopping to admire it, and I think that’s the difference between something that simply works and something that’s genuinely well designed.

Not because it was the most practical stereo ever built, but because it was memorable.

I sometimes wonder whether we’ve confused good design with invisible design.

Everything now seems designed to disappear into the background.

Speakers are built into walls, televisions are giant black rectangles and coffee machines all look as though they graduated from the same engineering school.

Individually, they’re functional designs. Collectively, they’re becoming a little forgettable.

Nothing is allowed to have personality anymore, which is strange because people have personality, and we’re naturally drawn to things that do too.

Nobody talks about the perfectly adequate toaster they owned in 1998, but they’ll happily tell you about Nana’s avocado-green fridge, the bright orange Formica table that somehow survived three generations of family dinners, or the gloriously impractical component stereo system they fell in love with and convinced themselves it was a sensible use of their student loan.

Those things became part of the family story, and perhaps that’s the real job of good design.

Not simply to make something work, but to make someone smile every time they see it. To spark a memory, start a conversation.

So, if you’re a young industrial design student wondering what the world needs next, here’s my completely unqualified advice.

Forget safe. The world already has enough sensible products.

Design something with a bit of personality.

Design something that makes people stop and point.

Give us something that people fall in love with, even if it takes up too much room, weighs a ridiculous amount or makes an accountant nervous.

Because history suggests we’ll forget the products that quietly blended into the background.

The ones we’ll remember are the ones that had the courage to stand out.

How to prune berry fruit for a better crop next season - Kem Ormond

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Blackberries are naturally thorny, so thornless varieties make pruning much easier. Photo / Phil Thomsen

Pruning, whether a fruit tree, berry canes or a shrub, seems to be the one job most gardeners dislike.

The reason being a lot of gardeners are not confident about what to cut and keep so it will crop well in the coming season, as well as maintaining the shape of the tree or bush.

There are some great videos available online that can be helpful if you are struggling with your pruning.

September is usually the time to think about pruning your cane fruit, one of the least-enjoyed jobs in the vegetable garden.

If you don’t have berries in your garden, they are something you should consider, especially if you have limited room for fruit trees.

Some to select from are raspberries, thornless blackberries, boysenberries, blueberries, currants, and brambles.

There are also cape gooseberries and gooseberries.

I have to say, raspberries are my favourite, and while I have friends who grow enough to freeze, I love to graze while working in the garden.

Finding those ripe little gems is my reward for the weeding that needs to be done!

And what I like even more is that you can get two fruitings from most varieties.

But beware of birds who think we grow them for them alone; you may need to throw the odd bit of bird netting over your berries when in full production.

They like moist, cool conditions, rich, well-fed soil, and good drainage.

These canes are vigorous, and when planting new canes, space them out about 40cm along the row.

They will grow to 1m to 1.5m, depending on the variety.

Now, you can get yourself into a mess if you don’t keep these canes under control.

You need to thin out the suckers that pop up around the root base.

When fruiting is finished, remove each cane at the base and allow the young suckers to replace them.

The old canes will be dark and need to be removed, whereas the new ones will be light golden in colour.

I try to keep order with my berries, so I use bamboo, placed horizontally to support them, or you could use wire.

Because most varieties fruit in late spring and late summer, after the spring crop, remove the fruited canes, as this will allow new canes to develop for the summer crop.

Blueberries prefer acidic soil, so keep lime far away.

If you need to increase your soil acidity, apply some sulphur.

They like to be kept moist, so mulching around the plants is a good idea.

The berries are produced on 1-year-old wood, so when pruning, remove old wood while maintaining the shape and size of the bush.

Currants have a few different habits.

They do like moist, fertile soil, but they also need a whack of winter to initiate the flower buds producing that gorgeous fruit.

Shallow-rooted, they like a good dollop of mulch on top to keep those roots cool and damp.

More of a small shrub than a cane fruit, blackcurrants fruit on 1-year-old wood, so thin out any fruited wood to let the new boys on the block through, ready for the following season.

The red currant differs from its brother as its fruit is produced from longer-lived spurs, and all that is needed is a good tidy up of any old wood to let new growth flourish.

I have to say, red currant jelly is superb.

Blackberries and boysenberries are forms of brambles, whereas a loganberry is a cross between a bramble and a raspberry; a little confusing, I know, so just go on taste.

Naturally thorny, thornless varieties are now available.

While they prefer cool conditions, they are hardy and adaptable in most places.

If you think about where wild blackberries pop up, they certainly are tough.

You do need to keep your plants watered when the fruit is ripening, as it will improve fruiting.

These canes grow quite long, so plant about 2m apart.

They are usually heavy croppers, so they would appreciate their stems being supported.

Berries are produced on 1-year-old wood, so after fruiting, cut canes down to ground level, and remove any excess suckers.

As much as we dislike pruning, it is necessary if we want some of those beautiful fruit jewels.

Kem Ormond is a features writer for The Country. She’s also a keen gardener.

South Auckland farming couple rebuild Hereford stud after 50 cattle stolen

New Zealand Herald August 22, 2026

Phillip Jackson, Kirstine Lereculey and Carter Jackson of Bluff Herefords in South Auckland.

Imagine investing in a stud of 450 prized Herefords, conducting your first bull sale, and then discovering a couple of weeks later that the hinges have been removed from one of the property’s main gates.

Tyre tracks are found, along with the remains of a trampoline mat and pieces of old carpet that had apparently been used to help a vehicle negotiate its way through the mud.

Then comes the devastating realisation: 50 head from the stud herd, all cows and calves, have been stolen, never to be seen again.

Such an experience would be enough to make even the most established farmer question their chosen profession.

For a young couple working hard to establish themselves and build a future in farming, the impact is even greater.

This is exactly what happened three years ago to farming couple Phillip Jackson and Kirstine Lereculey, who farm 200ha surrounding the Glenbrook Steel Mill, South Auckland.

While this was a devastating blow, this couple have to be admired for their determination and positive outlook, which enabled them to carry on breeding the stock Bluff Herefords is known for.

Once over the initial shock, they then had to scan everything to find out exactly what stock was missing, as the rustlers took what they could, leaving multiple bulls together in a single paddock, orphaned calves, and fretting cows.

Building a successful stud takes many years of careful planning, selective breeding, and investment.

When animals are stolen, the loss extends far beyond simply replacing the individual stock.

The greatest loss is the genetic value developed over generations, along with the considerable time, knowledge and resources invested in establishing those bloodlines.

These genetics cannot simply be replaced overnight.

Rebuilding a stud to the same standard can take many years, making the impact of such a loss both significant and long-lasting.

While Jackson and Lereculey work hard, they both say they wouldn’t have it any different.

They love the lifestyle, the animals and being able to bring their son up in such a lovely, healthy environment.

“We are the first to admit, leasing the land that surrounds the steel mill certainly comes with its own set of challenges,” Lereculey said.

“It is a busy site with daily visitors, and the hardest job is keeping the gates shut, the stock in, and educating people to scan the QR code at every gate so everyone can be accounted for.”

“We watch growth figures very carefully,” Jackson said.

“We are constantly reseeding, as most paddocks are kikuyu, and in the winter, silage is fed out to the stock.

“We want to stay true to our objectives, adhering to our breeding plan and facilitating our client base.

“We love the nice temperament of the Herefords and the good mothering instinct of the cows.

“It has taken a while, but finally we have our herd up to the same numbers as before the rustling, and we have our fourth bull sale happening [soon].”

The bulls are handled daily, ensuring they are quiet, well-mannered and have an exceptional temperament.

All bulls have been thoroughly tested and vaccinated, providing buyers with confidence in their health, soundness, and readiness for the upcoming breeding season.

The couple say they are pleased to welcome prospective buyers to arrange a viewing before the sale, providing an opportunity to inspect the bulls and discuss their breeding and individual attributes.

The Bluff Herefords 2026 annual sale is being advertised for Friday, September 4.

Cam Heggie of PGG Wrightson will conduct the auction on the day.
