Once sleepy and run-down, Italy’s largest island is full of wonders

Sydney Morning Herald August 23, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It’s just after 4am when I open my eyes to a strange, dimly lit hotel room. After a 29-hour trek from Australia my body clock is all over the place, but for once, I’m pleased to have a touch of jet lag. I throw the shutters of my room wide open to find Syracuse bathed in delicious golden light and strangely quiet – a deep, almost sinister, air of tranquillity that is distinctively Sicilian.

After a quick shower, I’m wandering the deserted streets of this honey-coloured southern Italian city. Camera in hand I snap almost everything I see from the boat-bobbing harbour to the flowering oleanders, the grand squares, picturesque alleyways and Baroque cathedral.

I’d visited Sicily many years ago and carry vivid memories of hanging out in Palermo before taking a very slow train (where is Mussolini when you need him?) to Naples, via a ferry across the Straits of Messina.

Back then Sicily was sleepy, intriguing, a little run-down perhaps, with pompous architecture and a taste for elaborate funerals. And like many travellers my view of modern Sicily is, perhaps inevitably, largely shaped by the prism of The Godfather movies and blood-stained news coverage of the Mafia, which culminated in the tortuous Maxi Trails of the 1990s.

On this visit, I’m keen to see how much Sicily has changed, explore the island’s fascinating history and visit some of the famous archaeological sites, some of the richest in the Mediterranean.

Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter

Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now.

I’m here to join an eight-day tour of the island run by Cox & Kings. Founded in 1758, the company built its reputation on these specialist, small group European itineraries, so I expect a busy schedule, decent hotels, reliable transport and expert commentary.

While my preference is to travel independently, the company’s Classic Sicily tour includes some of Sicily’s most important sites, including the Valley of the Temples and Villa Romana del Casale, while also showcasing the island’s mountain villages, stunning coastline and impeccable Norman and Baroque towns – impossible to do as a solo traveller.

After a 60-minute drive from Catania airport, I join my 14 travel companions, a friendly English bunch of various ages, for a glass of prosecco and a chat in the hotel dining room. I also meet our tour guide Rosalia Coci, a petite woman with huge knowledge of Sicilian history and a passion for archaeology. Her English is excellent and colourful.

“We Sicilians have been so many things over the centuries,” she explains. “We have been Greeks, Romans, Phoenicians – you name it. But I’m glad to say the Barbarians didn’t leave a lasting impression.”

DAY ONE | At the crossroads of conquerors | Syracuse + Noto

After a leisurely breakfast at the hotel, we board the minibus which will be our constant companion for the next week. There’s a short drive to the Parco Archeologico della Neapolis on the outskirts of Syracuse. It’s just after 9am, but the place is already packed. “Syracuse is a tourist town,” says Rosalia. “It’s always very busy here.”

Despite its garden-like appearance, the archaeological park is brimming with all kinds of wonders, including a Greek theatre, a Roman amphitheatre and a vast quarry dating back to the fifth century BC. The quarry’s most famous attraction is the so-called Ear of Dionysius, an artificial cavity in the rock, but the horror of this place is palpable. “Around 7000 Carthaginian prisoners of war were sent here,” says Rosalia. “They were used as slave labour and worked to death.”

We return to Syracuse for lunch and are free to explore the old part of the city, Ortigia, which contains several important sites, including the Temple of Apollo and the impressive seventh century cathedral. Returning to the hotel, I stumble on a small beach packed with sunbathers, a reminder that the European summer is already here.

Then it’s time for our afternoon tour of Noto, a UNESCO-listed hilltop town south-west of Syracuse. The original Roman city was destroyed by an earthquake in 1693 and rebuilt in the Baroque style. The use of honey-coloured limestone gives Noto a sense of warmth, but its civic buildings are grand and opulent.

I’m particularly intrigued by the Triumphal Arch which dates from the Bourbon kingship. Noto is a pedestrian zone, and it’s pleasant to wander along Corso Vittorio Emanuele, visit a couple of churches, and then sit on a restaurant terrace with a cold Messina beer and soak up the atmosphere.

DAY TWO | In the shadows of Etna | Catania + Cefalu

Rosalia warns us that today is going to involve a fair amount of travel as we venture north to Catania, a major provincial centre, and then onto Palermo, the capital of Sicily, with a lunch stop at Cefalu, a popular beach resort.

The distinctive shape of Mount Etna looms over Catania, Sicily’s second-largest city, and has played a major role in its history. When Catania was not being laid waste by invading armies, it was threatened by volcanic lava and earthquakes. A huge quake in 1693 flattened most of the city.

“The Greek history of the town is a series of invasions and destruction, but it became much more important during the Roman times under emperor Augustus,” explains Rosalia.

Today Catania is celebrated for its festivals, street food and fish market but will certainly wow lovers of architectural excess. I’m so smitten with the giant elephant sculpture in Piazza Duomo that I become separated from the rest of the party. After a few text messages we’re reunited, but I realise how dependent I’ve become on my fellow travellers.

Sadly, I miss out on both the massive cathedral and Catania’s favourite snack of roasted peppers and tripe but do squeeze in a visit to the Roman Amphitheatre, one of the largest in Italy.

It’s a 185-kilometre drive north to Cefalu which provides ample time to learn more about the Norman kings who unified Sicily and ruled over the island for 133 years.

After driving through wheat fields and rolling farmland we reach Cefalu. With its umbrella packed beach and cobbled alleyways this sunny village is the ideal place to kick back. I find a small bistro and order a plate of sardines and a glass of chilled Sicilian white. Bellissimo.

DAY THREE | Yes, there is no cannoli | Monreale + Palermo

Cox & Kings step up the accommodation for our time in Palermo. Housed in a former bank, the Grand Hotel Piazza Borsa is certainly grand with a delightful central courtyard and rooms like small apartments. It’s also terribly formal – staff don formal attire to serve breakfast.

While the major streets are busier and scruffier than I remember, the cathedrals, palaces, squares and public gardens look newly scrubbed.

The day begins with a 30-minute drive up to Monreale, a beautifully preserved Norman town in the hills above Palermo. On the city outskirts we see some of the country estates that once belonged to Palermo’s richest families and one gifted to Lord Nelson, where he scandalised English society by carrying out a passionate affair with Lady Hamilton.

The Cathedral of Santa Maria la Nuova in Monreale was a passion project for William The Good, King of Sicily, and blends Islamic and Norman architectural influences. This remarkable structure, which is beautifully preserved, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

Returning to Palermo we visit the Norman cathedral, or duomo, and the sprawling Palazzo dei Normanni, which includes the Cappella Palatine.

The interior of the chapel is covered with elaborate Byzantine-style mosaics representing scenes from the Old Testament. “This chapel was commissioned by Roger II [in 1130] and is quite remarkable,” says Rosalia. “The mosaics depict all the church fathers. Here you see St John, St Gregory and St Basil.”

We stop for a light lunch at a family-run restaurant before continuing our walking tour of Palermo. I persuade Rosalia to take a detour to the Monastery of Santa Caterina which is renowned for its cannoli – classic famous Sicilian pastries made of tube-shaped, deep-fried pastry dough shells filled with ricotta cheese – but we leave empty-handed. “There is no cannoli today,” she says. “Palermo has a water shortage and the bakery cannot operate.”

DAY FOUR | Of vanished cities and hilltop towns | Segesta + Erice

After another sumptuous breakfast at Grand Hotel Piazza Borsa, we board the minibus for a long drive that will take us across the top of Sicily and down the east coast to Segesta, stepping off point for the Valley of the Temples.

The terrain is harsher and drier here, but we are soon rewarded by our first glimpse of the Doric temple at Segesta, one of the best-preserved Athenian temples in the Mediterranean.

The remote, rural location adds to the sense of drama as we walk up to the temple which was built between 430 and 420 BC. Although Greek in style, the original settlers are thought to have been Trojan exiles. “The temple looks impressive, but it was never actually finished,” says Rosalia. “There were so many wars and other issues going on.”

Segesta was once the centre of the enigmatic Elymian civilisation, said to have been founded by Trojan exiles who were constantly shifting their allegiance between Rome and Carthage.

Today’s visitor enjoys a sense of serenity that the original settlers clearly never experience. The city that once stood here has vanished, so running your hands along one of these ancient columns is a bitter-sweet sensation.

Next stop is Erice, a flawless Sicilian village perched atop Mount Erice and commanding stunning views over the city of Trapani. “I think you will like Erice,” says Rosalia. “Because everyone likes it.” Fans of Erice include the poet Virgil who mentions the town in his famous work, the Aeneid, but its history stretches back to the Elymian and Phoenician times. Later came the Arabs, Normans and Spanish.

With its cobbled streets, alleyways, cafes and souvenir shops, Erice attracts plenty of tourists, but retains a relaxed, charming atmosphere. History buffs can explore the town’s two forts, one Saracen and the other Norman, or just sit on the old ramparts and enjoy the views.

DAY FIVE | On an amble through antiquity | Agrigento + Valley of the Temples

The town of Agrigento serves as our base from which to explore the Valley of the Temples, the centrepiece of this Classic Sicily itinerary.

This arid valley, dotted with almond trees, features eight Greek Doric temples dating back to the sixth century BC. Lost for centuries, these temples were only rediscovered by archaeologists in the 18th century.

“After the Greek period, the Romans built a 12-kilometre wall around the park, but the temples later fell into disrepair – the Temple of Concordia was converted into a church and is the best preserved,” says Rosalia.

Our morning saunter through the Valley of Temples is the most arduous of the entire trip but is exhilarating and informative. Our legs and brains are both aching as we drive to a small trattoria in the countryside between Agrigento and Piazza Armerina. For lunch, we have plates of hearty beef ragu and slices of chilled melon for dessert.

Two hours later we’re deposited at yet another archaeological site, but one that almost eclipses the Valley of the Temples. Dating from the fourth century, Villa Romana del Casale was once the centre of a vast estate. Buried under tonnes of mud by a flood in the 12th century, the property was rediscovered 700 years later, its beautiful mosaics as vibrant as ever.

Gazing down at the depictions of everyday Roman life, sea voyages, exotic African animals and lady athletes (the so-called bikini girls) is truly spine-tingling, transporting the viewer to a world so removed from our own.

“We believe this was a summer residence for a wealthy man,” says Rosalia. “The property is divided into several parts. There are the owner’s private apartments, an area for guests, a gymnasium, a banqueting hall and thermal baths which were open to the public.”

DAY SIX | Under the volcano | Taormina + Mount Etna

After the sensory and intellectual riches of the past five days, I’d imagined that the pace would slow down. How wrong could I be? The previous evening we’d driven to the medieval town of Taormina. A Sicilian version of Capri, this hilltop honeypot just oozes style, sophistication and money. An episode of The White Lotus was filmed at the Four Seasons Hotel here and at the town’s magnificent Teatro Greco.

Over the centuries Taormina has attracted European royalty, artists, movie stars and writers. D. H. Lawrence and his wife Frieda lived here for two years and I managed to track down his old house – now locked up – which has fine views over the Ionian Sea. “We love Taormina and in particular our house,” he wrote. “I love [watching] the sun rise over the open sea to the east.”

Our lodging is called Hotel Splendid and shares the same jaw-dropping vista that Lawrence enjoyed. After breakfast, we’re off for a morning tour of Mount Etna, Europe’s highest (3327 metres) active volcano – its last eruptions were in 2001 and 2002.

The drive takes us up through vineyards, citrus orchards and neat little villages. The rich volcanic soil is responsible for the area’s abundance of cherries, hazelnuts, pears, strawberries, pistachios and, of course, grapes.

“A national park was established in 1987 which covers Mount Etna and also protects all the communities that exist on its slopes,” says Rosalia.

After pulling into the visitor centre, we spend a happy hour clambering around its bare, greyish slopes and photographing the moon-like craters. Our lunchtime stop is at Murgo Wines, one of 150 vineyards in the Mount Etna DOC, where we enjoy platters of cured meats, cheese and pickled vegetables and get to sample some estate wines, including a refreshing Etna rosso and an inky cabernet sauvignon from its Catania vineyards.

Gazing down over the plains below us this seems like the perfect place to say farewell to Sicily, but we have a full afternoon of sightseeing in Taormina before us. After seven days on the road, we’re still eager to see more.

Escape to the Aeolian IslandsOlder Sicilians go all misty eyed at the mention of the Aeolian Islands. Known locally as the Seven Sisters, the archipelago off the north-eastern tip of Sicily has been a favourite holiday haunt for decades. Volcano Island, the closest to Sicily, offers the rare chance to hike on an active volcano plus taking a soak in the island’s health-giving thermal springs.

Sicily’s most charming villageSick of fighting the crowds in Taormina? Then head up the hill to the medieval village of Castelmola. Built around a ruined Norman castle, the village is remarkably unspoilt, with picturesque terrace houses, narrow alleyways and several ancient churches. Visitors who hike the five kilometres from Taormina are rewarded with sweeping views of Mount Etna and the Straits of Messina.

Enna: A city in the skyAt 931 metres, Enna is Italy’s highest provincial city and one packed with ancient monuments and archaeological sites. Known as “the navel of Sicily” Enna is a stunning mountain town but attracts few tourists because of its remote location. Over the centuries, Enna has been ruled by the Greeks, the Romans, the Byzantines, the Arabs and the Normans who have all left their mark. Its many attractions include Italy’s largest medieval castle (Castello di Lombardia), a 14th century cathedral, and a temple site dedicated to Demeter. It also stages several dramatic religious festivals, including Madonna of the Visitation.

Hike Cavagrande del CassibileCavagrande del Cassibile is a nature reserve near the towns of Avola, Noto, and Syracuse. Keen walkers can join a guided hike along a 10-kilometre stretch of the Cassibile River. The path passes through canyons and scrub and ends at the Cavagrande lakes. Other attractions include the necropolis of Cassibile, an archaeological site boasting a large system of caves and tunnels.

The world’s most beautiful cityDestroyed by a 1693 earthquake, Scicli was rebuilt in Baroque style. The writer Elio Vittorini described the resultant civic masterwork, 25 kilometres south of Ragusa, as perhaps “the most beautiful city in the world”. Today’s visitors to the town enjoy a wealth of ecclesiastic architecture, fine boulevards and imposing town squares set in a dramatic gorge.

TOURClassic Sicily is an eight-day Cox & Kings tour of the Mediterranean’s largest island visiting the key historical and archaeological sites, from Syracuse in the east to Erice in the west. Prices start from $5995 a person and include four-star accommodation, all entrance fees, breakfasts and some meals, private transport and a tour guide. See coxandkingtravel. com

FLYCathay Pacific flies from Sydney and Melbourne to Rome via Hong Kong several times each week, with connecting ITA Airways flights to Catania-Fontanarossa Airport. See cathaypacific. com

The writer travelled as a guest of Cox & Kings Australia.

Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since

Sydney Morning Herald August 23, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

There is a familiarity within the Australian creative scene that gives audiences a unique kinship with the actors who appear on our screens and stages. These are the faces we have grown up with, who we have aged with, and who we innately feel like — were we to run into them at the pub — we could share a beer with. It gives our home-grown productions a warm, fuzzy feeling because, not only do we recognise familiar streets, landmarks and cafes used as filming locations, but we feel an instant intimacy when recognisable faces appear. The pride is palpable.

Occasionally, a production comes along that is so successful in creating that feeling of familiarity you can’t help but smile when you watch it, even if the subject makes you cry or shift uncomfortably in your seat. And that, in a nutshell, is Dalliance.

The six-episode drama series charts the fallout from one big, life-changing event and the ways it radically upends a group of 60-something friends. Exploring everything from female friendship and the path to parenthood to sex, desire and ambition, it’s the latest endeavour from John and Dan Edwards, the father-and-son production duo behind Bump and The F Ward.

The series also marks a reunion for long-time friends and collaborators Heather Mitchell and Hugo Weaving, who star as would-be romantic interests, Dani and Billy. Their on-screen rapport is instant, but when you’ve shared stage and screen for over 40 years, that’s to be expected.

“I feel so blessed every time I get to work with him,” Mitchell says of her decades-long friend. “From when we first worked together … there’s always been a lot of laughter, a lot of fun and ease. It hasn’t changed, really, over the years. And that’s the thing about getting older. [With] people you’ve known for a long time, you sort of slot right back to where you were.”

The pair first met at the prestigious National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA) in 1979, began working together at Sydney Theatre Company in 1982, and, most recently, shared the screen in Binge’s acclaimed multi-generational drama Love Me.

“I adore Heather,” says Weaving. “Working with her is being embraced. She has a capacity to care about others like no one else and I consider myself hugely lucky to get to play with her whenever we work together.”

Dalliance is a reunion for many of the cast, and remarkable in that most of them are in their 50s and 60s. Mitchell was most excited by the prospect of giving talented friends, such as Catherine McClements, an opportunity to expand their creative horizons. “I loved watching her play a character who’s sexy, funny and complex when she’s so often cast as brittle and tough.”

She also knew the perfect person for the role of Rose, Billy’s wife of 40 years, pleading with Home and Away producer Julie McGauran to release Georgie Parker, who has spent 16 years working on the soap, for Dalliance. “I’ve known Georgie Parker since we were in our 20s, and I think this role shows people the depth of her talent.”

By nature of the series’ time-jumping format, Weaving worked mostly with Mitchell and David Wenham, who plays Billy’s volatile younger brother, but relished the chance to connect with old friends. “Our read-through days were very special, all the cast together for two days. It was so lovely to catch up with everyone.” And like all great 21st-century friendships, Mitchell adds, the WhatsApp group is still going strong. “We’re constantly writing to each other on because we formed such a close relationship between all of us. It’s beautiful.”

For 68-year-old Mitchell, this was a project particularly close to her heart. Despite a career rich with experience (she won her second AACTA Award in February for The Narrow Road to the Deep North), this is her first time in the producer’s seat. She was quick to accept when John Edwards made the offer. “One of the beautiful things about being older is the challenges are less risky because you’ve got less to lose, if that makes sense.”

“And I have loved it,” she adds, pointing out that her age gave her the confidence to ask questions. “I haven’t beaten myself up if I don’t know something. I just say, ‘Can you help me with this?’ I’d go to the production manager and say, ‘I have no idea what this means.’ I think as I’m getting older, I ask for help more.”

Camaraderie played a pivotal role in not only the chemistry between the actors and behind the scenes – Mitchell’s husband of 34 years, Martin McGrath, is the show’s director of photography – but also in the writing room, where lived experience and a willingness to be vulnerable gave depth to each character’s journey.

National TV editor

“We talked a lot about sexuality,” says Mitchell. “Passion, love, sex. People who’ve been through cancer, how medication affects your sexuality, how desire changes for each person as they get older. Some people just do not want to be touched any more. Other people long for it desperately. For me personally, I’m probably saying too much … [but] I’m more sexually satisfied in my 60s than I ever have been. And I know what I want.

“We really wanted to explore both men and women and whatever gender, that there is no time limit to love and companionship and sex. And that sex is not the driving thing for everybody. That often people go online looking for very different things. And sometimes it is sex with no other attachments. And other times, someone is really looking for a true love. The past can turn up.

“So we talked at length about what is sexuality, and how is it perceived? And I would hope that for younger people, if any younger people watch this show, that they will also feel that life doesn’t stop. You don’t stop growing. You don’t stop living. You don’t stop wanting.”

Dalliance, and Mitchell’s own sharpened focus on life, touches on what psychologists call “socioemotional selectivity theory”. It argues that we shift our priorities and goals depending on how long we think we have left. Young people who see the future as long and open-ended prioritise knowledge and building their social network, while those further along in life, faced with their own mortality, grow more selective. They chase emotionally meaningful goals, avoid obvious risk, and prioritise close relationships over new connections.

“The older you get, you’re looking closer to the idea of death. More friends die around you, more things happen which you might feel will result in an ending,” reflects Mitchell. “Certainly within this show, we want to say, no one’s ready to end anything. These characters aren’t thinking of endings, they’re thinking of beginnings, like how do I want to live the rest of my life? How do I want to be with the people I love?”

Sam Neill honoured at the Logies

Australian stars at the Logies pay tribute to Sam Neill, who passed away in July.

Endings, as it happens, are fresh in Mitchell’s mind. She recently starred in black comedy The Fox, which would become one of the late Sam Neill’s final roles (though with Neill as the voice of a magpie, they didn’t actually share the screen). “Sam was a very, very dear friend of mine,” says Mitchell, who also paid tribute to Neill at the recent Logie Awards. “I’ve spent a lot of time with him, and my husband was a close friend of Sam’s. He’s directed me, I’ve acted with him, but our main relationship is a non-professional one – I actually went out with him when I was 22 – and I still feel his presence enormously.

“And there again, a man in his late 70s who was working and had jobs lined up. So much of his identity and his love was in his work, the people and the industry. I think it’s important for people to know, he was not a weakened person. He was strong right up until the end.”

As with Neill, both Mitchell and 66-year-old Weaving show no signs of slowing down. Weaving is in pre-production for, among other projects, the long-awaited Priscilla Queen of the Desert 2 and returns in season six of Slow Horses next month. Meanwhile, Mitchell is fresh off a 350-show run of her acclaimed one-woman play RBG: Of Many, One and is already lining up her next credits.

“People talk about being invisible in their 60s or as they get older; I feel the reverse,” she says. “Your 60s is a wonderful period of self-exploration in a whole new way, consolidating what’s important in life and what’s right for you.” If you ever run into her at the pub, she’ll tell you all about it.

Dalliance premieres on Paramount+ on August 27.

Too pretty to be funny? Why Brooke Shields is still fighting to be taken at more than face value

Sydney Morning Herald August 23, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Brooke Shields can’t play funny because she is too pretty. So say some male network executives with whom she locked horns over her new murder-mystery, You’re Killing Me. In the series, by Mother of the Bride writer Robin Bernheim, Shields plays crime-romance novelist Allison Chandler, the bane of the local detective (Tom Cavanagh) in a cosy fishing village in Maine, the kind where nothing much happens – except a worrying number of homicides. Allison is funny, clumsy, sensitive and smart. But, according to the network higher-ups – despite Suddenly Susan, Lipstick Jungle and a legendary guest spot on Friends – Brooke Shields couldn’t be all those things at once.

“As an executive producer I’m privy to the comments from our bosses,” she says on a Zoom call from her home, an hour outside of New York City. Her expressive hands embellishing her words, Shields radiates warmth and passion. “A lot of it is still stuck in the old times. It’s like, ‘oh, no, she can’t be clumsy because she’s pretty’. And the more modern way of looking at this is: she’s all of that. She can be sexy and she can be faulted and that’s fine because she’s earned it. At 61 you earn all of your flaws and your experience. And it makes you so much more interesting. It was important for me to play a character like that to show the multifaceted nature of women.”

Strong, complex female leads are as old as storytelling itself, she says. Just look at Homer’s Odyssey, now a box-office hit.

“Anne Hathaway’s character [Penelope] and Calypso [Charlize Theron] – these are unbelievably strong women,” says Shields. “This is since the dawn of time … Women have been the forebears of strength before we even know. It’s why we have the children. I think that’s starting to become more part of the zeitgeist and not as threatening.”

The disconnect between Hollywood’s feminine ideal and the female experience is a topic she explored in her memoir Brooke Shields Is Not Allowed to Get Old: Thoughts on Ageing as a Woman.

“You look at Irene Dunne movies and Lucille Ball, who was a beauty queen,” says Shields. “You look at true female comedy back in that day. Even the Marilyn Monroes. They were brilliantly funny and used their looks as a vehicle. So that by the time they had more dramatic moments, your heart was breaking, because they threw you off balance.”

Much of the comedy in You’re Killing Me stems from the generation gap between Shields’ character and cocky true-crime podcaster Andrea Walker (Amalia Williamson from Canadian romance drama Sullivan’s Crossing), with whom Allison is forced to collaborate to solve the murder of a fellow writer. The Gen X-Gen Z misfires yield hilariously awkward verbal slapstick to match the physical theatre.

“A woman of this age needs this young person in her life,” says Shields. “She can teach this young person and she can learn from her, too. And together, they’re stronger.”

She needed look no further for dramatic motivation than her relationships with her daughters, Rowan and Grier, with her filmmaker husband, Chris Henchy.

“A lot of [inspiration] came from my trying to set up my phone with Apple Pay, and my daughters being like, ‘Oh my god, Mum! Here!’ Or I’ll be saying to them, ‘Are you on the polly?’ And they’re like, ‘It’s not polly, it’s molly [the street name for party drug MDMA], and no!’ They make fun of me all the time. And so I went to Robin [Bernheim] and said, ‘We’ve got to put this stuff in there’.”

Retaining the dignity of the characters amid the rivalry was “a fine line”.

“If you’re the one being made fun of, you get more leeway. And it’s never mean. My older daughter [Rowan] has all this TikTok stuff that she does, and most of it is her making fun of me. I’ll learn the dance or whatever it is. I don’t understand what they’re saying. But it’s funny and I don’t take offence.”

2:04

'I don't take offence': Brooke Shields is bridging the generation gap

The iconic '90s actor is back on screen - and taking tips from her daughters.

After Rowan was born in 2003, Shields suffered postpartum depression, the subject of her memoir Down Came the Rain, and an infamous clash with Scientologist Tom Cruise, who criticised her use of antidepressants. In June this year, Rowan made her reality-television debut, joining the cast of Bravo network’s Next Gen NYC, which follows young professionals making their way in the Big Apple. Her mother wasn’t happy.

“I was horrified. But she held her own,” says Shields. “I got a message from [the show’s host] Andy Cohen that said she maintained her integrity and she is the grounding force. I said to her, ‘Don’t be the one throwing up. Hold the hair back of the person throwing up. Do not succumb to being mean. That’s not going to get ratings. I don’t want to hear that from you because that’s not who you are.’ So she stayed pretty steady.”

Shields barely recognises the industry in which she got her break in 1978 in the film Pretty Baby, and then shot to stardom in 1980 with The Blue Lagoon, before becoming a Calvin Klein model and Time Magazine’s Face of the ’80s.

“I’ve had to hire people to help me with social media. I hate it,” she says. “I’m not good at it. My younger daughter was modelling for a while, and she had a contract, and she had to do all of her own photography. I was like, ‘You’re working for Tommy Hilfiger. How are you doing your own photography?’ She’s like, ‘That’s the way it is, Mum’. And I mean, the word ‘influencer’ – what does it mean? And [fame] is so short-lived but that’s where the money is going. Someone has this many followers or this many TikToks and they pay them numbers that they would never get paid for a hard job. How do you battle that?”

As president since 2024 of the Actors’ Equity Association, Shields is lobbying the US government for better wages and working conditions for performers, particularly those employed by Disney’s theme parks and the Trey Parker/Matt Stone-owned restaurant Casa Bonita.

“The battles we’re fighting right now are heartbreaking,” she says. “You’re watching people work so hard and they’re not compensated. They’re not protected. They weren’t part of the union prior and they want to organise now. We’re going up against this massive industry and this conglomeration that doesn’t care about the people that are busting their asses for them.

“At Casa Bonita you’ve got cliff divers and there’s no safety. The idea that ‘the show must go on’ is not fair. I’ve had so many injuries myself from being on Broadway – taping up my knees and continuing to go on. Actors are considered disposable, and the amount they work, and the money they generate, it’s amazing. And that’s male and female.”

In Washington, DC, where “everyone wants a selfie”, she has heard shockingly dismissive statements about her craft.

“If you’re a plumber, you don’t have to pay taxes on your plunger, right? Well, under [former US president] Reagan, if actors had to pay for anything to do with their field – tap shoes, headshots, singing lessons – they didn’t have to pay taxes on them,” she says. “And then, in 2017, that miraculously just went away. We obviously know why, and so that’s another thing that I’m fighting for. I’ve had people in DC say, ‘Oh, wait, so you want funding so someone can follow a hobby?’”

Her experience at the age of 18, appearing in Bob Hope’s variety show for US troops in Beirut, was an early lesson in the value of entertainment. “Those 20 minutes of gags, monologues and songs for all these fresh-faced young people who were staying on the USS Guam – that was all we could give them. And it meant the world to them. We’re talking about entertainment as a form of escape and medicine, in a way. I’m not overstating it.”

Her new show, she says, “is a little escape … It’s just entertainment. It’s not too heavy.”

But she hopes You’re Killing Me plays a part in challenging those pervading perceptions about women that she has faced throughout her lifelong career. “Attractive females can also be smart and not afraid to be flawed. I’m OK with not being pristine and perfect.”

You’re Killing Me is now streaming on Stan (which is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead).

Meghan’s casting in The Gentlemen reportedly withdrawn

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 21:23:18 GMT

Duchess of Sussex was believed to have been under consideration for season three of Guy Ritchie’s crime caper

The Duchess of Sussex’s reported casting in Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen has been withdrawn, it was reported.

Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, wrote on Saturday: “I learned this morning that the casting of Meghan Markle in season 3 of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series The Gentlemen has been withdrawn. The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward.”

The development comes a day after reports that the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to make her acting return in The Gentlemen.

According to Variety, Meghan was in discussions to join the third season, which has yet to receive an official greenlight.

The Gentlemen series is a spin-off from the 2019 crime comedy film of the same name, which starred Matthew McConaughey and Charlie Hunnam, with Guy Ritchie acting as creator of both.

The duchess made her name in the legal drama Suits, in which she played the character Rachel Zane for seven seasons.

Her other small-screen appearances include CSI: NY and 90210, while film roles have included a small part in the comedy Horrible Bosses and 2015’s crime thriller Anti-Social. She also led two Hallmark movies: When Sparks Fly and Dater’s Handbook.

She recently filmed a cameo playing herself in the Amazon comedy Close Personal Friends alongside Brie Larson and Jack Quaid.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to return to live in Britain this month, six years after leaving for the US, it is understood.

The couple and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate to a property believed to be outside London.

King Charles was reportedly informed last Sunday that his son and daughter-in-law would return to Britain.

Last year the Duke and Duchess of Sussex signed a fresh multi-year film and television deal with Netflix.

Harry and Meghan struck the original five-year deal in 2020, reportedly worth $100m (£78m), which resulted in a number of projects.

Meghan’s main release with the streamer was the lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. The show received negative reviews from many critics, with the Guardian’s Chitra Ramaswamy calling it “toe-curling stuff” in a one-star review.

Is this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream?

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 20:42:12 GMT

The Sussexes are returning to the UK with significantly reduced media deals in an industry where fame alone can no longer guarantee success

Having settled in California in the aftermath of their dramatic decoupling from the royal family in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced a partnership that appeared to set a clear destination for their new lives outside the House of Windsor.

With every global media stable clamouring for their signature, the couple revealed a deal with Netflix reportedly worth $100m. The ambitions were lofty and broad, including scripted and unscripted projects, shows for all ages and documentaries.

A $20m podcast deal with Spotify appeared to confirm their ambitions; the Sussexes were reinventing themselves in the competitive world of content creation, a media powerhouse in the booming universe of streaming and podcasting.

As the couple now prepare to return to the UK, they do so with those mega-deals either pared back or expired, and their media plans less clear. It raises the question: is this the end of their American dream?

As with all things Harry and Meghan-related, their various media forays have spawned copious amounts of reactionary content and commentary. Each appearance, commission and production has been dissected: there have been blockbuster hits, much-publicised misses and some brutal reviews along the way.

For Harry, the pull of returning to the UK, if perhaps not permanently, has been clear for a while.

He says he loves his country, and in an interview with the Guardian last year, he admitted he hankered for home.

“I have always loved the UK and I always will love the UK. It’s been good to reconnect with the causes I am passionate about. I have been able to spend some time with people that I have known for so long. It is hard to do it from far away.”

Perhaps more so recently because his father, King Charles, has been ill. And on the work front, it hasn’t been easy either.

Six years in the content game offers a case study in how difficult it can be to negotiate the shifting sands of a transformed media landscape, so difficult that even a Hollywood actor and a British prince are not guaranteed to succeed.

Those years have proved there is one bankable aspect of the Sussex brand: their relationship with the royal family continues to be devoured on an industrial scale. However, launching lifestyle brands and philanthropic pursuits that rely purely on name recognition – even with a packed contacts book of A-list friends to help – cannot guarantee reliable success in the cut-throat era of the attention economy.

“The Sussexes have kind of got caught up in the media’s awkward teenage transition,” said Evan Shapiro, a former US media executive turned leading analyst of the creator economy. “Just being famous is no longer enough … The last time Meghan Markle worked in show business [starring in the US legal drama Suits], it was a different era. It was top down: ‘We push it out, you watch it.’ That’s just how it worked.

“That era has passed. It’s fucking hard [now] … the competition is literally every human on earth. Eight billion people with phones who are all competing with Meghan Markle.”

The Sussexes could scarcely have had better timing for their eye-catching 2020 Netflix deal, via their Archewell Productions organisation – global streamers were scrambling for big names to lure subscribers.

The pair were in demand, talking with the likes of Disney and Apple before the Netflix deal was signed. Spotify was also pursuing big-name deals when it secured the Sussexes.

While the Netflix announcement talked of a raft of potential projects, the greatest prize was always the story of the Sussexes’ relationship with the royal family. The subsequent 2022 documentary series, Harry & Meghan, duly delivered, setting record viewing figures for a documentary debut and ranking as one of its most successful docuseries ever.

Other Netflix projects featuring the couple followed, including the Live to Lead interview series, Harry’s Polo documentary and two series of the cooking and lifestyle show With Love, Meghan.

Unsurprisingly, content without the royal intrigue could not hit the heights of Harry & Meghan. Polo failed to make Netflix’s top 10 lists around the world, while ratings for the second series of With Love, Meghan dropped off. It was the 1,217th most watched title on Netflix over the second half of last year. A mooted animated children’s series, Pearl, was cancelled.

Netflix also ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, after seven months. The company said handing full control to Meghan was always the plan. However, the relationship endures. Netflix renewed its partnership with the Sussexes, but slimmed it down to a “first look” deal.

As for podcasting, the Spotify deal was ended by mutual consent in 2023, having only produced Meghan’s 12-episode podcast Archetypes, featuring interviews with people such as the former tennis champion Serena Williams and pop star Mariah Carey.

Meghan subsequently launched another podcast series, Confessions of a Female Founder, in 2025, with Lemonada Media. Only nine episodes were made. She revealed last year that there would be no second series, saying she was focusing on As Ever.

In line with all of Harry and Meghan’s exploits, there have been some acerbic assessments of their media production efforts. Most notably, the Spotify executive Bill Simmons called them “fucking grifters” after the company’s deal with the couple ended.

Less incendiary industry analysts point to the significant timing. The Sussexes’ narrowed Netflix deal and split with Spotify coincided with content providers cutting back on their big celebrity bets, and the chaos being wrought by the rapid rise of the creator economy.

“This isn’t a story about nobody being interested in [the Sussexes],” said Matt Navarra, a social media consultant who has worked with broadcasters. “It’s quite the opposite. They can generate attention almost on demand. The harder thing is converting attention into a repeatable media proposition.

“Harry and Meghan arrived in Hollywood with almost every advantage imaginable, but audiences now effectively have infinite choice. They don’t care about how expensive the deal was, or how famous the person is.

“I think that’s one of the brutal lessons of the new media world: that fame can buy you the first click, but only the content earns the second … Their original Harry & Meghan series was pretty much a blockbuster. What they’ve struggled with is repeatability.”

Several industry insiders noted the comparisons with the Obamas, whose Higher Ground production company’s multi-year deal with Netflix narrowed to a “first look” deal in 2024. Their Spotify deal also ended in 2022.

Shapiro said the Sussexes had not yet proved they could draw big audiences beyond content directly related to their dealings with the royal family. “By no fault of their own, the Sussexes were not prepared for the current moment,” he said. “It turns out, other than marrying a prince, Meghan Markle just isn’t that special. Other than being born into royalty, Harry’s just not that interesting.”

Navarra said: “Enormous curiosity exists around them, but curiosity about a person isn’t necessarily the same as demand for everything that person produces. Celebrity is a distribution advantage, but it isn’t a content strategy.

“Harry and Meghan show that you can inherit enormous attention and still have to earn the audience every single time. To me, that is the really interesting shift.”

It is perhaps understandable, then, that Meghan is reportedly returning to a bankable acting career that she put on ice after her marriage to Harry. Initial reports from Australia of a UK-based role for Meghan were backed up by Tina Brown, the former Vanity Fair editor and founding editor of the Daily Beast.

Brown said it had been fuelled by Meghan’s positive experience as a celebrity judge on MasterChef Australia last month. “She finally realised how much easier – and more fun – it is to perform in a hit baked by someone else,” Brown wrote.

“She was back on the market, and it did not take long for Hollywood’s mega-deal machine, WME, the talent agency that still represents her, to get her a role.”

Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied the reports.

On Friday night it was reported that Meghan was in talks to return to acting in Netflix’s series The Gentlemen. According to Variety, she was in discussions to join the third season of the Guy Ritchie-created series.

On Saturday Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, reported that Meghan’s casting had been withdrawn due to “backlash in the UK”.

But the couple are not out of the media production game. Archewell has evolved into a more traditional production company. Its forthcoming Netflix projects include a polo drama and a film adaptation of the romantic novel Meet Me at the Lake. Several sources familiar with the company said there were also projects in the works beyond Netflix.

In practical terms, the move back to the UK creates few issues for their media ambitions. It is not unusual for major production companies to sit outside Hollywood and make shows away from the US, and the UK remains a major production hub.

As for Harry, he – or anyone else – will struggle to replicate the runaway media success of his memoir, Spare. He is focusing on his Invictus Games coming to Birmingham next year. Meanwhile, Meghan has suggested any return as a business podcaster may depend on the progress of her lifestyle brand.

“I would love to bring the show back when I am at a different end of my founder journey,” she said last summer, explaining why she had put her Confessions of a Female Founder podcast on hold. “I think a different time will be so exciting to compare and contrast.”

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 20:27:08 GMT

‘We are not in the right physical condition’

Spurs beaten 3-0 at Brentford in Premier League opener

Roberto De Zerbi said that Tottenham are “not a team” after they opened their season with a humiliating 3-0 defeat away to Brentford.

Spurs are looking to kick on after almost going down last season and are expected to spend more than £300m this summer but they were handed a rude awakening at the Gtech Community Stadium. Brentford outclassed the north Londoners and left De Zerbi rueing a lack of fight from his players, bemoaning his side’s physical conditioning and suggesting that the pre-season tour of Australia was less than ideal.

“We are not a team yet for a lot of reasons,” the Tottenham manager said. “Before you become a team you can’t say what you can do. We are not in the right physical condition for a lot of reasons. Some players came back late from the World Cup. In Australia we don’t work in the right way but it is not excuses. It is a normal situation when building a new project.

“I don’t want time but we have to pass through these problems. I cannot lose confidence in my players. I believe in my players, my club, myself. We are working well. We have to improve quickly. We could fight stronger than we did today. We lost too many duels today. We arrived second in the second balls. We didn’t win one second ball, one duel, one tackle.”

Spurs handed debuts to Andy Robertson, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali. They are close to strengthening their attack by signing Omar Marmoush and Savinho from Manchester City but De Zerbi needs to build a collective.

“There are steps to become better,” he said. “Now the target is to become a team. You can’t become a team from the transfer market on paper. You become a team when the players find a connection, a spirit, a soul. It’s a project.”

De Zerbi pointed out that he was without Pedro Porro, Kevin Danso and Micky van de Ven. He said that Rodrigo Bentancur, who started on the bench, came back late in pre-season.

It was a fine way for Brentford to start their second year under Keith Andrews. Keane Lewis-Potter, Vitaly Janelt and Michael Kayode scored and there was an outstanding debut in midfield from Mamadou Sangaré, the £39m signing from Lens.

“The club deserve a lot of credit for getting that deal done,” Andrews said of Sangaré. “You’ve seen today what he’s capable of, the attributes he has. It adds to a talented midfield. I really enjoyed his performance today. He’s slotted in really well. He’s a humble young man who’s very, very hungry.”

The moment I knew: Days after September 11, we flew through turbulence – all I could say was ‘I love you’

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 20:00:12 GMT

In 2001, Scott Westerfeld travelled from New York City to Sydney to see Justine Larbalestier. In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, they navigated the crisis as best they could, together

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

I noticed Justine before she noticed me. We were at a literary award ceremony and she was wearing a dress, upcycled from a black Velvet Elvis painting, talking to a man three times her age.

I asked my friend, Carol, who knew everyone, why I’d never seen her before. Carol explained that she was an Australian academic, researching the history of publishing, and led me across the room.

“Justine,” Carol said. “You’re researching science fiction in New York. This is Scott, he’s a science fiction writer in New York.”

Justine turned from the older man, glanced at me, then shook her head. “Not my period.”

I was too young. She was studying science fiction’s golden age, a time before either of us was born. No one under 80 was relevant, or worth remembering.

A week later, we ran into each other at a reading. This time we talked. We discovered we’re both fans of Samuel R Delany, Octavia Butler, Ursula K Le Guin, eggs with hot sauce, bushwalking, and exploring new cities.

We were seeing other people at the time, but continued to run into each other at science fiction gatherings. Then came Justine’s last week in the city before returning to Australia. At a big farewell dinner, we were sitting directly across from each other, with lively conversations on either side, and we made eye contact, momentarily alone together.

“I just broke up with my girlfriend,” I told her.

“Me too,” she said.

We spent her last weekend in NYC together.

Then Justine was back in Sydney, and we spent months talking on the phone and emailing. This was our romantic jet lag era, 10 time zones apart. She was waking up when I was going to sleep, and vice versa.

In early September 2001, I flew to Sydney to see Justine’s city, her family, her friends. It was spring and everything was in bloom. The harbour was sparkling, and the big local news was a host of flying foxes invading the Royal Botanic Gardens. I was utterly charmed.

Until bigger news happened. Justine and I were at one of Sydney’s finest restaurants, Tetsuya’s, eating an extraordinary degustation, discussing each and every dish and drinking too much. When we left at midnight, (10am in New York), the staff seemed oddly sombre. The taxi driver didn’t speak much English. We didn’t learn what had happened until the next morning when Justine ran into her addled flatmate on her way to the bathroom. “She says the Statute of Liberty exploded?”

We turned the radio on and lay in bed holding hands, listening to what had happened to the city we both loved. We tried to call friends, but reached only overloaded circuits.

We had a flight booked to Melbourne the next day, to meet more of Justine’s friends. We’d heard from our New York people by then. All of them safe, but shaken.

It felt like tempting fate, boarding an aircraft on 13 September 2001. Even the cabin crew wasn’t pretending it was a normal flight. Justine and I huddled in our row of two, staring out the window, holding hands again.

Halfway to Melbourne, we hit a stretch of turbulence. And it struck me: passenger jets were now weapons of war. International travel as we knew it might be over. What if I went back to the US, and couldn’t see Justine again for years?

I opened my mouth to say all this, but instead said: “I love you.”

My voice was calm and level. Here, with her, I felt certain, despite the tumult outside.

“Me too,” she said.

Australia felt very far from Ground Zero. Normal life was still under way, except when people asked where I was from, and I became the focus of a sweet, unnerving kindness, treated gently, given free drinks. Once, an actual fruit basket.

The fruit basket became a running joke, one of many we had that week. Part of navigating a crisis with a partner is knowing how to change emotional gears. Justine and I would talk about the coming war one moment, and about sulphur-crested cockatoos the next. We were skinless, our feelings always close to the surface.

With the world reorganising itself, we had to let each other feel the weight of history, but also remind each other to taste the wine in front of us.

There was a deeper question, one that many New Yorkers asked themselves in the days after 9/11: Who do you want to spend the apocalypse with? Who can you trust to make the right silly joke when the world is demanding to be taken so seriously?

Turned out, I’d found that person just in time.

Jets kept crossing the oceans, of course, and Justine returned to New York much sooner than expected: in November, to meet my parents. We were already married by then, eloped upstate without telling our friends, and have been together ever since.

The Mortons by Justine Larbalestier and Scott Westerfeld is available now through Penguin ($AU34.99).

Aston Villa upheaval is a risk but Emery can release v2.0 and reap rewards

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 19:00:11 GMT

After exodus of key players, youthful arrivals over the summer amount to a fresh beginning with plenty to get excited about

Last season was the greatest Aston Villa have enjoyed since they won the European Cup in 1982. They claimed their second European trophy by lifting the Europa League, but even without that would have secured Champions League qualification by finishing fourth in the Premier League.

Despite a miserable start during which they failed to win any of their first five league games, there was even a spell around Christmas when it looked as though Villa might be challengers for the title. The question after a season like that is always: where next?

The answer is probably less clear now than it was amid the delirium of Istanbul in May. A reasonable consideration, even a couple of weeks ago, would have been: was that a one-off high, the limit of the club’s ambitions, or was there more? The danger for any team, but particularly one relatively unfamiliar with success, is to rest on its laurels, to be too loyal to those who have brought the long-awaited silverware.

It’s an understandable enough impulse: any transfer comes with a risk, so why make changes when what was there before worked? Why offload players to whom there is a sense of gratitude? Villa have not rested on their laurels.

Three major players – Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Ezri Konsa – have left, Emí Martínez seems likely to join them and Ollie Watkins might go as well. This is not a fire sale. Nor is it a club cashing in while it still can. But it probably wasn’t quite planned this way either. The exodus is a combination of accepting that certain players are ready to fly the nest and trying to make as much money from them as possible for a rejuvenation of the squad. The danger is that too much is being changed too quickly.

Those changes have not just been among the playing staff. Two physios and the head of the medical team went to Arsenal. Jaime Arias Galán, a technical assistant, has left. The individual development coach, Rodri, went to Como. Most significantly, Unai Emery’s assistant, Pako Ayestarán, departed, while the set-piece coach, Austin MacPhee, went to Chelsea. There are always changes among backroom staff and the impact is hard for outsiders to assess but, still, the departures add to the sense of flux and uncertainty.

There is logic in the changes to playing personnel, though. Rogers is 24 and had been at the club for two and a half seasons. He scored 14 goals in all competitions in each of the past two seasons, many of them spectacular. He squeezed in the third goal in the Europa League final and will be remembered with great affection by Villa fans but he wanted to go for the better salary and perceived better opportunities (a risk, frankly) at Chelsea.

Once a player’s mind is set on leaving, there is rarely much point in standing in their way. An Alexander Isak at Newcastle situation helps nobody. Far better to accept the cash and reinvest it. For a player who cost £15m, a fee of £117m, less the 20% owed to Middlesbrough, represents excellent business.

Konsa is 28 but had two years left on his contract. A fee of £51m feels reasonable. Tielemans went after Manchester United triggered his £35m release clause. There was nothing Villa could have done but, given the Belgian is 29, they can at least console themselves that they’re selling a player they picked up on a free in summer 2023 for a reasonable price before any decline has begun. While no club enjoys losing high-class players, trading is a necessary part of squad development – and there is reason to be excited about Villa’s recruitment.

Johan Manzambi is a hugely gifted young attacking midfielder, Zion Suzuki is recognised as one of the most promising young goalkeepers in the world, João Gomes has already shown signs of the tenacity he can bring to the midfield and Matteo Ruggeri probably represents an upgrade on Lucas Digne at left-back. Alejandro Garnacho is a loan signing with potential. The Argentinian winger clearly has talent; the issue is releasing it consistently. Aaron Wan-Bissaka, reliable cover at right-back, has joined from relegated West Ham.

And all that with a net surplus of £160m, plus whatever they may get for Watkins should he leave. More signings will arrive. There is need of a defender to replace Konsa. Chelsea’s Nicolas Jackson represents an obvious option to replace Watkins, given his capacity to exploit the space behind opposing defensive lines. The thought of him and Manzambi linking with Brian Madjo, the 17-year-old centre-forward who made such an impression in the Uefa Super Cup defeat by Paris Saint-Germain, is undeniably enticing.

Sign up to Football Daily

after newsletter promotion

Another central midfielder looks essential, particularly after Amadou Onana tore his anterior cruciate ligament at the World Cup. There will probably be at least one and possible two more creative players, one to operate centrally and one in the left.

That means potentially seven or eight major arrivals over the summer, and that is a lot. It hasn’t always been easy for new signings to adapt themselves to Emery’s methods. The Spaniard has insisted there are “six or seven contenders” who are better equipped than Villa this season.

Managers habitually try to play down expectation and, given the changes, it’s understandable Emery should take that stance. It may even be accurate. But it’s also true that a lot of sides have undergone a lot of change this season – and Villa at least have retained the same manager.

It may even be that this is a necessary stage of development, of rejuvenation and of the accumulation of capital before a renewed assault on the heights. Certainly the shift from Profitability and Sustainability Rules to squad cost ratio should suit Villa. But in an ideal world, all three of Rogers, Konsa and Tielemans would not have gone in the same summer; to undergo this much change at once is an enormous risk.

It is, though, risk with a potential upside, whereas sitting back and relishing the memory of last season would have led inevitably to decline. One phase is ending, a new one beginning and, while it might go wrong, Emery 2.0 may, in time, be even better for Villa than the first version.

Kayode seals emphatic Brentford victory in wake-up call for sorry Spurs

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 18:40:35 GMT

Continue down this road and it will not be long before the chants of “Lincoln away” start up again. This was the start of Tottenham’s brave new era but there was no sign of any change. The old flaws were still there in a cowardly display – with and without the ball – and after a summer of extravagant spending it will alarm Roberto De Zerbi that his side opened the season looking like relegation candidates rather than contenders for European football.

If anything it was a reminder that winning the transfer window is not the same as winning on the pitch. There has been plenty of excitable predictions about Spurs, whose outlay is likely to soon surpass £300m, but are they based on anything substantial? Not on the evidence of this game. There were no patterns of play from Spurs. They were timid in possession and chaotic at the back. They failed to perform the basics and they crumbled in the face of relentless pressing from Brentford, whose blend of power, speed and skill revealed a team determined to kick on in their second season under Keith Andrews.

Spurs could count themselves fortunate it finished 3-0. Brentford should have scored more – Igor Thiago, normally so reliable from the spot, marred an intelligent forward display by missing a penalty – but this was a joyous start to their campaign. Keane Lewis-Potter, Vitaly Janelt and Michael Kayode scored the goals and in the final analysis it was impossible not to dwell on a sparkling debut in midfield from Mamadou Sangaré, who already looks a bargain after joining from Lens for £39m.

How do Brentford keep picking up these gems? Spurs broke their transfer record this summer, signing Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m. They spent £85m on Mateus Fernandes, who came on for his debut, but Sangaré was head and shoulders above any of De Zerbi’s midfielders. The Malian offered energy, showed quality in possession and made the opening goal with a lovely piece of play, tearing Spurs to shreds by playing a clever one-two with Thiago before pulling the ball back from the right for Lewis-Potter to run in from left-back and beat Antonin Kinsky from close range in the 12th minute.

It helps that Sangaré, working in tandem with Janelt and Mathias Jensen, has slotted into a cohesive unit. Brentford have enjoyed a calm window and are well drilled by Andrews. “There’s real trust in what we’ve built,” the Brentford manager said.

In contrast Spurs were fragmented and undercooked. They stared into the abyss last year, averting relegation on the final day, and have so much to improve. De Zerbi, who saw a lack of fight, will worry that his side appeared to believe an extravagant transfer window meant they could stroll to victory.

It will take more than moving on from the constraints of Levynomics for Spurs to regain their place in the top six. De Zerbi has to raise standards. Spurs have moved at dizzying speed in their first summer since moving Daniel Levy aside as chair but De Zerbi needs time and was honest in his assessment of this defeat, admitting that the performance was bereft of soul and was emblematic of a team of individuals.

These are still early days. Spurs started with four debutants and have players to come back from injury. Even so it was worrying to hear De Zerbi say his side did not win a single second ball. Spurs could not have been weaker. They had three new faces in their back four – Andy Robertson was at left-back while Jan Paul van Hecke partnered Marcos Senesi in the middle – but Brentford found wide open spaces from the start, created havoc with deliveries from the wings and had chances to score before Lewis-Potter’s goal.

Much is made of Brentford’s threat from set pieces but this was proof that they can be just as effective in open play. Spurs were sliced apart and they continued to ship openings. Thiago headed against the bar and Dango Ouattara twice went through on goal, only to take a heavy touch on both occasions.

Brentford were rampant. Thiago bullied Senesi and Van Hecke while Kevin Schade had fun running at the Spurs captain Archie Gray on the left.

It was not until Brentford were 3-0 up in the second half that Spurs created a chance of any note. De Zerbi will hope that bringing in Omar Marmoush and Savinho from Manchester City will add more bite in attack. However, disappointing displays from Richarlison, Mathys Tel and Mikey Moore were far from the only problem for Spurs. There were frailties in every department. Lucas Bergvall was at fault for the second goal, losing a 50-50 with Jensen. Kinsky then failed to push Jensen’s shot to safety, leaving Janelt to convert the rebound.

Bergvall and Conor Gallagher were removed at half-time. Brentford, though, soon stamped out any hope of a fightback by scoring from a corner. Nathan Collins nodded down at the far post, Sangaré shot, Kinsky saved and Kayode rammed the loose ball into the roof of the net, leaving Spurs humiliated and De Zerbi with much to ponder.

‘I was rooting for Josh’: Pogacar wins Vuelta opening stage with Tarling third

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 18:27:45 GMT

Pogacar edges out Ethan Hayter in Monaco time trial

Josh Tarling third a week after death of brother Finlay

Tadej Pogacar stormed to victory in the individual time trial to claim the leader’s red jersey after the first stage of the Vuelta a España on Saturday.

The overwhelming favourite, aiming to complete a career Grand Tour treble, completed the 9.4km ride just 0.09 seconds faster than Britain’s Ethan Hayter.

Joshua Tarling finished third, four seconds behind the top two, to complete the podium a week after his younger brother, Finlay, died in a road accident while racing in the Tour of Portugal.

Pogacar clocked 10min 57sec for the short and technical course through the streets of Monaco, where he now lives, in the opening stage of the 81st edition of the Vuelta. Pogacar, who won the Tour de France for the fifth time last month and triumphed in the Giro d’Italia in 2024, is expected to finish in the red jersey in Granada on 13 September.

“It’s a weird feeling to win the time trial on the first stage and by such a small margin,” said Pogacar. “I was not expecting it. I’m really happy. This red is a really nice colour.”

The Slovenian said home advantage was the key to his victory. “That 0.09 happened when I passed my apartment because that was the most technical part, and I walk and cycle there every day.”

Pogacar said he had been hoping Tarling could win the stage after his brother’s death. “When I was going to the start line I saw that Josh had the best time. I was really wishing he would win today. I was going to give my best, but it was a strange moment, I was really rooting for Josh as well.

“Then I came to the intermediate point and I hear a different name. I hear Ethan Hayter is in front of me by three seconds. So I thought: I will give it everything, but no risks – I’ll see what happens.”

A Vuelta victory would make Pogacar the fourth rider to complete the Tour-Vuelta double in the same season, while only eight riders have won all three Grand Tours. His compatriot, Primoz Roglic, is chasing a record-equalling fifth Vuelta victory, but came in 24th.

Tarling (Netcompany Ineos) had been among the leading contenders for the opening stage, on a route designed to favour specialists, and moved into the lead before Hayter (Soudal Quick-Step) and Pogacar (UAE Team Emirates) usurped him.

The race continues on Sunday with a gruelling 214.3km stage from Monaco to Manosque in France. Monday’s stage runs 174km from Gruissan to Aude in southern France, with stage four taking place in Andorra before the race returns to Spain.

One of the videos referenced a 2015 attack in which a masked swordsman killed a teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhättan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by police.

Several party leaders cancelled planned speeches on Saturday, pausing campaigning ahead of Sweden’s 13 September general election.

It wasn’t a classic, but a statement victory by the All Blacks to which South Africa must respond in the coming weeks. By the end, South Africa had two men in the sin-bin and, given their status as the world’s leading side, this must go down as a disintegration. There will be a backlash – it is hard to remember a time when South Africa were so inaccurate with the ball in hand – but credit New Zealand for producing a masterclass at weathering the storm and taking their chances. It is 30 years since Sean Fitzpatrick led the All Blacks to a first series victory in South Africa, but the class of 2026 are off to a flying start.

The All Blacks chalked up five tries to South Africa’s one and they were even calling for scrums late in the second half, having found parity to nullify the Springboks’ only threat on the day. The last meeting between these sides in Wellington ended 43-10 in South Africa’s favour. This was some revenge mission.

South Africa, for their part, may wonder how New Zealand kept 15 men on the field during a period of sustained pressure near their line early in the second half. Their profligacy in the New Zealand 22 should be of more concern to Rassie Erasmus and his assistant coaches, however.

The pre-match verbals had all centred around speed. New Zealand wanted a fast-paced game, South Africa supposedly wanted to slow it down. It matters little what tempo you play at if you cannot catch the ball.

Andy Burnham was in the posh seats to see how his beloved Everton would fare without the key additions that even the prime minister has voiced an opinion on. No right-back, no new centre-forward, no problem: Everton contained enough quality to overcome a wasteful Crystal Palace.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Iliman Ndiaye delivered a timely reminder that, despite the missing pieces in the squad, there is pedigree and Premier League knowhow available to David Moyes as he attempts to sustain a challenge for European qualification this season.

Dewsbury-Hall swept home an outstanding finish to give Everton the lead and sweep away any lingering resentment over how last season flatlined. Ndiaye supplied the superb cross that invited Thierno Barry to seal Everton’s first opening game win since 2021. It was a brutal introduction for the new Palace manager, Pierre Sage, who lost defender Chadi Riad to a potentially serious knee injury late on.

“I spoke to the prime minister on the phone,” Moyes said. “Andy Gray came down into the office [before the game] and his assistant Peter Reid phoned down.”

Reid was Burnham’s chaperone for the day – along with a phalanx of security – and put the prime minister on the phone during his call to Moyes. His good luck message was answered, thanks in part to Palace’s profligacy.

There were no radical changes in formation or personnel from Sage for his first Premier League outing. A lack of cutting edge was familiar from the Oliver Glasner era, too. The visitors created three clear opportunities before Everton took the lead and failed to take any. Misfortune played its part in two of the chances, with Jordan Pickford’s left post struck twice, but that did not diminish the torment for Sage and the travelling support. A sense of the inevitable from Everton increased with each one.

Palace denied reports that Ismaïla Sarr had refused to play because of a desire to join Galatasaray – the Senegal international was absent due to a groin injury, according to his manager – and the disruption had no effect on their start. Eddie Nketiah created an early opportunity for Jean-Philippe Mateta, but his strike partner volleyed over at the near post.

Chance number two came from a sublime pass by Adam Wharton, the midfielder who Sage has insisted is going nowhere despite interest from Manchester City. Wharton found Nketiah free inside the area with a perfectly weighted ball over Merlin Röhl, forced to deputise at right-back in the absence of a conclusion to Everton’s almost farcical search for Séamus Coleman’s successor.

Nketiah had time to pick his spot but Pickford produced a superb save to tip the shot on to a post. Mateta struck the same post from another Nketiah cross and Everton took full advantage of their reprieves.

Everton grew into their opening game, with the summer signings Hayden Hackney, Tyrique George and Röhl all impressing. Creativity was initially in short supply from the home side, despite George’s constant probing on the left, until Dewsbury-Hall and Ndiaye imposed themselves on proceedings.

Victoria Fuller, the chief constable of Cleveland police, said it was an “incredibly sad day” for the force.

“The loss has been felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies,” she said.

She described Blades and Clough as “brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift”.

Fuller added that she had visited the families of both officers to “offer our condolences and support”.

The force confirmed that all occupants of both vehicles were pronounced dead at the scene.

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), said it understood the officers had been pursuing a suspicious vehicle when the accident occurred at 3.39am.

It has launched a mandatory investigation and is working with officers from Cleveland police to establish the circumstances surrounding the crash.

“This tragic incident will be felt across Cleveland, within our communities and throughout the entire policing family,” Fuller added.

“We are providing specialist support to all families involved at this extremely difficult time.”

Fuller said Cleveland police would “cooperate fully” with the IOPC investigation.

“While this investigation takes place, we strongly urge people to avoid speculation,” she said.

Writing on X on Saturday afternoon, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Devastated to hear that two police officers have lost their lives while on duty in Cleveland this morning, as well as five members of the public.

A spokesperson said: “Sadly, despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene.

Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this.”

Lauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling today.

“Our colleagues who should have been going home to their loved ones at the end of their shifts are not. And that is just unfathomable.

“Cleveland police federation will be offering full support to our fallen colleagues’ families and they have all of our love and care at this time.

“When the time is right we will pay full tribute to our brave colleagues. But we can assure that their sacrifice will never be forgotten.”

“Two of the seven people who have lost their lives were Cleveland police officers, on duty serving our community. “I cannot begin to imagine how difficult this has been for the emergency services responding to such a devastating incident. Thank you to every one of them for their courage, care and professionalism.”

The crash marks the first time in 14 years that more than one police officer has died on duty while responding to the same incident.

In September 2012, the Greater Manchester police officers Fiona Bone, 32, and Nicola Hughes, 23, were killed in a gun and grenade attack in Mottram, Tameside, during what appeared to be routine burglary call.

They were lured to their deaths by Dale Cregan, now 43, who was already on the run, having committed several other murders. He was given a whole-life jail term in 2013.
