Chemical suppression: why the UK is exploring libido control drugs to treat sex offenders

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 16:00:07 GMT

Treatment is already required by parole boards in several countries, but some feel the practice is unethical

Thousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugs

For some prisoners with problematic sexual arousal (PSA), “images of sex flood their minds” all of their waking hours, according to Prof Belinda Winder, a leading forensic psychologist who has evaluated the use of drugs to control libidos.

“I remember talking to one guy a few weeks after he started taking the medication. He said: ‘It’s amazing. I followed a film plot. I wasn’t just looking for when I could see bra straps, when I could see nipples, when someone’s going to bend over so I could see their bum.”

“Without the drugs, these images were going around his head all the time. He did not want them any more,” she said.

Drugs used in the UK to treat PSA include antidepressants, which help control obsessive urges, and anti-androgens, which lower testosterone levels.

The treatments, typically taken as pills, are not suitable for some offenders such as those who are primarily motivated by anger, or who struggle to moderate their behaviour while using alcohol or drugs.

A similar approach has been used in some European countries. In Denmark and France, the use of chemical suppression has only been administered on a voluntary basis.

In Germany, the Dunkelfeld project provides free and confidential therapies including medical interventions to men with paedophilic or hebephilic obsessions.

An advert on YouTube urging men to contact the project shows unidentified men saying: “In therapy, I learned that no one is to blame for their sexual preference. But everyone is to blame for their behaviour. I don’t want to be an offender.”

But many other countries have taken a harder line. Poland introduced mandatory chemical suppression for some sex offenders.

South Korea became the first country in Asia to legalise chemical castration, passing a law in 2010. The law grants courts and a Ministry of Justice committee the authority to order involuntary hormone treatment for convicted sex offenders to suppress their testosterone.

In Australia, several states grant courts and parole boards the power to order anti-libidinal treatment for high-risk sex offenders which can then become a condition of release. Kazakhstan and a number of US states including California and Florida already have mandatory prescribing of anti-libidinal drugs to some sex offenders.

Officials in the UK have explored whether taking part in programmes such as these could be made a condition of a parole licence, similar to a scheme in California. However, ethical dilemmas remain over whether it would be right to give someone parole based on whether they take a drug that can be life-changing.

In the 50s, hormone treatments were given to men convicted of crimes related to their homosexuality with the promise that they could avoid jail. Alan Turing, the computer scientist and codebreaker, who was convicted of “gross indecency” in 1952, accepted chemical castration as a way of avoiding imprisonment. He took his own life two years later and received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.

The side effects of anti-androgens in particular can be severe. Some men experience fatigue, hot flushes, muscle loss, mood changes, weight gain and a loss of bone density.

Experts acknowledge that problems remain. The medication is not a cure and does not change underlying behaviours. Some programmes have high drop-out rates.

Each offender would have to be assessed by the Parole Board on their merits, according to Winder. “It is never going to be so simple that a decision will be taken on whether to give someone parole based on whether they are taking their meds,” she said.

Winder added: “Parole Boards take such decisions by assessing many factors, including how receptive they are to staff and how they interact with their peers. It is really important that people are trained in understanding what it means if someone is taking this medication and how that might affect a person’s behaviour.”

Thousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugs

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 16:00:07 GMT

Exclusive: Voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing medication to expand to 20 prisons and expert says it could be rolled out widely by late 2028

Chemical suppression: why the UK is exploring libido control drugs to treat sex offenders

Drugs that help control the libidos of people who have committed sexual offences could be rolled out for thousands of male prisoners in England and Wales from December 2028, an expert has said.

Prof Belinda Winder, who has evaluated the use of sex drive-suppressing medication in prisons, said about one in four sex offenders – equating to 3,750 current prisoners – would be considered for the treatment.

Government sources have told the Guardian that Andy Burnham’s administration is keen to expand the voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing drugs amid a scramble to ease the prison overcrowding crisis.

However, ministers are re-evaluating whether to press ahead with Shabana Mahmood’s pledge to explore mandatory chemical castration of serious sex offenders, such as paedophiles and rapists.

About 15,000 prisoners in England and Wales are serving a sentence for a sexual offence, and more than 850 men a month are arrested on suspicion of online child sexual abuse offences.

A pilot programme, the medication to manage problematic sexual arousal treatment pathway (MMPSA), will be expanded from 10 to 20 prisons in November. The next phase will extend from south-west England into two additional NHS regions, the north-west and north-east.

It is meant to target sex offenders who experience intrusive, persistent and intense sexual thoughts, persistent arousal, and unhealthy sexual urges and sexual behaviours. Prisoners on the trial can be offered drugs including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as sertraline, which helps to limit invasive sexual thoughts, and anti-androgens, which reduce the production of testosterone and limit libido. In some cases, it reduces testosterone to pre-pubescent levels.

Winder said officials could be ready to launch the drugs in prisons and probation services across England and Wales within 28 months if the pilot continued to progress.

“They [the Ministry of Justice] could be ready in December 2028 to roll the programme out if the interim findings look useful,” she said.

Those on the scheme would have to receive clinical support if they were to commit to taking the drugs and not reoffend, Winder said. “I am optimistic that a properly resourced, voluntary national MMPSA pathway could ultimately be developed … A good national service needs appropriately trained clinicians, clear referral routes, appropriate psychological support alongside medication,” she said.

Last year Mahmood, the then justice secretary, told MPs she was exploring a national rollout of voluntary chemical castration for sex offenders and whether it could be made mandatory.

Two experts have told the Guardian that the plan will not work. Winder, a co-chief investigator of a Prozac clinical trial with sex offenders, said she had significant concerns.

“A mandatory approach would require screening a very large prison population to identify the much smaller group for whom treatment might actually be appropriate,” she said. “It would have substantial clinical and resource implications.”

There were also concerns that if it was mandatory, there could be a breakdown of trust with offenders and it could be open to abuse, she said.

“Trying to impose and monitor daily medication among people who do not necessarily want to take it could be extremely inefficient. It could also introduce a range of consequences that we simply do not yet understand, including effects on trust, disclosure, engagement and the therapeutic relationship.”

She rejected characterising the drugs as a form of “chemical castration”. “People say that because some people like the idea of castrating people who commit sexual offences,” she said. “But these drugs are not permanent, unlike castration, and must be taken consistently to work.”

Burnham announced earlier this month that prisoners convicted of rape, grooming and serious child sexual offences would be excluded from the early release scheme that is due to begin in October. Other sex offenders serving sentences of less than four years will still be eligible to leave prison early.

There are comparatively low reoffending rates among sexual offenders compared with other cohorts. According to government data, 11.7% of sex offenders reoffended in 2023, compared with 53.9% of those with an index offence for theft.

Prison campaigners have urged caution before going ahead with a national programme. Critics have previously pointed out that long-term testosterone suppression can cause osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease. There is limited data because randomised controlled trials remain scarce.

Andrew Neilson, the director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “The history of prison-based treatment programmes in this area has proven troubled, which is both a reason for exploring alternatives but also a reason to exercise caution before expanding new approaches more widely. It’s also important that nobody is forced into these chemical interventions and that participation is truly voluntary.”

Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers’ union the POA, said: “Anything that potentially protects the public is welcome but I would be cautious about the rollout until we are in receipt of evidence that proves success.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “This government is determined to tackle the root causes of sex offending, which is why we’re working at pace to extend the existing pilot to a further two regions.”

Lando Norris surges past Russell and Antonelli to snatch Dutch GP pole

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 15:42:22 GMT

Norris outperforms Mercedes pair against the odds

George Russell wins the sprint race convincingly

What a title fight Formula One would have on its hands if McLaren could make the final steps with their car. This was demonstrated to dramatic effect on Saturday as Lando Norris hurled his ride around Zandvoort to claim pole position for the Dutch Grand Prix. It was a prize secured against the odds and his own expectations, hours after he had bemoaned being in no position to fulfil his hopes of mounting a successful title defence.

The McLaren car is immensely quick through the fast corners, perhaps the class of the field, but is haemorrhaging time through the slow stuff, the package not quite complete, or suboptimal as Ron Dennis would have had it. Yet Norris managed to eke out its very best across the circuit to see off the Mercedes of George Russell and Kimi Antonelli into second and third place. The season’s dominant car was subdued by Norris in qualifying for the second race in succession, after he took pole in Hungary.

Earlier in the day the defending world champion was disgruntled at best with his ride. Russell had won the sprint race with a controlled dominance from pole position, but Norris had gone from second to third, struggling for grip and pace, passed late on by Charles Leclerc. His assessment was blunt.

“We don’t have the pace in general, slow-speed corners we struggle so much compared to others. There is nothing we can do,” he said. “The upgrades have all worked and they allowed me to be P3 today, but we need more if we want to be fighting for a championship.”

A turnaround had not been expected, but with fresh tyres and low fuel the McLaren was a less recalcitrant beast and Norris delivered a mighty lap in the final runs to see off Russell and Antonelli by a tenth of a second.

“Our biggest losses were still the same places, the same corners, as it was this morning,” he said. “It’s just new tyres, low fuel. It just seems to mask quite a few of our issues and that was probably still the case today. I just drove well, I put a lot of things together.”

Which sets up an intriguing prospect for Sunday’s race. With tyre wear and fat with fuel he will have to fight hard to keep the two Mercedes behind him.

With Russell’s sprint victory and Antonelli only fourth, the Briton trails his teammate by 56 points, in third place in the championship. Lewis Hamilton is 53 points back in second and Norris 90 points in arrears.

Most notable is how much more comfortable Russell has looked in the car this weekend, after struggling with problems around its energy deployment that had left him frustrated and examining his driving style. Having said he intended to drive more instinctively here he came into the weekend confident, took pole and then victory in the sprint race. While he was beaten to pole in qualifying, Russell was quicker than his teammate.

Certainly he appeared to be enjoying himself once more. “I just feel way more relaxed. I don’t feel like I’ve got anything to lose. The pressure’s off,” he said. “I’m just going to go out and enjoy it. I don’t even really feel in a fight. It’s not mine to lose. It’s mine to gain. So that’s the mentality I’ve got, I feel it’s going to help me, I’m just enjoying driving.”

Norris went on to win from pole in Hungary and with Piastri taking the win here last year and Norris in 2024, McLaren may still make it three in a row, which would be a testament to their impressive work. Their car development has been ferocious and most importantly effective, including another swathe of developments brought here, fulfilling the expectations of the team principal, Andrea Stella, whose calm assurance at the helm has once more been a striking piece of management as the team adjusted to the new regulations.

All of which may yet shake down into a tense title fight and the teenager Antonelli was aware his rivals were watching closely to see how he handles it, a task which comes with the territory. “It was a very good wake-up call this weekend, that you can never lower your guard,” he said. “When you do that, I made a mistake yesterday and today I made a mistake in Q3.

“It’s not that I’m driving more tense or anything but I feel this weekend is a good wake-up call to just put things in the right place at the right time and deliver the result when it counts.”

It all sets the scene for a showdown beside the North Sea on Sunday.

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 15:41:27 GMT

Bruno Fernandes: ‘We gave too much of the ball to them’

Sergej Jakirovic happy Hull proved critics wrong

Michael Carrick says he will not overreact, but has called for improvement after Manchester United started the season with a 2-0 defeat at Hull. United lost their opening game for the fourth time in the past seven years as Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy took advantage of poor defending from set-pieces.

The United head coach presented a professional exterior despite United’s performance not reaching the desired standard as they were deservedly beaten by Hull, who finished sixth in the Championship last season.

“I’m talking to you quite calmly, but I’m not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day, so there’s a big difference,” he said. “I played [for United] for a long time. You don’t get to play here for a long time without just going day by day, the results, the ups and downs, but you just carry on as normal.

“It’s 100% not that, and trust me, it’s not that. It just doesn’t mean that we all have to shout and scream and come out and create some chaos just because of it. Inside we’re hurting and we need to get better. But the calmness doesn’t mean there’s no emotion in it, for sure.”

He added: “The result’s the result. We got beat, we’re hurt and it’s not a nice feeling. It doesn’t mean it’s going to change the whole direction of how we’re going as a team or as a football club.

“It’s one game and results can happen in football, we all understand that. It’s not nice when they do, but it does happen.”

United barely threatened throughout the 90 minutes. “Same mistakes as we did last season, every away game,” Bruno Fernandes said. “We gave too much of the ball to them, in the first 20 minutes the goalkeeper had more touches on the ball, too much time. We need to press a little bit more, be more aggressive, and set-plays – we need to work on it, to be more aggressive and try not to concede these types of goals.”

We need to be honest about the Hundred: it feels as real as Ted Lasso

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 13:03:31 GMT

The shirts, the songs, the supporters, the rivalries. Somebody created the whole thing and it’s all disconnected from county cricket’s culture and history

I went to Old Trafford expecting to watch a game of cricket. Instead, I left thinking about history, identity and whether you can manufacture belonging. Walking through the concourses, I found myself surrounded by the faces of Lancashire’s greats. Farokh Engineer. Sir Clive Lloyd. Players whose stories are woven into the fabric of the ground. The Sir Clive Lloyd Stand is a reminder that this place has accumulated meaning over generations.

And then, almost everywhere else, Manchester Super Giants.

At first, I was impressed. The ground seemed full of supporters in new shirts, waving flags and chanting MSG. I remember looking around and thinking they had done an extraordinary job. Somehow, in almost no time at all, they appeared to have persuaded thousands of people in Manchester to buy into a completely new cricket team. Then I discovered they were giving the shirts and flags away for free.

I played at Old Trafford many times. But in this form it felt like a completely different space, a different entity plonked down, unconnected to all that culture and history.

It reminded me of watching Ted Lasso. You switch on the television and see a packed football stadium, thousands of people in the same colours, chanting passionately for their team. For a moment you wonder who they are and how you have never heard of them. Then you remember that AFC Richmond doesn’t exist. The shirts, the songs, the supporters, the rivalries, somebody created the whole thing for the television programme. There was something of that feeling at Old Trafford.

Every boundary brought another booming chant over the speakers. MSG, MSG, I assumed. Except when I listened more closely, it wasn’t MSG at all. It was LSG, Lucknow Super Giants, the Indian franchise from which this new Manchester identity has emerged.

It was strangely disorientating. Here we all were in Manchester, wearing Manchester Super Giants shirts, waving Manchester Super Giants flags, apparently chanting for Manchester Super Giants, while the sound system was playing the chant of Lucknow Super Giants.

There was something almost gladiatorial about it. Loud, colourful and undeniably entertaining. But also slightly surreal. At moments I felt less like a supporter and more like a participant in an enormous live experiment. Here is your shirt. Here is your flag. Here is your chant. This is your team.

A major question that hasn’t really been answered is: what do the players think about this? I have spoken to one or two. There is a divide. Do they think this is a good thing? Naturally, they do if they’re playing. They get paid really well, it’s short and full of energy. For the women’s game, it has been a massive economic and visibility driver.

If they’re not playing, the opposite can be true. Some of them undoubtedly hate it. You’re not working. You’re not in that narrow spotlight. Your summer is just passing by.

On the other hand, the children around me at Old Trafford certainly weren’t worrying about authenticity or history. They were watching sixes disappear into the stands, waving their flags and joining in. The crowd was engaged and there was energy in the ground. Whatever I thought about how it had been created, people were enjoying themselves.

My other reaction was more personal. I have spent most of my life either playing or coaching cricket, and I sat there bemused by what I could add to what I was watching. It felt almost uncoachable.

That isn’t to say the players aren’t highly skilled or brilliantly coached. Clearly they are. But it felt separate from the cricket I recognise as a coaching proposition. I found myself wondering what I would tell a young player to take from it or what conversation we would have about it afterwards. Beyond the extraordinary execution, I wasn’t sure. Perhaps that is partly the point. The Hundred isn’t really asking me to coach it. It is asking the crowd to watch it.

This product is totally disconnected from red-ball cricket, technically and emotionally. It is a separate thing. We probably need to be honest about this rather than dancing around it.

Sign up to The Spin

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

There was, though, a connection between what was happening on the field and what was happening around it. Both felt invented. A new format of cricket, surrounded by a newly created team, with newly created rituals, colours and identities. None of that stopped it being fun. Judging by the children around me, it was great fun.

But it also felt detached from what came before. Underneath the barrage of MSG branding, you could still make out the old murals. Engineer. Lloyd. The names and faces of people who didn’t need a marketing campaign to make them part of the place. Their significance accumulated through performances, stories and generations of people watching them.

English cricket is now experiencing something fascinating. For years, the gravitational centre of the game sat here. Now, the money, influence and cultural confidence of franchise cricket increasingly flows in the opposite direction. An Indian franchise identity can arrive in Manchester and be laid directly across one of English cricket’s most historic grounds.

There is something almost like a reversal of cricket’s old journey around the world, although this time it isn’t colonialism, but commerce. Maybe Manchester Super Giants will develop its own stories. Maybe children wearing those free shirts will still be wearing them in 20 years and by then the thing that felt manufactured to me will feel completely authentic to them.

Perhaps the same is true of the cricket. What feels slightly alien and uncoachable to me may simply be cricket to the generation waving those flags. I can sit there surrounded by a game I have spent my life in and feel strangely separate from it, while a child sitting 10 seats away is completely absorbed.

For now, walking through Old Trafford was like seeing a new coat of paint applied over something much older. However bright the new paint is, you can still see the history underneath.

The Secret Cricket Coach is a former professional cricketer, now an elite-level coach.

Andy Burnham says he wants to bring men’s World Cup back to UK in 2042

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 12:13:28 GMT

PM tells regional mayors during informal discussions he is keen for tournament to return to British Isles

Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring the men’s World Cup to the UK in 2042, returning the tournament to Britain for the first time in almost eight decades.

During informal discussions at No 10 North in Manchester on Friday, the prime minister told regional mayors he was keen for the tournament to be played in the British Isles.

The World Cup took place in England in 1966, when the home side beat West Germany 4-2 in the final after extra time – the only time the country has either hosted or won the contest.

Burnham, a keen football fan who has a season ticket at Everton, said earlier this month that it was “insane” only one World Cup had been held anywhere in the UK.

It is understood an application to stage the competition could also involve other home nations, none of which have hosted any World Cup games.

In recent years, joint bids between countries for major football tournaments have become more common. Alongside the Republic of Ireland, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will host the men’s European championships in 2028.

Work has not yet begun on any official bid for the 2042 event but it is understood Downing Street would support the FA should it choose to pursue it.

Sources say Burnham has “broad aspirations” and “a general ambition” to bring more major footballing events to the UK.

England made a doomed bid to host the 2018 World Cup, which was awarded to Russia amid allegations of corruption.

In 2014, while serving in the shadow cabinet, Burnham said he was uncomfortable that the tournament was still allowed to take place in Russia after its annexation of Crimea.

Under Fifa regulations, no European country would be eligible to stage the World Cup until 2042.

In 2000, Fifa introduced rules that meant the tournament would be rotated around its six continental confederations. It led to South Africa hosting its first World Cup in 2010, but the strict system was scrapped in October 2007.

Countries are not allowed to bid to stage a World Cup if either of the previous two tournaments have taken place on the same continent.

The 2030 World Cup will be hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with some early matches taking place in South America to mark the tournament’s centenary. The first World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930.

Fifa has also confirmed that the 2034 tournament will take place in Saudi Arabia. The location of the 2038 World Cup has not yet been announced, but under the rules, it is likely to be played in North America or Oceania, which includes Australia and New Zealand.

Burnham is also understood to have spoken about the possibility of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the north of England in the 2040s at Friday’s meeting.

UK Sport was commissioned to assess whether a bid would be viable earlier this year under the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer.

It is understood that the government is considering the possibility of a “multi-city bid” in an attempt to spread any economic benefit between several northern cities.

A government spokesperson said: “The UK is committed to delivering world-class major sporting events with pride, with the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes Grands Départs 2027 and Uefa Euro 2028 secured, and active bids for the 2029 World Athletics Championships and 2035 Women’s World Cup. “As the prime minister has made clear, we will continue to pursue sporting events that bring communities together, drive regional growth and create jobs across the country.”

Auntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBC

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 12:00:04 GMT

Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms

The millions who subscribe to the content creator Simon Squibb’s social media channels are usually delivered tips and hacks on how to turn their dream business idea into reality. But they were recently presented with something completely different.

In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from the BBC and other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not.

Squibb is one of many major UK content creators outraged by a proposal included in a government paper earlier in the summer that would boost content from traditional broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 in the all-powerful algorithms of YouTube and TikTok.

The idea has been pushed collectively by public service broadcasters as a way of boosting trusted material and preserving distinctly British content.

Ministers want to help them survive in a world in which audiences are ditching traditional TV for digital platforms. They prefer a voluntary deal with digital platforms, but have pointed to using legislation if necessary.

Video-sharing platforms and streaming services accounted for 74% of all video time for audiences aged 16-24 in 2024-25, and 69% for 25-34s. YouTube is the most-watched service for children aged four to 15, accounting for 28% of their video viewing.

But the measure has slowly but surely been causing anger and disbelief among content creators, who see it as shifting the goalposts to allow bigger players to stay on top. If the broadcasters go up the algorithm, they reason content creators will be pushed down.

They have been holding private meetings, putting out emergency videos and urging viewers and fellow creators to speak out before the government’s consultation ends at the end of the month, featuring dramatic warnings about “the end of YouTube”.

Squibb and others have even raised comparisons with authoritarian state control. “Russia pushes its channels that it believes the people should watch,” he said.

“I just think it’s a very bad thing to push. Trust has to be earned. If the BBC is selected as one of the trusted sources, does that also mean that Dragons’ Den is going to get prominent coverage over my education and business content? You have to let the public decide.”

Ben Ebbrell, whose Sorted Food channel started as a small project among friends and now has 15 million viewers tuning in each month, said the idea would undermine 16 years of investment in building an audience, a period in which the TV world ignored the growing popularity of YouTube, he said.

“At first, the TV world almost looked down upon content creators, but it’s completely flipped now, where we feel like we’ve got the stardust.

“It was just quite a shock when they said almost that they didn’t want to start playing the game, they wanted to move goalposts – or possibly even running off the pitch with a ball and a bit of a sulk … it’s kind of embarrassing.”

Jade Beason, a creator with 310,000 YouTube subscribers who has worked with traditional broadcasters on their digital content, said they should concentrate instead on making content that works for digital platforms – something the BBC and others are trying to do.

“I don’t think it’s going to get them the results that they need and I think it’s going to disrupt creators in the process,” she said. “To me, it just feels like you’re pushing the queue, you’re jumping ahead.

“[Traditional broadcasters] don’t need more help for people to find them … people aren’t struggling to find TV news, they know where it is. They’re choosing not to watch it. That’s the challenge we should be focusing on.”

Grace Andrews, a content creator who helped set up the Diary of a CEO podcast, is among those coordinating the pushback against the idea and rounding up responses before the end of the month. YouTube has also been encouraging creators to respond.

“Now obviously [traditional broadcasters] are scrambling for eyeballs and instead of adapting to that world, they’re trying to legislate their way back into it,” she said. “Nobody who actually understands why people watch what they watch in 2026 was in the room when this document was created.

“I don’t want misinformation on my feeds either, but I don’t think this is the solution. Social media works because people are choosing what they see. That’s the entire mechanic. The second that becomes something enforced instead of something they picked, they don’t trust it any more.”

A spokesperson for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “We want to ensure that content from public service media providers such as the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and others is easily discoverable on video-sharing platforms, like YouTube, and we have urged the industry to come together and move quickly on voluntary solutions.

“We do not see this as a zero-sum game between traditional broadcasters, content creators and other video platforms. We want to create an environment where PSM [public service media] providers, high-quality news providers and content creators can all thrive.”

It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 12:00:03 GMT

A Democrat’s remarks have resulted in impassioned defenses of the Trump aide. The right has discovered misogyny

Jon Ossoff is quite the miracle worker. Perhaps the Democratic senator can’t turn water into wine, but he has managed to turn whining conservatives into impassioned feminists.

During a rally last Sunday, the Georgia senator delivered a takedown of Donald Trump, which included a reference to his aide Natalie Harp. “He doesn’t want to do the job,” Ossoff said of the president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Those three words – travel with Natalie – were deliberately loaded. Harp was in the spotlight at the time because of the decoy plane story. The 35-year-old was one of a handful of people Trump had taken onto a different plane via a catering truck when he was worried about a potential assassination attack targeting Air Force One. Intrigue as to the exact nature of the relationship between Harp and Trump was heightened by the fact that Melania Trump, the president’s third wife, hadn’t been seen in public for weeks at the time. (Funnily enough, she magically reappeared on Thursday, a few days after Ossoff’s comments, for a press conference where she lovingly held hands with Trump. Very cute.)

Ossoff’s remarks about “Natalie” might have been something of a cheap shot, but it’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist. Suddenly, everyone from Fox News to prominent conservatives are very worried about a professional woman not being taken seriously.

The former House speaker Newt Gingrich, for example, said on Twitter/X that Ossoff owes Harp an apology. “If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job.”

The conservative commentator Scott Jennings, who is rumoured to be a potential replacement for Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, was also appalled. “[Ossoff] unleashed a comment so vile against a young Republican woman working in politics that every woman in this country, no matter your ideology, ought to listen carefully and never forget it,” Jennings said on his podcast.

Meghan McCain also clutched her pearls at the coverage Ossoff’s comments sparked. “The egregious sexist attacks on Natalie Harp are absolutely insane – and they’re coming from prestigious journalists,” she wrote on X. “What is wrong with everyone?! Every president has close aides and sometimes they are females. Like what year is this?!”

It’s 2026, Meghan. And in the year 2026 I think the masses have generally understood that simply criticizing a woman is not in itself misogynistic. I’m not saying there hasn’t been any misogyny in the Harp coverage, but the main reason there has been so much attention on the story is because the White House has had a completely unhinged response to Ossoff’s comments and kept it in the news. More importantly, the reason so many people aren’t taking the Trump aide seriously isn’t because she’s a woman; it’s because she’s not a serious person.

And I’m being diplomatic with that choice of language. After all, we’re talking about someone whose nickname is “the human printer” because, while working on Trump’s re-election campaign, she reportedly ran around after him with a portable printer, handing him hard copies of flattering coverage. You could write that off as a canny career move from someone who understands flattery gets you everywhere with Trump, but that’s also one of the least weird things Harp has done. Per a CNN report, which has pictures of the incident, back in 2023, Harp jumped in the trunk of an SUV because she wanted to be close to Trump and there was no room in his motorcade. Once Trump won re-election and Harp joined him in the White House, she apparently worked for a year without security clearance. According to reporting by MS NOW, she declined to complete the clearance process for unknown reasons.

And then there are the “adoring letters” Harp sent Trump, first mentioned in the book Regime Change, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Two were later published in the Daily Beast. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote in one letter. Other memorable lines included “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work’”; she also called Trump her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”.

To state the obvious: these are deeply weird things to say to your boss. (It’s also weird that Harp shares Trump’s unconventional approach to capitalization.) I should note that Harp, who says she is a cancer survivor, seems to believe that Trump saved her life by signing legislation that gave her access to experimental bone cancer treatment when she was younger. While that might make her obsession with Trump more understandable, it does not make her general conduct any more professional. So spare me all the lectures from the right about sexism, please. If you’re worried about how women in politics are treated, you should probably focus your attention on the adjudicated sexual abuser who is president.

Trump can’t seem to stand it when a woman doesn’t fawn over him and has a history of attacking female journalists. The latest object of his ire is the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes, who asked the president about Ossoff’s comments regarding Natalie Harp. Trump called Holmes a “loud boisterous person” and instructed her to be “quiet”. Meanwhile, the White House’s social media account posted about Holmes multiple times. In one post they wrote: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”

New York mayor Zohran Mamdani hosted the city’s first Parents’ Night Out. The city provided free childcare for nearly 300 kids so parents could have a little time off. This is what “family values” and being pro-life actually look like: supporting parents, not forcing women to give birth.

‘Penchant for bling’: can Sports Direct’s Mike Ashley take a bigger slice of luxury retail?

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 12:00:03 GMT

Frasers billionaire bought Harvey Nichols and increased Hugo Boss stake despite tough times for high-end stores

What billionaire doesn’t love to splash the cash on a luxury item? Some may buy watches or yachts, but Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has been snapping up entire brands.

Harvey Nichols is the latest bauble to drop into his shopping basket after his company bought the Knightsbridge department store out of administration earlier this month. It sits beside a large slice of Hugo Boss, a chunk of Mulberry, a snippet of Burberry, the remains of Agent Provocateur and the entire Flannels and House of Fraser chains.

After a rough few years for the sellers of luxury goods – as the cost of living crisis has crunched the spare cash aspirational consumers might have had available for the occasional treat, and Asian and Middle Eastern shoppers have become less inclined to travel to Europe – Ashley’s buying spree might seem out of sync.

However, the string of acquisitions closely match the entrepreneur’s established modus operandi – picking up bargains during tough times and finding the value where he can.

Sports Direct, now part of Ashley’s Frasers Group, built its business by snapping up struggling independent sporting goods chains and bumped up its profits by getting the UK rights to ailing sportswear brands – from Head to Slazenger – and using them to decorate its own products.

Since first buying a stake in Flannels in 2012, then a menswear store in Knutsford, Cheshire, Ashley has been slowly building a luxury portfolio.

The strategy has had its ups and downs. Flannels has expanded to about 75 stores and now sells brands from Gucci to Stone Island to Maison Margiela. This week, Ashley celebrated lifting his stake in the German label Hugo Boss to 48%, just short of taking full control, despite opposition from the company’s board.

The Harvey Nichols deal is a classic tactic to gain access to intransigent brands, adding lustre to the portfolio that could make some designer marques previously shy of engaging with the king of discount trainers sit up.

Ashley is likely to take a pragmatic approach to the wider Harvey Nichols estate, having said he intends to convert at least some of the five UK outposts outside London to the Flannels brand.

However, labels pondering whether to continue supplying the department store chain might do well to consider the events at the luxury online fashion seller Matchesfashion. Frasers bought the business for £52m at the end of 2023, only to place it into administration months later, leaving millions of pounds owed to designer brands.

House of Fraser is another cautionary tale. On buying the House of Fraser chain of 60 department stores out of administration almost exactly eight years ago, he set a mission to become “the Harrods of the high street”. Today there are just five stores left trading under that name.

There are another 15 stores badged as just Frasers, some of which are converted department stores while others are somewhat smaller sites. The Frasers name is also being used on a Luton shopping mall in the group’s property portfolio, which contains a House of Fraser discount outlet.

Such a confusing brand story is unlikely to entice large international labels to engage. Even the Flannels chain, Frasers said in its latest annual results published in July, was “now near complete”, indicating it did not intend to add many more stores.

Sales at the group’s “premium lifestyle” division, which includes House of Fraser and Jack Wills, fell almost 7%, while profits fell by almost £10m to £147.6m. Frasers said this included a rise in sales at Flannels, but gave no figures, so it was unclear if that was driven by adding new stores.

Luxury fashion acquisitions by Frasers do not appear to have flourished. Jack Wills, once widely sported by partying public schoolers on their holidays in Cornwall, now has just five independent outlets, down from about 100 when Frasers bought it in 2019.

Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital, said that if one examined the group’s spending on upmarket brands then “from a financial perspective it has not been a roaring success.

“The premium end of Frasers has been a burden for the wider group. The mothership is Sports Direct and that’s what is funding the wider diversification strategy.”

He suggested the strategy was more driven by Ashley’s personal aspiration to be taken seriously by these big names. “He has developed a penchant for bling in his 60s,” Black said. Whether “buying assets at the bottom” will lead to a benefit if and when the market improves works out “only time will tell”, he added.

Luxury market experts are also sceptical. One told the Guardian he would not have chosen to buy Harvey Nichols as its brand had become degraded and customers had gone elsewhere.

He suggested the building’s freeholders – the Cadogan Estate – had long discussed a plan to turn Harvey Nichols into a hotel or apartments and this might be the ultimate future of much of the Knightsbridge site.

Another industry insider said that, while rivals Selfridges and Harrods had been revitalised, Harvey Nichols “just feels like its lost its way”.

The old hand suggested Ashley’s scattergun expansion may yet lead him astray, pointing to the failed retail empires of Sears and Arcadia, and Marks & Spencer’s ill-fated efforts to expand overseas with Brooks Brothers. He suggested that running luxury brands such as Hugo Boss and Harvey Nichols might be a “bit of an overreach. It’s very different to a volume play.”

He said it was clear Frasers had a weaker business than Next, where chief executive Simon Wolfson’s buying spree is strictly limited to strong brands with effective management teams that need help to succeed online using Next’s expertise and infrastructure.

“The world of retail is littered with big organisations with an existing business that liked to acquire other brands and it doesn’t manage to succeed or end well,” the insider said. However, he added of Ashley: “I wouldn’t bet against him.”

The businessman has a long history as a gambler, famously producing a wad of £50 notes from his pocket when taking journalists through security screening on a visit to the company’s Shirebrook warehouse in Derbyshire.

He is not averse to risk but most of his business deals are underpinned by the value of stock and or property, which can be traded to raise cash if other tactics fail. The future for Harvey Nichols and its new luxury brand stablemates might not be pretty, but Ashley is likely to make money however it turns out.

Frasers Group declined to comment.

‘Perfect for kids’: the best (and worst) supermarket ketchup, tested and rated

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

It’s a saviour at family mealtimes, but which bottle of red sauce does our reviewer relish the most? (Spoiler: it’s not Heinz)

The best supermarket mayonnaise

I was that kid who put ketchup on everything, from fries to french toast, and if my parents wanted me to eat vegetables, they’d have to cover them in the stuff (the sugar cravings of my youth have subsided, but I still love ketchup mixed into peas). So I was pleasantly surprised by this test group, because even the most economical sauces performed well.

Tomato content varied greatly (though not always in line with price), with the most tomato-heavy products containing almost twice as much fruit as the least. This information is presented in two ways: the first is the amount of raw tomato used before the sauce is cooked down into puree (more than 200g per 100g of finished product is high, less than 150g is low); the second is a straight percentage of tomato puree used, which is a more transparent measure (above 50% is high, while less than that I’d consider low, so check the label if you want more fruit in your sauce). Products made with fewer tomatoes are sometimes thickened with modified maize starch. I’ve also listed the total sugar content.

Ultimately, every product did “what it says on the tin”, and while not necessarily delicious straight from the spoon, all were great with chips. Some of the top-end sauces suit a more mature palate, with a richer, spiced flavour, but they still have that classic burst of umami-sweet-sour tang.

★★★★☆

A squeezy bottle of vivid red sauce with a sweet and complex aroma. Contains a high percentage of fruit – 242g per 100g (tomatoes, plus surplus pears/apples) – which adds sweetness and a fruity depth layered with spice. Contains the preservative potassium sorbate and 20% total sugars.

★★★☆☆

A squeezy bottle of thin and smooth puree, with a classic, inoffensive and unremarkable flavour profile (sweet-sour, tomato), making it perfect for kids. A simple, additive-free formula with 16.4% total sugars.

★★★☆☆

A squeezy bottle of thick, deep red sauce that’s sharp on the nose but with a tempting, savoury aroma. Sweet and easy on the palate, too, with a slightly higher total sugar content of 22% and a ratio of 167g tomatoes per 100g sauce. Contains modified maize starch.

★★★☆☆

A squeezy bottle with a clean tomato puree aroma, rich colour and that classic, sharp-yet-sweet umami flavour. Total sugars stand at 20.9%, plus, at 38%, a relatively low percentage of tomato puree. Certified organic.

★★★☆☆

A glass bottle of very thick, smooth ketchup with the comforting and uncomplicated aroma of cooked tomatoes. Lively on the tongue yet classic and simply flavoured, with a dominant sweet-and-sour tomato flavour. A high percentage (80%) of tomato, too, and 16% total sugars.

Thomasina Miers’ recipes for spiced lamb-stuffed aubergine with aleppo chilli butter, and berry ripple ice-cream

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 11:00:02 GMT

A meaty, Middle Eastern style stuffed vegetable feast finished off with an ice-cold berry dessert

There’s something delightfully retro about stuffed vegetables. They take me back to Delia Smith’s iconic Summer Collection cookbook, which blew my tiny mind when it came out in my early teens. Too sheltered to know about the e rage that had inspired Delia, I delved into my mother’s vegetable crisper with reverence, stuffing courgettes, tomatoes and aubergines with a zeal that had escaped me at school. How could the roasting, reducing and condensing of ingredients create such explosions of flavour? I was hooked. I have recently been returning to this technique with glee, a simple solution for turning seasonal vegetables into feasts.

Serve these richly seasoned aubergines with warm, herb-flecked bulgur, rice or flatbreads, and a parsley and onion salad.

Prep 15 minSalt 20 min Cook 1 hr 30 min Serves 4-6

5 medium aubergines Salt and black pepperOlive oil 400g lamb mince 2 small onions, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 green pepper, halved, stalk, pith and seeds removed and discarded, flesh cut into 1cm dice200g cherry tomatoes, chopped 2 tsp ground cumin 1 tsp ground cinnamon 3 tsp aleppo chilli 2 tbsp Turkish red pepper paste, or tomato paste400g tin finely chopped tomatoes1 bunch flat-leaf parsley, picked and chopped 50g unsalted butter 200g Greek yoghurt, to serve

Cut the aubergines in half lengthways, then slice a lattice of crisscrosses over the flesh of each cut side, being careful not to cut down through the skin. Lay the aubergines flesh side up on a baking dish, sprinkle generously with salt, and leave for 20 minutes. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.

Using kitchen paper, blot away any moisture from the aubergine flesh, then drizzle over a tablespoon or two of olive oil. Roast for 30 minutes, until browned and softened, then remove and leave to cool.

Meanwhile, make the filling. Put a large pan on a medium-high heat, then add a tablespoon of olive oil and the lamb. Season generously with salt and pepper and saute for seven to eight minutes, until the meat starts to catch and brown. Stir in the onions and garlic, turn down the heat down to medium and cook, stirring often, for 10-12 minutes, until the onions have softened.

Add the green pepper, cherry tomatoes, cumin, cinnamon and one teaspoon of aleppo chilli, and cook for another 10 minutes. Add the pepper paste and half the chopped tomatoes, and cook for a further 20 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning, then stir in half the chopped parsley.

Carefully spoon the filling over each aubergine half. Mix the remaining half-tin of chopped tomatoes with 200ml boiling water and season with salt and pepper. Pour the mixture around the aubergines in the tin, cover with foil and bake for 20 minutes. Remove the foil and bake for a further 10 minutes.

In the last 10 minutes of cooking, put the butter in a small saucepan over a medium-high heat. Once sizzling, cook for 30 seconds before adding a generous pinch of salt and the remaining two teaspoons of aleppo chilli. Pour the butter over the baked aubergines, sprinkle on the remaining parsley and serve with the yoghurt.

An easy, no-churn ice-cream to finish; the tahini adds a nutty, salty note against the backdrop of intense berry deliciousness.

Prep 5 min Cook 25 min Freeze 4 hr+ Serves 4-6

200g mixed berries (blackcurrants, redcurrants, raspberries, say), thoroughly washed2 tbsp runny honey 100ml tahini 2 tsp vanilla essence150ml condensed milk 200g greek yoghurt 400ml double cream

To serveYour favourite biscuits2 tsp toasted sesame seeds (optional)

Pop the berries in a saucepan with the honey and cook over a low heat for eight to 10 minutes, until they start to break down. Take off the heat and leave to cool.

Spoon the tahini into a small bowl and slowly whisk in the vanilla essence, followed by the condensed milk. Fold through half of the yoghurt, then fold in the rest.

In a second bowl, whisk the cream to soft peaks, being careful not to over-whisk. With a large spoon, fold in the yoghurt mix little by little, until well combined.

Spoon half the tahini cream into a freezable container, then pour over half of the berry sauce create a ripple effect with the blade of a knife. Repeat with the rest of the cream and sauce in a second layer, and ripple that, too. Freeze overnight, or for at least four hours, then serve with your favourite biscuits on the side and perhaps a sprinkle of sesame seeds.

Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 11:00:02 GMT

A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger

The abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it.

So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally when Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general.

The vote, in which Blanche was confirmed by a margin of one along party lines, was conducted in the wee hours of the morning on 8 August. Maybe that’s because the Republicans who confirmed him didn’t want anyone to see what they were doing. Blanche has, after all, been shockingly subservient to Donald Trump, and seems poised to complete the president’s long-brewing transformation of the country’s chief law enforcement agency into a vehicle for score settling, personal vendettas, distributing favors to the administration’s friends and suppressing dissent from its political enemies. But perhaps most incendiary is what Blanche has said, publicly and privately, about how he intends to use the justice department and its vast array of oversight powers, legal prerogatives, and investigatory purview to curtail abortion access nationwide – and to shut down the life-saving distribution of mifepristone, in particular.

In a call facilitated by the White House faith office just days before he was confirmed, Blanche reportedly told Christian conservative leaders that as attorney general, he would move more aggressively than his predecessor Pam Bondi to outlaw the mailing of mifepristone across state lines, and target the Democratic-controlled states that have protected abortion most effectively. Blanche, who was then the acting AG, told the religious group Intercessors for America that the justice department was working “so that the Dobbs decision becomes permanent in every single state.” “We don’t have complete victory yet,” Blanche said, “but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and, and, and it will be permanent.”

Exactly how Blanche intends to secure his victory over women’s freedom is unclear. But as AG, he has several paths at his disposal. His comments on the call prompted widespread speculation that Blanche could call for enforcement of the Comstock Act, a long-dormant law from 1873 that has been unenforced for years and has been partially repealed in the past. Anti-choice advocates say it could be used to legally ban the mailing of abortion pills, thus cutting off access for many women who live in states with bans. In 2022, the Biden justice department declared that medical providers could not be prosecuted under the Comstock Act for mailing abortion pills; as the attorney general, Blanche would have the power to reverse that decision. The Comstock Act’s application would be particularly significant, as it could be used to halt virtually all commercial traffic in abortion pills – not only mifepristone, but also misoprostol, the second drug, which has sometimes been used to induce abortion on its own. Such a move would reverse the miracle of the pills, pushing many desperate women towards methods that are less effective and can carry grave dangers.

Another path that Blanche could take to restrict abortion access would be to sue the states that seek to protect it. On the call, Blanche explained his reasoning: “If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that. They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.”

Here, Blanche appeared to be referencing shield laws, legislation passed in a number of Democratic-controlled states that prohibits state authorities from participating in other states’ abortion-related investigations and prosecutions. The laws mean that doctors operating out of states like New York or Washington can prescribe and ship abortion drugs to people living in places such as Texas or Arkansas, safe in the knowledge that their own state police will not come knocking at their door to serve another state’s warrant or extradition order. Blanche’s comments suggest that his Department of Justice might sue to have the shield laws declared illegal, thus significantly curtailing liberal states’ rights to choose their own law enforcement priorities and granting conservative states the power to enforce their own laws even beyond their borders.

Blanche also appeared to indicate that he would seek to restrict abortion access using other agencies’ powers. On his call with leaders of the Christian right, he said his department was “working hand in hand” with health agencies to make Dobbs permanent. The FDA, which expanded access to mifepristone in 2021 under the Biden administration and made the change permanent in 2023, has been under intense pressure from anti-choice allies in the Maga coalition to revise that guidance, making the drug ineligible for telehealth prescriptions and requiring patients to retrieve it from providers in person, a regulatory move that would also serve to cut off access in Republican controlled states. But the anti-abortion movement is pushing the FDA even further: it has succeeded in getting the agency to initiate a “review” of mifepristone’s safety (though the safety of the drug has been proven by nearly four decades of use worldwide and hundreds of studies), which is widely seen as a pathway for the FDA to create a pretext to remove mifepristone from the market. That’s not fast enough for some on the misogynist right: Louisiana has sued the FDA, asking it to forbid mifepristone from being prescribed via telehealth, in a case that is set to be heard by the ultraconservative fifth circuit next month. So far, the justice department has supported the drug’s online availability in court. Under Blanche, it could reverse that stance.

Trump has been gunshy about pursuing the agenda of his antiabortion allies since returning to office. He appears to have been spooked by the political reaction to Dobbs, which was credited for the Democrats’ better-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms, as well as with a slew of pro-choice victories in special elections in the years that immediately followed the decision. The anti-choice movement has even been angry with Trump for the slow pace of his anti-abortion agenda since his return to power in 2025. Which is not to say that the Trump administration has given the movement nothing: enforcement of the Face Act, a federal law meant to stop anti-choice protestors from physically blocking clinic entrances, has been all but abandoned since Trump returned to the White House; some who were prosecuted under the law have even been pardoned and remunerated by Trump, at taxpayer expense. But until now, Trump has faced a looming threat that seems to have slowed the pace of his anti-abortion policymaking: the 2026 midterms. Soon, that obstacle will be removed. The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights: more abortion restrictions can be expected in 2027.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

The faces behind the feeds: Gen Z’s private lives and public posts – in pictures

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 11:00:01 GMT

For the first digital natives, there are two places to express yourself: in the comfort of your own room and online. Photographer Niccolò Rastrelli set out to find out how the identities compare

Social media arrived just as I, a younger millennial, was on the brink of teenhood. My friends and I signed up for accounts on Facebook, Myspace and Twitter, as well as less remembered sites such as the now defunct Bebo. We didn’t know what we were doing; no one did. We posted indiscreet messages and photos on public feeds that we wouldn’t want any future employer – or really anyone, for that matter – to see. Then gradually we, and our parents and their parents, too, learned what it means to live with that world-changing phenomenon that we term social media. We started to find different ways to adapt, a process that is ongoing.

But what is the experience like for gen Z, the first generation of “digital natives”, for whom the language of the internet is a mother tongue? That is the question that led the Italian photographer Niccolò Rastrelli to embark on the project IRL (the online acronym, of course, for a phrase denoting our offline existences: in real life).

Rastrelli has long been interested in the way people construct their identities through self-presentation. “In the last few years, I’ve also worked a lot with younger people. I’m older and don’t have children, so I want to understand their point of view,” says the photographer, who was born in 1977, making him a member of generation X. Past works include a project exploring the rising popularity around the globe of the youth subculture of cosplay. Now he felt it was time to broaden his focus to a more ubiquitous experience: being on the “socials”.

“I wanted to portray the diversity in gen Z,” Rastrelli says. He recruited subjects across the full span of the generation, from 14-year-olds to adults in their late 20s. Most were in Italy, but he also visited the UK, Morocco and France. Each portrait has two paired components. On one side the subject is photographed in their bedroom, whether in their family home or in a flatshare or university halls. They are intentionally posed, nearly always making eye-contact with the camera. S ome clutch their phones, or sit by a computer. Often there is the familiar sight of a tangle of cords and plugs in an extension cable by the bed.

“I decided to shoot in the bedroom because when you’re young it’s such an important place. It’s really your first solo home,” Rastrelli explains. “Before social media, it was also the main place where you could build your identity.” Your room and the things inside it – posters, paintings, books, an electric guitar, a barbell, a massivestuffed unicorn – tell a story about what kind of person you are and want to be.

Nowadays, the same goes for social media. And so, alongside those portraits, Rastrelli asked each of his subjects to pick snapshots of their phone screens that represented their usual activity. Nearly everything is from Instagram, one of gen Z’s main apps of choice – and many of the images are from temporary “stories” rather than posts on the feed. There are selfies with silly filters, casual snaps of friends and food, black-and-white portraits taken with film cameras. It was important to Rastrelli that the youngsters “co-curated” the selection, just as they had arranged and posed in their bedrooms.

Rastrelli also gave his subjects a questionnaire about their relationship with social media. Many responses surprised him – for example, that they often maintain more than one account on a single platform. Lana, who is 16, has multiple Instagram profiles with varying levels of privacy. “Only on my most private account do I feel free to really be myself,” she told him. He was also struck by how many young people see social media less as a site of personal expression than as a work tool. The clearest example was 23-year-old web developer and social media manager Francesco, who doesn’t post on his own account. As Rastrelli observes, “It’s like when you meet chefs. They all say they don’t cook at home because they’re cooking all day in the restaurant.”

Recent years have seen growing debate about the potential dangers of social media for young people. In the UK, a ban for under-16s is set to be enforced from next spring. (In Italy there are no such plans.) But from his conversations with gen Z-ers, Rastrelli doesn’t think they seem any more affected than their elders: “Many of them use social media less than people from my generation.” The primary difference is the platforms they go to. For example, Facebook, now associated with boomers, barely came up. It’s made Rastrelli consider repeating the project but focusing on the older generation instead: “We are all involved with social media.”

A student from Pennsylvania, Stevie is now studying abroad in Rome. He says he has two Instagram accounts: a public one and a private one, and tends to shift in tone and identity depending on which he’s using. He dreams of becoming a media personality.

Lana’s first smartphone – obtained aged 11 after longnegotiations with her parents – opened up a new world, from group chats to shared photos. Social media is integral to her daily life: TikTok is more of a pastime while Instagram is like a diary. Her bedroom is the place she feels most authentic, she says. She reads a lot, from YA novels to heavier authors like Dostoevsky and Freud, who help her better understand herself and the world around her.

Sofia attends an art school where she studies animation, a passion she discovered thanks to a digital creator who makes content about the history of cartoons. Her online life is limited: her parents have blocked Instagram and TikTok, so she uses WhatsApp to share drawings, homework and memes with friends.

Born in Italy to a Ghanaian family, Roberto has lived in London for the past eight years and currently works as a personal trainer and a bartender. He didn’t get his first smart-phone until around 15 or 16 – before that he used a basic phone so his parents could keep track of him. He is cautious about what he shares and views: mainly fashion and fitness content.

Mark, who was born in Nigeria and raised in Italy, paid for his first smartphone himself aged 12, by doing odd jobs and reselling customised clothes. He used to alter his features in photos, removing elements like his nose to escape identity labels. Now, as a freelance creative, he mainly uses Instagram as a tool for research, and rarely posts.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

Melina, who studied 3D animation, relies on Instagram for tutorials and discovering other artists. She also follows friends and humorous accounts. She shares infrequently, mostly drawings rather than photographs of herself, rarely edited beyond an occasional filter. She keeps a second account with no other followers, where she stores images to remember moments of her life.

What excited Anna most when she got her first phone, aged 11, was the ability to photograph and film the world around her. Now her dream is to work in film, and she says social media will be a useful way to share work and find opportunities. In the meantime, she uses Instagram mostly as a source of creative inspiration. When she posts, she likes to avoid putting herself at the centre of the image.

Andrea maintains two separate Instagram accounts, a personal one and a professional one for his work – as well as appearing in a local theatre troupe he performs solo as a drag artist. He says his approach is consistent across both his accounts: showing himself without filters , whether beautiful or deliberately grotesque, retouching images in Photoshop only to make a scene more “editorial”.

Ali’s first proper smartphone, after years spent using broken old ones, changed everything, allowing him to take and share photos for the first time. These days he works in social media marketing, helping companies and projects grow and gain visibility. He says that he sees his bedroom as a place to rest and think, while online is where he can express his personality and take inspiration from others.

Silvia says she feels like herself both offline and online, in different ways. At home she is more quiet; on social media, more extrovert. She says her family hasn’t always approved of her lack of filter on the internet, but she continues regardless. Music is central to her life – she’s part of a techno collective and performs as a DJ.

To see more images from Niccolò Rastrelli’s project, go to instituteartist. com.

Chinese robot runs 100m sprint quicker than Usain Bolt’s world record

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 10:25:01 GMT

Lightning the humanoid ⁠robot clocks 9.32sec in Beijing

Quicker than ​9.58sec men’s world record set 17 years ago

A ⁠robot named Lightning ⁠has run ​the 100m in 9.32 seconds, ⁠beating the human world ⁠record, China’s ​state broadcaster ‌has reported.

The humanoid, developed by the Chinese smartphone manufacturer Honor, ‌reached a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second during ‌a test event for ​the second World Humanoid Robot Games, which ⁠began on Saturday. The ​performance surpassed ​the ​9.58sec men’s ​100m world record ​set ​by Usain Bolt 17 years ago at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin.

China has been promoting humanoid robots as an emerging industry, with policymakers and companies ‌betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their deployment in manufacturing, logistics ​and consumer applications.

Lightning also won the Beijing half marathon in April in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the men’s world record. The robot stood 169cm tall and ​had ​95cm-long legs at ​the half marathon. Researchers have since lengthened ​its legs ‌by 10​cm for these Games.

More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the five-day games, now in its second year, a spectacle intended to demonstrate China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and football.

The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week as Beijing held the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. China makes the majority of the world’s humanoid robots.

Last month, the US Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations.

At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organisers and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation on to the field in a massive display of synchronised coordination.

In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games . It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid.

Experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research – at least for now – and it will take time to achieve mass real-world deployment. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities.

Humanoid robots are “evolving rapidly”, said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. “At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.”

Yang Shangzheng, another spectator, said: “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing.” Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer”.

This year’s robot games – which the organisers say has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the US – also includes other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.

Four blokes and a zebra crossing: the banality and beauty of the Beatles’ Abbey Road cover

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 09:00:04 GMT

Much-copied and parodied picture captures dynamic between the individuals and the band with eerie perfection

It’s not really the four blokes on the zebra crossing who make the cover of the Beatles’ Abbey Road memorable, but the street behind them. Vanishing towards a perfect blue sky, with summer trees veiling in bright green what might otherwise be dour brick houses, it could be a hyperreal vista painted by David Hockney. The black and white stripes of the crossing and the white line down the middle of the receding north London road are fresh and crisp, enhancing the clarity of this psychedelic daydream.

Of course the four blokes do play a part. The Beatles were so transcendently famous by the time Iain Macmillan took this picture on 8 August 1969 that seeing them do something as ordinary as cross the road becomes a magical mystery.

All the tourists who continue to recreate this photograph, the acts – from the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Kanye West to Franciscan friars and Booker T and the MGs – who have parodied it, as well as Sam Mendes, who this week recreated it for his four Beatles biopics, are hypnotised by its enigmatic marriage of banality and charisma. Just four people on a zebra crossing, but they’re gods!

The Beatles played on the same impossible everydayness months before this picture was taken when they performed live on the roof of Apple Corps in London’s Savile Row in January 1969. These were not just among the group’s last appearances together; they were manifestations against London backdrops of four individuals who had become archetypes.

What Abbey Road freeze-frames with eerie perfection is the dynamic between four individuals and one unit that made the Beatles so appealing: the character of each Beatle coming together, or so fans still wanted to believe, in perfect step, as this photograph catches them.

John Lennon leads, yet seems absent and absorbed: he is the only one whose face you can’t fully see and if he is the pacesetter, he might also be trying to get away. There I go. There’s a self-consciously symbolic quality to this picture that invites you to insert whatever allegory you please. I can picture Lennon walking away because that’s what he told the group he was going to do that September.

But at the time, notoriously, it was Paul McCartney’s bare feet that fed bizarre speculations he was dead. According to this conspiracy theory, the black-clad Ringo Starr is the undertaker and George Harrison the gravedigger.

It’s not such a bad interpretation and answers the picture’s demand to be decoded: surely it must be saying something! But the “Paul is dead” theory was doubly daft since McCartney was the picture’s creative author along with Macmillan.

This was not a photograph taken by chance. It is a piece of conceptual art – something the Beatles were very familiar with, what with Lennon marrying one of the world’s most radical artists, Yoko Ono, that year. After an idea of being photographed in Nepal was rejected, it was McCartney who suggested they just do it in Abbey Road, outside the music studios in north London’s St John’s Wood. His sketches planned out the picture, with the four of them as stick figures on the zebra crossing and a view from above of the tree-lined street. On the day, they got a police officer to stop traffic, and Macmillan stood on a stepladder to get this perspective.

Sign up to Sleeve Notes

Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week

after newsletter promotion

It’s not an accident; it’s art. McCartney started collecting paintings by René Magritte in 1966 and this picture’s combination of a haunting, almost too real perspective and a confounding yet deadpan foreground scene is highly evocative of the Belgian surrealist. These are not the Beatles. This is not Abbey Road.

It is definitely London, though. In these days of national self-loathing the wonder of the Abbey Road cover has to be its celebration of a very British moment. Zebra crossings are British: you know this is London, not New York.

The Beatles are walking into their separate futures, but here McCartney, the most passionate believer in the band, freezes them for ever outside the studios where they’ve worked. He doesn’t want to go anywhere – he’s taken off his shoes.
