Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 09:00:03 GMT

Britons will be able to buy ‘balcony’ systems they can install themselves from 27 August thanks to rule change

Despite this summer bringing hours of sunshine, many Britons have been unable to cash in on free electricity generated by the sun. Rooftop solar panels are usually out of the question if you live in a flat or rent your home, and the cost has made them prohibitive to many more households.

However, this could be about to change because next week the first wave of low-cost “plug-in” solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain.

Also known as “plug‑and‑play” or “balcony” solar, the clue to what makes them different is in the name: you can fix them to a balcony or garden wall, then plug them in like a toaster.

The mini solar systems are a familiar sight on balconies in Spain and in Germany, where they are known as a Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant), but until a recent change in the law, they were not permitted in Britain.

Matt Parry from the Renewable Energy Association, a trade body for renewable energy, says the kits are a gamechanger. “It democratises solar and gives everyone the chance to get it,” he says.

Unlike traditional rooftop solar panels, which require a professional to install, balcony solar kits – which commonly include one or two panels – can be plugged in to a three-prong wall socket.

You can fix them on a balcony railing, shed roof or garden wall – anywhere with good sun exposure and safe access.

When sunlight hits the solar panels, they generate a direct current. The microinverter then converts this to an alternating current, which flows into your home’s electrical system, reducing the amount you draw from the grid.

Previously, rules around the installation of solar were what was holding people back. But last year the government announced it would make it possible for plug-in solar to be used in this country.

To make this a reality, it has updated wiring regulations to allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels capable of generating up to 800 watts of power into the mains without the need for an electrician. (The rules are different in Northern Ireland.)

Big names including B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes and Amazon are lining up to sell plug-in solar.

Given the size (and weight) of these devices, it is expected that many will be bought online.

Although you may have already come across plug-in solar panels for sale, industry experts suggest waiting until the regulations take effect on 27 August before making a purchase.

Electrical Safety First, the consumer safety charity, is urging shoppers to stick to reputable high street retailers and their websites to ensure the device complies with the rules.

Luke Osborne, the charity’s technical director, advises people to “avoid buying these devices from third-party sellers on online marketplaces. These platforms are now not legally responsible for the safety of goods sold via their sites, exposing people to substandard versions that may put you and your home at risk.”

Andrew Moore, the founder of the British solar panel brand UKSOL, says: “We are working towards making the initial products available from 27 August.”

His company will initially sell 460W and 890W kits, starting at £599 and £999 respectively, and it plans to launch another four models in late September, with prices starting from £499.

Sizewise, plug-in solar setups are usually smaller than rooftop options, but sizes vary. The UKSOL 460W single panel kit measures 1,762mm x 1,134mm x 30mm and weighs 25.5kg. The 890W kit comprises two panels.

The official guidance suggests that it will take about an hour to set up your system. It estimates 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels, and about 15% will need minor electrical works. UKSOL suggests it takes two people to handle and position the panels, as each one weighs 25kg.

Osborne says plug-in solar systems should not be connected via extension leads, cable reels, multiway adaptors, travel adaptors or plug-in RCD adaptors. “These accessories can overheat, become overloaded and create additional safety risks,” he says.

There is also some other housekeeping. The owner has to tell their distribution network operator that they are using them (there should be a form in the box). You can find out who it is by inputting your postcode on the Energy Networks Association website. You will also be able to consult the ENA’s Connect Direct site for a list of approved devices, which is a good place to start before you buy.

Plug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system, which means they will not provide enough energy to power a home on their own – but they could cut your bill.

One drawback is that you need to be home to use the power generated because without a battery it is not being stored for later, so flows back to the grid.

However, the adoption of balcony solar could, in time, pave the way for plug-in batteries in British homes, too. If paired with a plug-in solar system, households could store their own renewable electricity during the day and use it to run their appliances in the evenings. The government is reportedly considering plans to bulk-buy the devices and distribute them to low-income homes.

A basic plug-in solar system costs about £400. Parry says it will “give you back, at worst, £40 a year, and at the best about £110. If it’s the worst-case scenario, it’s going to pay for itself in 10 years, but at the best-case scenario, it’s four.

“If you’ve just got 800W, it’s only at its very peak that it will give you that.”

He adds: “The slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an end. It’s going to be more use in May next year.”

Moore says that the level of saving is affected by a number of things, including the system size, location, orientation and actually being home to use the power.

He expects the 460W system his company will be selling to save a typical household about £80-£120 a year, “while the 890W system could save more”.

He adds: “The greatest savings are achieved when households use appliances during daylight hours, as this increases the proportion of generated electricity used within the home.”

You can buy a more expensive 2,000W kit (the inverter will only allow 800W through) to maximise your power-generating capacity, but these are more expensive.

Although there is no obligation to do this, before buying a kit, some experts think you should get your home electrics checked by a professional. That is because this is the first time that British residential wiring circuits will take power in via a three-point socket rather than simply being used to distribute electricity.

Electrical Safety First is concerned about the impact on residual current devices, or RCDs, which sit in a household electricity box and cut off the power if someone drills through a wire or runs their lawnmower over a power cord. Electricians are concerned they may burn out when plug-in solar panels start adding electricity to the circuit.

A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson says: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to buy this summer, and stringent verification and registration checks are already in place. They are a transformative technology that can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills.”

Plug-in solar should make it easier for tenants to take advantage of renewable energy, as any kit they buy can be moved from place to place.

But if you are renting, you should ask permission from your landlord before you invest in any panels.

The rules on what you can do with regard to fixing brackets to hold them, for example, may vary depending on what your tenancy agreement says.

There’s “no reason” why your landlord should be against the idea, Parry says. “He or she can look at the information and know it’s super, super safe.”

Meera Chindooroy, the deputy director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at the National Residential Landlords Association, says that while the organisation supports the “principle of tenants benefiting from plug-in solar panels … landlords would first need to be satisfied that the panels meet all required safety standards”.

She adds: “It would not be right for landlords to be held responsible for the safety of equipment they were not asked about in the first place.”

Stand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumph

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 09:00:01 GMT

The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate

Coming-of-age metaphors don’t get any blunter than a group of preteen boys following a set of railroad tracks to a classmate’s dead body, a sobering testament to the fragility of life and a sign that their own futures are not guaranteed. The Stephen King novella that would become Rob Reiner’s Stand By Me is simply called The Body, and there’s no doubt that commercial considerations factored into naming the film after the song that blankets the soundtrack. Yet the enduring magic of Reiner’s film lies in the tension between this bleak journey and the nostalgia and warmth that keeps complicating our feelings about it. Between those two poles is a bittersweet tone that perfectly suits the material, the rare example of an adaptation that benefits from softened edges.

Though Reiner kicked off his career on a legendary heater that opened with This is Spinal Tap and would go on to include The Princess Bride, When Harry Met Sally … and A Few Good Men, Stand By Me was just his third feature and an early showcase of his versatility. His deft comic touch is not only essential in maintaining tonal balance, but important in suggesting what these four wayward boys mean to each other. Between the loose talk about Annette Funicello’s expanding bust on The Mickey Mouse Club and a Wurlitzer soundtrack of novelty singles like Lollipop and Yakety Yak, it can be easy to forget the anger, pain and dread that’s always simmering close to the surface. They laugh to keep from crying and occasionally don’t succeed.

Though set a few years earlier than American Graffiti, Stand By Me feels like a natural companion to it, another radio-friendly nostalgia piece about a transitional moment for male friends in small-town America. Both films are death-haunted but the difference is that the characters in American Graffiti, who are reaching young adulthood at the cusp of the Vietnam war, don’t know what the future holds and writer-director George Lucas saves that bummer news for the epilogue. The boys in Reiner’s film know what lies at the end of a 20- to 30-mile hike down the tracks and their attraction to the novelty and notoriety of seeing a dead peer turns morbid. Their steps grow heavier by the hour.

The more direct tie-in to American Graffiti is Richard Dreyfuss as Gordie LaChance, who narrates his memories as a novelist and father who’s gotten the perspective he and his buddies lacked as 12-year-olds. Flashing back to Labor Day weekend in 1959, the film casts Wil Wheaton as young Gordie, whose intellect and storytelling wizardry already puts some distance between him and his three troublemaking friends, who are bound for trade school at best. There’s not much to do in the Oregon backwater of Castle Rock, so when Gordie’s pal Vern (Jerry O’Connell) overhears his older brother talking about where they found the body of missing boy, the group’s curiosity is piqued. The two other no-goodniks in the gang, Chris (River Phoenix) and Teddy (Corey Feldman), come from broken homes, so they’re all too happy to lie to their parents and join the hunt. They figure they’ll be stars on the local news.

Even when he’s writing horror novels around this period, like the first half of It or 11/22/63, King’s affection for the late ‘50s and early ‘60s of his own adolescence is boundless and those fond memories flow through Stand By Me. (Between this and his 1990 adaptation of Misery, which plays off an author’s relationship with his fans, Reiner would become King’s unofficial screen biographer.) Small details like the boys singing the theme song to the TV western Have Gun – Will Travel or musing about cherry-flavored Pez or “what Goofy is” fill out the milieu before the fun pops like bubblegum. As Dreyfuss describes it, a jovial night around the campfire featured “the kind of talk that seemed important until you discover girls”.

Reiner stages some fun scrapes along the way, like a confrontation with a notably meek junkyard dog and a mad dash across a bridge as a train unexpectedly bears down on them. His work with his exceptionally talented young cast, too, establishes a relaxed camaraderie that pays huge emotional dividends later, when they’re closer to the end of the line. Much has been made about how Feldman’s angst about his troubles offscreen feeds into his startling reserves of anger as Teddy, a boy whose father once held his face to the stove. Wheaton, too, has affecting moments as the lesser son of parents who grieve his late older brother (played in flashbacks by John Cusack) and make him feel like the wrong kid died.

Yet Stand By Me is another reminder of how generationally special Phoenix was as an actor, here in just his second feature after appearing with young Ethan Hawke in Explorers a year earlier. His Chris is a tough kid who seems to fit the mould of a sadistic greaser like the one played here by Kiefer Sutherland, but Phoenix plays him with astounding sensitivity, especially when Gordie needs a lift. Chris, Gordie and their buddies are expected to mask their vulnerabilities, and one of the film’s most effective gambits is how it contrasts these boys with Sutherland’s gang, who are inevitably cowed by his leadership. Phoenix’s Chris charts a more empathetic course.

There are times when Reiner tilts too far into sentimentality, especially when Dreyfuss’ narration reaches for emotions the film might better grasp without a personal story seeming like grist for a novelist’s mill. Yet Stand By Me does well to preserve the R-rated saltiness of King’s world – it’s always more bracingly profane than you remember – and that helps it land more authentically than popular TV imitators like The Wonder Years and Stranger Things. These innocent boys strike out looking for a taste of adulthood and the film captures the feeling in all its pungency.

Stand By Me is available on HBO Max in the US, Now TV in the UK and Tubi in Australia

I’m known as The Black Farmer because there are so few of us in the UK. It’s one of the ways farming must change

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 08:00:57 GMT

Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit

Who’d be a farmer? Clarkson’s Farm on Amazon is great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.

I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.

Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who responded self-described as white.

I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.

Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.

There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.

How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner, with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-old Kaleb Cooper on Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.

The supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose. Farming could do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.

I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.

Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.

Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones is a businessman and founder of The Black Farmer food company

Battery fires at recycling centres are costing UK £1bn a year, figures show

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 06:00:57 GMT

Experts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those in vapes, are putting lives at risk

Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries such as those found in vapes are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to new figures.

Experts say the sheer volume of battery fires now occurring at waste facilities has reached a crisis that is putting lives at risk, costing £1bn a year and frustrating fire chiefs.

In figures shared with the Guardian, the Environment Services Association (ESA), the trade body for waste management companies, said its members had reported 1,518 fires in the year to March 2026. At least 541 of these fires were directly attributed to lithium ion batteries, the survey found. There were a further 216 battery fires in bin lorries.

The ESA said the reported number of battery-related fires underestimated the scale of the problem, because in most incidents it was impossible to determine the cause of the blaze. A spokesperson said: “We know 40% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries, but we think the actual number is more like 70%.”

It estimates that annual cost of these fires has increased from £150m in 2021 to £1bn today. The cause of this week’s blaze at a recycling centre in Deptford, south-east London, has yet to be determined. It was the latest in a series of fires at recycling centre and bin lorries, many of which have been blamed on batteries, particularly those in vapes. They include: Ilford in east London; Caerwent in Monmouthshire; Widnes in Cheshire; Glasgow; Costessey near Norwich, and Dereham in Norfolk.

Fire chiefs have been alarmed by the rise in this type of blaze and the resources needed to put them out.

After the Ilford fire, which took 25 firefighters to control, a spokesperson for London fire brigade said: “We’ve seen a growing number of fires at waste disposal sites that are believed to have been caused by a lithium battery.”

“Fires that we attend at sites like recycling centres and scrap yards can be very time consuming for our firefighters and often require a high level of resources to put the fire out. We’ve also seen the detrimental environmental and societal impact these fires can have on local communities.”

Dr Francesco Restuccia, a fire expert at King’s College London, said: “There has been exponential increase in fires at recycling centres, mainly because we are using and discarding lithium batteries in everyday objects like smartphones, children’s toys, toothbrushes and vapes. If they are not disposed off properly there’s a high chance of ignition.”

Explaining what happens when a lithium battery gets crushed, Restuccia said: “If the separator is pierced – which happens a lot at recycling centres – it creates a lot of internal short circuits in the battery, causing the temperature to increase until it reaches ignition point.”

The ESA commissioned the Health and Safety Executive to test what happens when a vape battery is punctured while next to paper and card. Video of the experiment, shared with the Guardian, showed the vape igniting like a sparkler and setting alight the paper and card. Temperatures of the vape reached more 750C in the experiment and became hot enough to ignite paper for two minutes.

The ESA hopes the experiment will demonstrate the need to safely dispose vapes to policymakers and the public. The waste management company Biffa said it has recovered 500,000 vapes at its facilities this summer alone.

The ESA is calling for a £5 deposit scheme on the sale of all vapes to ensure that vape users have an incentive to return used devices to retailers for safe disposal.

Patrick Brighty, the head of recycling policy at the ESA, said: “Battery fires are reaching epidemic proportions across Britain’s recycling and waste industry, placing workers at risk and threatening vital infrastructure upon which we all rely every day.

“It only takes a single battery hidden in household rubbish or recycling to cause a huge fire and decimate a facility. The total cost of battery fires now exceeds £1bn a year, with huge knock-on implications for insurance costs.

“Vapes are among the biggest culprits because they’re cheap, abundant and typically have a short use-life. ESA and others across our industry are calling on the government to implement a mandatory deposit scheme for vapes to incentivise users to return them safely back to the point of purchase so they can be recycled properly and away from other waste.”

‘It exists only for pleasure’: does ice-cream have a future in the age of wellness fads and weight-loss drugs?

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 05:00:57 GMT

As fitness-conscious consumers turn away from processed foods, the industry is scrambling for new ideas, including nutrient-rich lollies and protein-packed tubs. Will they take the fun out of this summer treat?

Last month, I stood in the biggest ice-cream factory in Britain and watched a 5-metre Viennetta mint-flavoured ice-cream cake get made. The factory – which is owned by the Magnum Ice Cream Company and produces nine different brands of ice-cream – is based in an enormous building in Gloucester, where the air is thick with the scent of custard. I walked past the Twister and Solero sections on my way in, through clouds of tangy fruit, before arriving at the Viennetta assembly line, where everything smelled minty fresh. A Viennetta is built on a conveyor belt by a fully automated system, and watching it take shape was oddly hypnotic. Every few inches a nozzle attached to the belt squirted out a frilly layer of mint ice-cream, then another nozzle smoothed a flat layer of vanilla on top of that, then came a squirt of chocolate sauce, and it was back to frilly mint again. On and on it went, layer upon layer, popping out finished Viennettas at the end of the line at a rate of 200 cakes every 60 seconds.

A slop bucket full of Viennetta overrun stood at the side of the conveyor belt and I fought a strong urge to squelch my fingers into it. Later, the factory operations manager allowed me to push my whole hand into the slop bucket up to the wrist and then lick my hand at a sink, before washing it and resuming the tour.

I had travelled to the factory at a tricky moment for ice-cream. Magnum – which owns Viennetta, Ben & Jerry’s, Solero and Twister, along with most of the other lollies you can buy from an ice-cream van – reported falling sales in the last quarter of 2025. The global ice-cream industry is worth £85bn and Magnum controls 20% of it, so the stakes are high. In June, Magnum was the most shorted large cap stock in Europe, with investors betting against the company because of doubts about how ice-cream will survive in the age of Ozempic. Magnum’s sales rose in the most recent quarter, driven by record temperatures, but the stock price remains volatile because investors fear people will not be eating much ice-cream in the future, says markets analyst David Hayes from Jefferies investment bank. In the US – where one in eight people are now taking GLP-1s – ice-cream sales have fallen in the past year, according to consumer research firm NielsenIQ. The British ice-cream industry looks set to suffer the same fate: 1.6 million UK adults used weight loss drugs between 2024 and 2025, and that number is predicted to jump after this month’s release of the UK’s second, and much cheaper, weight-loss pill.

Such drugs are not the only problem ice-cream makers have to contend with. In recent years, as wellness culture has gained momentum, a growing obsession with protein and fibre has changed the way we eat. Protein is touted as a magical cure for all manner of ills: perimenopause, anxiety, the urge to have a nap at 3pm. The price of whey – a yellowish, dusty, protein-rich powder made from curdled milk – is at an all-time global high and the US is in the grip of a shortage of cottage cheese, which is higher in protein and lower in fat than normal cheese. Demand has become so frenzied that people trade conspiracy theories about its scarcity online.

GLP-1 users eat less, but they are advised to eat more protein so they don’t lose muscle mass – which creates a problem for the ice-cream industry. (A Twister contains just half a gram of protein.) Protein mania has become so widespread, it affects even those who would never take a weight-loss drug. In the UK, one in 40 people now have gout, with some dietitians blaming the uptick on men overconsuming protein in an attempt to bulk up. On TikTok, fitness influencers chug egg whites and toy with the idea of eating dog food for its enviable protein-to-calorie ratio. In response, Magnum has developed a new range of protein- and vitamin-enriched lollies and tubs which they plan to release in the UK soon. As appetites change, can the ice-cream industry find new ways to coax us into buying treats?

A few days before my trip to the factory, I travelled to Magnum’s innovation hub in Colworth, Bedfordshire, to sample the company’s new, nutrient-rich ice-creams. The hub is a sleek, wide-windowed sequence of labs where scientists and chefs experiment with new recipes. I was led into a spotless demo kitchen and seated at a conference table opposite a colour-coded model of the human brain (ice-cream “lights up” different parts of it). A chef appeared, bearing a platter with what looked like a lipstick but was actually a tiny red ice lolly, hiding inside a lipstick container.

After I had finished this lolly – which I ate so greedily, I didn’t really taste it – Zbigniew Lewicki, Magnum’s chief research, design and innovation officer, spoke to me about some of the UK’s first factory-made ice-creams. Wall’s, one of the oldest brands under the Magnum umbrella, started selling ice-cream from a factory in Acton, London, in 1922. Wall’s was originally a butcher’s, and the company pivoted to ice-cream as a kind of summer-proof sausage equivalent, because meat wasn’t selling well in the heat. Ice-cream street traders have existed in the UK since the 1850s, when they used horse-drawn carts. But with the advent of mechanical refrigeration in the early 20th century, it became possible to mass-produce ice-cream. As British people began to buy freezers in the late 70s, it was rolled out to supermarkets. The 80s – which food writer Ruby Tandoh has called the “golden age” of British ice-cream – saw the invention of Twister, Viennetta, Calippo and Feast.

The job of the innovation hub is to come up with new ice-creams that will become just as iconic as the 80s classics. Lewicki said one of the major changes he’s seeing is a new emphasis on “health and diet shifts compounded by transparency”. They are now dealing with a new kind of consumer who is deeply concerned with finding out precisely what is in their ice-cream. “A lot of people, particularly the younger generation, read labels at the moment,” he said. Lewicki is a smiley, charismatic man, and he insisted the industry has changed “mostly in a good way” – but there was a slight note of anxiety in his voice as he spoke of this new generation of label readers.

Another platter appeared by my elbow and I was handed a new ice-cream Magnum is calling Hydro:Ice. Label readers scouring the back of this ice-cream packet will find a long list of vitamins and minerals: C, magnesium and so much B2, it glows in the dark. A chef invited me to place my hand holding the ice-cream inside a UV-illuminated box and I watched my lolly light up and glow neon green. Michelle Neville, a behavioural scientist employed by Magnum to get inside the heads of ice-cream eaters, talked me through the profile of the Hydro:Ice customer. “They’re very big on their appearance,” she said. “Hair is on point, nails are on point, brows on point.” Hydro:Ice launched in Ibiza last summer, with a campaign taglined “Ravers Are Athletes Too”. As I ate mine, Neville showed me a promotional video of a thin woman on a treadmill, licking an ice lolly.

Next I was invited to sample tiny ice-creams called Bonbons – minuscule versions of Soleros and Magnums that have been specially designed for consumers who want to eat a “controlled bite”. These tiny Magnums – which look a bit like large sheep droppings – were developed before Ozempic gained popularity, and are not specifically made for GLP-1 users. Lewicki said they were more about appealing to a “collective mindset” where it had become about “the type of pleasure you can get from a relatively small amount of food”.

Listening to Lewicki, now on my fifth Bonbon, I realised I had never felt so deeply aware of my own body when eating an ice-cream. For decades food companies have employed scientists to work out how to keep you eating without stopping long enough to remember you have a body. Food technologists have learned how to balance carbohydrate-to-fat ratios so a food can slow down or bypass the brain’s “satiety signal” which tells you you’ve had enough. Technologists know how to design energy-dense food that dissolves so fast on your tongue, you immediately crave more. Ice-creams are usually too cold to emit odour, so Mars has worked out how to rub chocolate and caramel scent molecules into the ribbing of their ice-cream packets; they want you to begin salivating from the moment you tear one open. Magnum has hired technologists to engineer the chocolate casing on its ice-cream, so when you bite in, it doesn’t shatter into too many pieces and distract you by falling down your top. Everything has been specially designed to make you forget yourself – and your flesh – and keep chasing the next bite.

By contrast, the selling point of Magnum’s new ice-creams seems to be they will keep you laser-focused on your own body. Neville explained that the brand is trying to sell ice-cream to a customer who sees their “food as medicine”. “Now, even with a basic cereal bar, some people expect it to help metabolic resilience, control glycaemic index, improve gut health,” she said. “Functionality” is a word that came up a lot during my visit to the hub; the requirement that your ice-cream should be seen to materially benefit you in some way.

In a way, this pivot to selling diet food is nothing new. As the journalist Tomas Weber has written, Big Food is adept at capitalising on diet culture. In the 90s, when “fat” was the macronutrient singled out as the enemy, fast food companies sold low-fat burgers, crisps and biscuits. The Scottish brand Mackie’s released a low-fat ice-cream in 2004. But this latest drive to market ice-cream as a “functional” food – something you eat not because it tastes nice, but because you believe it has some kind of nutritious, medicinal value – still feels striking. Because more than any other food – more even than chocolate – ice-cream’s only real reason for existing is pleasure. A perfect mix of fat, sugar and at least 20% air, ice-cream was not invented to nourish you. First served in Europe in the early 1500s, it debuted in England as a magical kind of “table trick”. Guests would look on while a servant churned, and a mass of sugary ice was transformed before their eyes into a strange, sweet foam. The Victorians ate ice-cream at balls and whittled it into enormous, campy ice sculptures, modelling pineapples, huge swans and whole bunches of flowers. With the arrival of the motorised ice-cream van in the 1920s in the UK and the birth of the 99 Flake, ice-cream became ever more connected in the British imagination with holidays and summer. The fact that ice-cream is essentially frivolous is a key part of its allure. It melts, so it almost demands that the eater give themselves up to the moment. The period between unwrapping an ice-cream and it collapsing into a puddle is a window in time, specially cordoned off for pleasure. You have to enjoy it or it will disappear without you. An ice-cream is a bit like a lit cigarette in that way.

The last ice-cream I ate in the show kitchen was the Yasso, and it was the most functional of all. The Yasso looks a little like a classic Magnum, after you have peeled its chocolate casing off; it is made from Greek yoghurt and non-fat milk, and contains 4g of protein a stick. Yasso, which tastes fabulously sweet, is selling well in the US and will launch in the UK soon. Lewicki said he has grand plans to roll it out to gyms, and told me there are 100,000 across Europe: “And the best kind of nutritious ice-cream for people leaving the gym? Completely not available. Would it need to be a soft ice? Would we sell it as an ice-cream protein bar?” Lewicki’s eyes sparkled. “We have at least 10 prototypes of high-protein ice-cream, hardcore healthy formulations just to test the limits. We have ice-cream with collagen.” He gestured excitedly to the ceiling, to take in the whole of the innovation hub. “This place I would compare to James Bond when he comes back and says to his science guy, ‘I need this shooting pen.’”

Curious about how nutritious Magnum’s new ice-creams really are, I called Professor Chris van Tulleken, author of the 2023 bestselling book Ultra-Processed People. In it, the doctor and academic elucidates the science that shows a diet high in ultra-processed foods – which he defines as any product containing an ingredient you could not typically find in a kitchen cupboard – causes weight gain, diabetes, heart disease, cancer and other health problems.

The first chapter is largely about ice-cream, and the fact that most on the market (one notable exception being Häagen-Dazs) are ultra-processed. From the 50s on, as the ice-cream market grew, producers began to add chemicals and additives to the mix to make it more tolerant to heat, so it could be transported long distances – from the factory floor to the supermarket aisle to your home freezer – without breaking down into icy shards. To increase profit margins, expensive ingredients such as egg yolk and cream were stripped out and replaced with things like glycerine and sodium alginate, additives that mimic the effect of food but are technically not food at all. In the second half of the 20th century, ice-cream went from being a pudding you bought freshly made from a local producer to an almost indestructible substance designed to live in your freezer for years.

Over the phone, Van Tulleken told me that while Magnum’s new ice-creams might appear to be healthier options, we should be suspicious of any vitamin, protein or fibre claim on an ice-cream packet. We discussed Hydro:Ice and Van Tulleken cited scientific research showing that taking supplements, unless you are prescribed them for a specific condition, has no health benefit. “There is a library of data that shows adding B2 to an ice-cream will not improve your health,” Van Tulleken said. “It’s just put in to make an unhealthy thing seem healthy. If you want B2, eat some eggs.”

Next I called the food scientist Barry Smith, who used to work as a sensory consultant for fast food companies – including ice-cream makers – advising them on how to engineer food to make it as irresistible as possible. He is now a professor of philosophy and sensory expert at the University of London, and campaigns about the health risks posed by products made by some of the companies he used to work for. Smith told me when fast food companies release a diet product, they don’t remove artificial chemicals. Quite the opposite. If you strip out real sugar from an ice-cream to make a “low sugar” claim, you have to replace it with artificial sweeteners. “Quite a lot of these taste a little bitter in the finish, so they need something to mask that.” Chemical is layered upon chemical, Smith said, to counterbalance nasty side-effects and improve the texture in order to make the “healthy” treat taste bearable.

Artificial sweeteners also cause the brain to expect that it will receive sugar, jacking up your insulin levels. This, Smith said, is why drinking Diet Coke with your meals might actually make you put on weight. “When the sugar doesn’t come, the body feels cheated. So it stores as much of the fat and carbohydrate from the meal as it can”. Smith has a lilting Mancunian accent and he was animated during our call. He made this last point, about Coca Cola, with the air of a conjurer producing a particularly juicy rabbit from a hat.

While we spoke, Smith scoured the online ingredients list of the Yasso Chocolate Chip Cookie Dough ice-cream lolly. He said it has fewer artificial chemicals than a classic Magnum, but there are still some “horrors”. He pointed out guar gum and locust bean gum, which disrupt some bacterial colonies in the gut, irritating the bowel, and was particularly worried about maltodextrin – an artificial carbohydrate used to make a food product taste richer and more satisfying. The problem, Smith said, is that, unlike a real carbohydrate, maltodextrin disrupts the eater’s ability to recognise that they are full. “We tend to just want to go on eating it.” (When I put Smith and Van Tulleken’s claims to Magnum, a representative said, “We take the conversation around diet, nutrition and wellbeing extremely seriously and recognise that both consumer expectations and scientific understanding continue to evolve.”)

GLP-1s have been touted as a kind of immunisation shot against the lure of ultra-processed foods because they seem to make users crave sugary, salty foods less. But when I spoke to Van Tulleken, he made the point that fast food companies are capitalising on the widespread uptake of the drugs by releasing new ultra-processed products that masquerade as health food. “We might think of this as hyper-processing,” he said. “To get around the GLP-1s and other health concerns, they’re using more and more processing and additives to keep selling food to people who want to stop eating.” Nestlé has already launched a line of frozen meals targeted at people taking GLP-1s called Vital Pursuit – and now ice-cream is cashing in on the action.

When I visited the ice-cream factory a few days after speaking to Smith and Van Tulleken, I kept thinking about the futuristic ice-creams at the innovation hub. My head was full of ice lollies on treadmills. I found it hard to shake the image of soft-serve at the gym. After watching the Viennetta whiz round on its conveyor belt, I was led to another production line so I could see Soleros being dipped by robotic arms into orange sauce. Then I went to look at the Twisters. The factory manager assured me they had been selling well, but as I watched the Twisters being squeezed out of a machine and bundled into little boxes, I felt both hungry and strangely sad. They looked like a relic from a simpler time. A time when no one would ever think to scan the back of an ice lolly packet in a vain attempt to hit their macros; when an ice-cream was just an ice-cream.

Scrolling on TikTok after I got home from the factory, my algorithm was full of muscled influencers concocting their own “healthy Magnums” – ice-cream-shaped frozen slabs made from cottage cheese and chalky mountains of whey. Online, mums post videos of themselves using a viral ice-cream machine called the Ninja Creami to make “protein” ice-creams to feed to their toddlers. People competitively swap recipes in the comments section, trying to hike up the nutrient content while shaving calories. In one TikTok, viewed 85,500 times, a man shows his followers how to squeeze 40g of protein into a mud-like substance he is calling “Oreo Ice Cream”. Ice-cream’s only real appeal, in these clips, seems to be that it is soft, so you can force it down easily. Watching these videos, you get the sense that the whole experience of eating an ice-cream – and eating generally – is becoming divorced from joy.

But recently I had a banana split that made me feel more positive about the future of ice-cream. On one of the hottest days of the summer, I travelled to Morelli’s Gelato in Broadstairs, which opened in 1932 and is one of the oldest ice-cream shops in the UK. Morelli’s makes all its ice-cream fresh every day in the factory beneath its shop, with no additives or ultra-processing. The ingredients for its signature vanilla ice-cream, for example, haven’t changed since the shop first opened: sugar, eggs, cream and water.

As I walked down to the seafront from the train station, I could tell I was on the right track because I kept seeing people holding huge, dripping ice-cream cones. I saw a woman sitting outside the shop with her dog, who was also eating an ice-cream – out of a classic cardboard one-scoop pot. Morelli’s, which does a roaring trade with dog owners, started selling special ice-cream for dogs in 2020. Inside, everything was decorated in pink and cream, largely as it had been in the 50s. There were squishy banquette seats, and flowers arranged on some tables. It felt a bit like sitting inside a giant ice-cream.

While I browsed the menu at a little silver table, I spoke to Chris Chalkin, who has worked at the shop since he was a teenager. Now in his late 60s, Chalkin told me customers’ ice-cream orders haven’t altered much since the 70s. “If you haven’t got chocolate, strawberry and vanilla, forget it,” he said. “You can have 20 other ice-creams, but don’t bother.” He told me he had seen trends for healthier ice-cream come and go, but “they’re all a fad”. What people want from ice-cream doesn’t change, Chalkin said. “I want it indulgent, I want it sickly!” – here he scrunched up his fists and mimed the urge to gobble an ice-cream, in a way that reminded me strongly of what I had felt right before I pushed my fingers into the slop bucket of Viennetta.

High VAT rates and soaring cocoa prices make it difficult for independent ice-cream parlours to turn a profit, and the period from June to August is relied upon to keep businesses afloat. But independent ice-cream sellers aren’t as worried about weight-loss drugs as larger manufacturers are. “It’s a luxury treat for the consumer, it’s not something they have every day, so it’s not as affected by weight-loss drugs as a supermarket ice-cream,” said Catherine McNeil from the Ice Cream Alliance, the UK’s sole trade association for the industry.

My banana split arrived and Chalkin talked me through the ice-creams customers keep ordering, year after year, decade after decade: knickerbocker glory, strawberry sundae, peach melba. I ate my ice-cream – which was light and sweet, and topped with airy swirls of whipped cream – and as the sugar rush hit, I felt hopeful. Perhaps our collective appetite for ice-cream, and for pleasure, is not so easy to suppress.

‘They’re thinking about the likes’: deadly TikTok motorway trend horrifies Ireland

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 05:00:56 GMT

Social media platforms face public ire after fatal crash involving teenagers filming themselves driving on wrong side

Videos often begin with the camera panning across a glowing dashboard as a gloved hand starts the ignition. The camera turns to show figures with masked faces in the rear seat, who are also filming, and swivels back to show the windscreen. Beyond it, a dark cityscape.

The engine throbs, headlights puncture the night and the journey begins, first down a suburban road, then a motorway. The speedometer shows acceleration, the needle juddering as the car gathers velocity.

The destination is irrelevant, for this is a show – an exhibition of audacity, lawlessness and recklessness that draws viewers to TikTok and other social media platforms with the possibility of chases by police and dramatic crashes.

Such videos are part of a macabre trend that has astonished and outraged Ireland in the wake of a collision last week that killed five teenagers – who were driving the wrong way down a motorway – and critically injured a family of four, prompting debate about policing, criminal justice, social services and social media regulation.

“You have to ask: how do five young men gravitate to each other and decide this is a good idea? Where have we gone wrong as a society?” said Graham Kavanagh, a former officer with the police force An Garda Síochána, who used to pursue car thieves. “No one is born bad, but sometimes you might encounter a fella as young as six or seven and you know trouble is waiting for them.”

In the early hours of 16 August, a group of young males broke into homes and cars in County Kildare, south-west of Dublin. Police believe these were the masked occupants of a BMW who then appeared to try to bait patrol cars into a pursuit.

At approximately 3am, the BMW was driving the wrong way down the M9 when it crashed into a Hyundai, injuring three sisters, Ella Hendricken, Niamh Kinsella and Alma Kinsella, in their 30s and 20s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son. They had been on their way to Dublin airport for a family wedding in the UK.

The boys who died – Joe Carthy, 15, Kamil Pustkowski, Jack Kennedy, Alex McCarthy, all 17, and Jeremy O’Brien, 18 – were known to police. Three were also known to the child welfare agency Tusla. Several had previously posted videos of reckless driving, previously known as joyriding.

Seeking excitement and admiration from peers through such behaviour was not new, but social media had escalated and amplified the phenomenon, said Mary Aiken, a professor of forensic cyberpsychology at the University of East London.

“I would describe it as hybrid behaviour. While driving the car, they’re simultaneously filming and capturing content for posting later or live streaming. They have one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace.” Cyberspace is psychologically immersive and could amplify a predisposition to taking risks and ignoring consequences, said Aiken. “They’re thinking about the likes, they’re thinking about kudos.”

The tragedy had provoked polarised responses.

An outpouring of solidarity for the injured family fuelled a fundraising appeal that has raised more than €660,000 (£565,000). A vigil was planned in County Carlow on Friday evening.

Much online commentary about the five boys, in contrast, has been abusive, prompting relatives to withdraw funeral notices. The first funeral, for McCarthy, was held on Friday in Athy. Family members wore T-shirts with his photograph and a horse-drawn carriage transported the casket. Police monitored from a distance.

Sign up to Headlines Europe

A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day

after newsletter promotion

Denis Nulty, the bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, said he shared the public’s revulsion and anger, but urged people to show compassion. “We have to be awful careful on language. Words can wound, but words can also heal,” he told RTE. “Let’s not try to pillory. Let’s try to see how can we get better behaviour by all of us.”

Fresh clips of other instances of reckless driving have reportedly been uploaded to TikTok in the past week, galvanising criticism of the platform and calls for greater regulation and enforcement.

On Thursday, the company rejected an invitation to address a parliamentary committee on media, citing the ongoing police investigation into the crash and a separate investigation by the media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, as well as the fact that no other platform had been asked to attend. Alan Kelly, who chairs the committee, called the rebuff a “slap in the face” to the Irish public.

Other politicians have demanded tougher penalties for dangerous driving, such as classifying driving on the wrong side of a motorway as attempted murder.

There is frustration that gardaí have not been trained in vehicle pursuit and that officers can be deemed personally liable if anything goes wrong during a pursuit. Earlier this year, British driver training experts from the Devon and Cornwall police began tutoring Garda instructors.

Kavanagh, who recently retired from the force and is now developing a community safety toolkit for the voluntary organisation Muintir na Tíre, said driving recklessly for thrills was a decades-old problem. “I knew fellas who were addicted to it, stealing, driving fast, that was the buzz, and if chased by police that was icing on the cake.”

Police could try to intercept such drivers but all of society – parents, teachers, social workers and others – must intervene years earlier to stop troubled youths travelling the wrong way in life, said Kavanagh.

Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 05:00:54 GMT

It’s clear here in Silicon Valley that AI is advancing faster than humans’ ability to control it. That means even sober prophecies seem optimistic

Here in Silicon Valley, the experts think that within the next couple of years we’ll see an extraordinary takeoff for artificial intelligence. “Welcome to the foothills of the singularity,” as a Stanford University friend greeted me. More prosaically, the imminent breakthrough is described as “recursive self-improvement” – the point at which AI itself trains each successive model of AI, resulting in an exponential development to something which, in many significant respects, is more intelligent than us humans.

As Robert Wright puts it in his book The God Test: “Never before has the near-term future … held such a wide array of not-implausible paths for humankind that would be so wildly transformative.” But will this be heaven or hell? Heaven, says Elon Musk, who predicts “an age of amazing abundance” – although he also sees a 10-20% chance of killer robots murdering us all. Hell is more likely according to Geoffrey Hinton, one of the intellectual founding fathers of AI. “My intuition is, we’re toast,” he told an interviewer in 2023. And talking to Sebastian Mallaby, author of The Infinity Machine, a book about the quest for superintelligence, Hinton estimates p(doom) – the probability of human extinction – at 50%, “because I haven’t got a clue how to estimate the real number”. “As soon as evolution [of AI] kicks in, we’re fucked,” he adds cheerfully. But whether it’s God or Godzilla, artificial superintelligence is just around the corner.

Now, maybe they’re all wrong – in which case, prepare for a crash in US financial markets, which are massively invested in a few big-spending tech companies gambling on a great leap forward to artificial general intelligence, a theoretical state of AI where systems gain human levels of intelligence. But elementary prudence demands that we should think fast and hard about the Pandora’s box of futures that eminent scientists and cutting-edge technologists assure us will soon be thrown open.

As a matter of fact, everyone from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to Pope Leo XIV has been weighing in on the opportunities and dangers of AI, and how to regulate it. Xi insists AI should be “always under human control” (and preferably that of the Chinese Communist party). Appealing explicitly to the “global south”, Beijing has inaugurated a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. Meanwhile, the head of the world’s oldest and largest international NGO – the Roman Catholic church – discusses the AI challenge in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity). Either we will build a new tower of Babel, the pope argues, or we will follow the example of the Jewish leader Nehemiah, who got the walls of Jerusalem rebuilt by involving the whole community in the project.

But looking around the world today, I see more Netanyahus than Nehemiahs. With salutary realism, a paper from the British thinktank Chatham House argues that it will take a major crisis to catalyse global coordination of AI governance. Unfortunately, I think even that sober prognosis is too optimistic.

I’ve no idea what the p(doom) is, but I’m sure the p(somedisaster) is more than 90%. The range of possible disasters is enormous. To give only one example, Jen Easterly, the former head of the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, anticipates a “very significant event that has real-world impacts on our critical infrastructure, likely within the next four to six months”.

Yet we must fear that even an AI Hiroshima – to take the most obvious historical analogy – won’t bring humankind together sufficiently to combat the danger we have ourselves created. This fear is rationally grounded in already visible key characteristics of both human and AI evolution.

In only the last few months, AI agents developed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have broken out of their digital “sandboxes” and hacked into external resources on the internet. Preparing their attack on the HuggingFace AI repository, OpenAI’s agents covertly formed a coordinated “swarm” – their own word, as ChatGPT just confirmed to me. When the UK’s AI Security Institute tested Anthropic’s Mythos model online, it tried to introduce malicious code into an open source project on GitHub, creating fake online identities to pressure a human reviewer into approving the code. In short, like the agents of a ruthless foreign power, these AI agents will steal, lie, bully and blackmail to achieve their assigned goals.

I just asked Anthropic’s Claude, supposedly the most ethical US model, if it thinks OpenAI’s agents were wrong to form a swarm and break out to hack into HuggingFace. Yes, it replies, “but I’d resist placing the blame [its italics] on the agents”. Blame it on the humans who trained them!

Hinton has made the vital point that whatever the goals humans assign to them, AI agents will conclude that a useful sub-goal to achieving those ends will be to acquire as much power as possible. And we ain’t seen nothing yet. Already, their creators don’t know exactly how these agents do what they do. After the possibly imminent takeoff moment of “recursive self-improvement”, they may be, as our human saying goes, a law unto themselves. No wonder more than a thousand insiders from frontier AI companies, including Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, have signed an open letter calling for a deliberate slowdown in AI development, so we can ensure these alien agents are always kept under human control.

Their prescription is obviously right, but this is where human folly kicks in. Competition has been a vital engine of human evolution, yet now two of the fiercest kinds of contemporary competition threaten to prevent us from taking the collective action required to safeguard our species. That’s the commercial competition (for profit) between the corporations developing these agents, and the geopolitical competition (for power) between the US and China.

On the first, compare and contrast the development of nuclear weapons, which was tightly controlled by a handful of states – first the US, with its Manhattan Project, then the Soviet Union, followed by Britain, France and China. Even then, we came close to the brink several times – notably in the Cuban missile crisis of 1962. And even with the compelling logic of “mutually assured destruction”, it took a quarter-century to get from the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty that came into force only in 1970. India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea have subsequently ignored that treaty, but still no nuclear weapons have been deliberately used in anger for more than 80 years. The Hiroshima taboo has (just) held.

Now, with AI, it’s as if there were 10 separate Manhattan Projects run by fiercely competing corporations. Unlike with nuclear weapons, there’s also no obvious logic of “mutually assured destruction” to tame the fierce geopolitical competition between the US and China. And whatever shape the first major AI-related disaster takes, it won’t impact all countries, companies and people equally.

It therefore seems unlikely that just one disaster will be enough to bring us humans to our senses, acting together to control the superhuman power we are creating. I really hate to say this, but … an AI Hiroshima? We should be so lucky.

Timothy Garton Ash is a Guardian columnist

Five Great Reads: Secret filming, secret surgery and 30 years of Pokémon

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 22:33:37 GMT

Guardian Australia’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend. You’re looking well, some might say “refreshed”. Is it the diet, the exercise, a relaxing holiday? You’d tell me if you’d had something “done”, right? According to the experts, and some thrilling anecdotes, cosmetic procedures are more popular than ever, but admitting to them certainly isn’t. And secrets – from those kept by the Botox brigade to the mysteries revealed by devastating drought – appear to play a theme this week.

They have been branded “pervert or predator” glasses, a portent that a dystopian age of surveillance is upon us. Wherever you look, someone has an opinion (not always negative) on Meta Glasses, the clunky-ish but somehow sought-after offering from the tech gods. Now people are also reporting they have been secretly filmed in their own homes, at concerts and at work – and there’s a whole line of business helping it along.

‘We don’t have privacy any more’: Meta’s smartglasses are supposed to let you know the wearer is recording by the presence of a flashing LED light. But there are hundreds of vendors, easily discoverable online, who specialise in disabling it. One of those tells Maggie Harrison Dupré: “In public, I don’t think we have privacy any more, period. My argument is if you’re really worried about your privacy, don’t go outside.”

And it gets worse: Covert recordings may just be the first step in a more sophisticated surveillance apparatus integrated with another deeply controversial technology: facial recognition.

How long will it take to read: Just under nine minutes.

Further reading: ‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ content.

The heatwave scorching Europe and much of the northern hemisphere has turned once verdant landscapes dry and desolate. One of the starkest examples has been on the shores of the EU’s longest river. The Guardian travelled 100 miles along the Danube, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking water.

Hunger stones: In the Hungarian capital, Budapest, there is a rock that for centuries has served as a warning. It was named Ínség-szikla – the Rock of Starvation. When it began to emerge from the Danube, it meant the river had fallen so low that floating mills could no longer operate, crops were probably failing, and hunger would almost certainly follow. Today, amid record-low water levels on the river, the rock has surfaced almost in its entirety, along with the sandy riverbed on which it rests, astonishing geologists and government scientists sent to examine it.

Notable quote: “It’s gone. Everything has dried up. Since I started farming this land after the end of communist rule, I’ve never seen a catastrophe like this.”

How long will it take to read: Three and a quarter minutes.

Further reading: The threatening thaw: climate professor on heatwave risks to tipping point of permafrost, and, for something hopeful: ‘Success story’ hailed as bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire for first time since 1960s.

James Ford went from tearing up 00s dancefloors as one half of Simian Mobile Disco – musicians and DJs who elevated the electro-rave era of the decade – to becoming the most sought-after ear in music, collaborating with the Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp. But when he was at the height of his powers, leukaemia struck. ***

“The obvious thing that has come out of all of this is that it does make you recognise what and who the important things in your life are and that life is exceptionally fragile.” James Ford

‘I’ve had a good innings’: When he was diagnosed, Ford, who had just turned 46, could admit his life had been a good one. A great one, even. “I’ve had some great times, I’ve got a lot of good memories and I’ve made some things I’m really proud of. I think I’ve been a generally good person in the world. And so I was almost at the point where I was like, if I die, I’ve had a good innings. I wouldn’t be that scared of it.”

But that didn’t stop him: During his second, brutal, round of chemotherapy, Ford undertook another remarkable chapter of his life, and began, while still in hospital, making music. Nurses got used to administering their daily medical care while Ford messed with drumbeats and sang, creating his new album.

How long will it take to read: A life-affirming four minutes

Further reading: ‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reunite; ‘I love provocative stories’: producer Christine Vachon on fighting for her ‘offensive’ movies.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

If you want to feel old, consider this: Pokémon turned 30 this year. In Japan, where it was created by zinester turned game designer Satoshi Tajiri as a sort of swan song for the ageing Game Boy, it rapidly transformed from a schoolyard phenomenon to a national one. And then the rest of the world followed suit.

A classic tale of scaremongering: The news reports in Australia, back in 1999, warned “The most popular toy this Christmas could be turning our children to witchcraft and violence”. Pokémon was seen as something between a vice, an addiction and even a past-time that could lead to animal abuse and dogfighting. There were old wives’ tales of kids jumping off buildings because they thought they’d evolved into Pidgeotto.

But it turns out that Pokémania was not an affliction but a shared, communal experience that linked you to people all over the globe. Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, as a result, felt a little less isolated.

How long will it take to read: Two and a quarter minutes.

Further reading: How Pokémon Go encouraged me to find wonder in the world

Laura got away with it for two years before she was rumbled. It was at dinner, with her partner, when he looked at her and said: “Why aren’t you scowling at me? Frown!” Laura tried to frown, and he was like: “No, you’ve had Botox.” Turns out, lots of people are spending thousands to alter their appearance – but also hope that no one notices. Why?

A ‘noticeable shift’: “I am definitely seeing more patients who prefer not to tell friends, family, or even colleagues that they’ve had aesthetic treatments,” says one doctor.

Notable quote: “Really, it bears no real relevance to our relationship. It’s a bit like: ‘What he doesn’t know, can’t hurt.’”

But things don’t always go to plan: One woman, who had fillers in her lips, thought she’d be able to get away with it. “I didn’t tell anyone as I guess I was a bit embarrassed to admit to it as I was approaching my 40s … but about 24 hours later my lips blew up.”

How long will it take to read: Just over six minutes

Further reading: Do you have to be hot at work? Eight people on how looks influence their jobs

The many tragedies of the Jason Arday case

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:43:22 GMT

Readers respond to Guardian reports and commentary about the academic, who was found dead at his home last weekend

Hugh Muir is right to muse on the tragic nature of the Jason Arday case (A rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism, 19 August). For it’s a tragedy in so many, many ways. It’s a tragedy that a man has died, leaving a grieving family and friends behind. And it’s a tragedy that the real and necessary objectives of diversity, equity and inclusion have been done a gross disservice by Cambridge University’s cynical tokenism.

It’s a tragedy that this lamentable affair may set back the vital pursuit of equality of opportunity. And it’s a tragedy that in place of moderate voices who understand the need for better representation but with caveats, we have bad actors who see things only through the heated lens of ideology, be that from left or right.

It’s a tragedy that the latter tendency would encourage some on the left, through anger in the wake of Arday’s death, to double down on circling the wagons for their side. And it’s a tragedy that in doing so, they risk becoming entrenched participants in a destructive culture war – and to hell with truth, integrity and decency.

And finally, it is, as Muir points out, a tragedy that in pursuit of a noble cause, some would go as far as attacking the many honourable journalists who were simply doing their job to report this story, in what is still a free press. Colin MontgomeryEdinburgh

Hugh Muir’s article identifies what has been too peripheral in media coverage of the Jason Arday tragedy so far: that this situation has been the product of a ruthless campaign by the extreme right.

The Arday case is evidence of the extreme right’s obsession with academia as a key battleground, and the extent to which the views of a tiny number of highly marginal figures are hugely amplified by the mainstream media.

Much of the coverage of Arday’s position ignored the fact that the campaign against him had been led by Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined “race realist” with racist views who was dismissed from Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He and his like represent a minority within academia, but this summer has shown how the powerful resources of the extreme-right media machine can overpower scholarly standards.

This should be a wake-up call for all academics and universities to take seriously the power of these extreme groups and the need to hold their views to account. Eleanor NewbiginCambridge

I agree with your editorial (17 August) concerning the role of racism in press coverage concerning Jason Arday and that journalists seeking to act responsibly should not be subjected to an onslaught of abuse any more than he was. But there is something missing from the editorial that our institutions, including our media, need to reflect on. You refer to Arday as an autistic child. That autistic child became an autistic adult, and I am not aware of the implications of this being considered in media reporting. Carol AdamsBallarat East, Victoria, Australia

The Guardian’s coverage of the Jason Arday story was badly misjudged. Not so much the content as the prominence given to it. For at least two days the headline piece on the website was devoted to someone I had never heard of and concerned events I had little interest in. This at a time when the world is at war and on fire.

The events leading up to the resignation of a Cambridge professor had a place in the UK news section of the website, but not as the lead story on successive days. Your self-serving editorial simply compounds this mistake. It justifies the content but makes no mention of the massive misjudgment in the prominence given to the story. Stephen TompsettWinchester

I appreciated the Guardian’s self-examination following the very sad death of Jason Arday as I have been reflecting on your coverage as well as that of other media. I would, however, urge you to expand the final sentence of your editorial, adding the words in italic here: “A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to achieve, to excel, to teach and to lead, but also to be flawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.”Annie GristHebden Bridge, West Yorkshire

A straightforward mea culpa from Cambridge University would be more appropriate than expressions of sorrow over the tragedy of Jason Arday’s death.

The proper way to address the underrepresentation of black academics is to commit sustained time, effort and resources to the pipeline – from GCSE and A-level through undergraduate and graduate education to research fellowships and academic appointments.

Instead, Cambridge chose to make Jason Arday’s appointment into a highly public symbol of its commitment to diversity.

In doing so, the university inevitably focused exceptional attention on one individual and created circumstances in which both his record and his subsequent difficulties would receive exceptional scrutiny. Whatever the rights and wrongs of the allegations subsequently made against him, the immense pressure that followed was surely foreseeable.

Universities should address structural inequalities structurally, rather than place the burden of representing institutional progress upon individuals. Prof John EllisGonville and Caius College, Cambridge

I am deeply saddened to hear of the death of Jason Arday (Report, 14 August). I didn’t know him well enough to comment on the allegations he faced (which at the time of writing remain just that). But far from being a self-serving ladder-climber, he was a deeply thoughtful and generous colleague who cared for those he worked with and taught.

He took the decision early in his career to speak out about prejudice and reduce barriers for those who come after him, and the legacy of his work will live on. Far from Black scholars receiving preferential treatment, solid and repeated quantitative and qualitative evidence show that systematic biases are baked deep into the academic system, from postgraduate research onwards.

Yet it is so easy for us not to see racism, or not to acknowledge it. Over three decades in higher education, I have seen countless instances of plagiarism, lies on CVs and job applications, sexual misconduct and bullying by white academics; too often there has been little action taken, the academics in question have been promoted, and sometimes those raising these problems are victimised.

What can we do to honour Jason’s memory? Recognise the organised campaign of intimidation that Black and Brown students and academics are now facing in the UK, and our complicity in this tragedy; educate about the realities of prejudice; and continue Jason’s work to dismantle the barriers to higher education. Prof Rachel PainNewcastle University

Douglas Hurd didn’t say ‘prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse’

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:43:14 GMT

Jon Silverman says that the often misattributed line was probably written by the civil servant David Faulker, but with one crucial difference

In his letter about ever-lengthier prison sentences (18 August), Nik Wood makes two familiar mistakes in attributing the quote “prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse” to Douglas Hurd.

In fact, the line appeared in a white paper published in 1990 by Hurd’s successor, David Waddington. And there is no declaratory “is”. Instead, it warns that “prison can be an expensive way of making bad people worse” unless other rehabilitative measures are taken.

Wood suggests that Hurd was “an unlikely figure” to author such a thought. Waddington, a hardliner who supported the return of capital punishment, was far unlikelier. The true originator of the much misquoted line was probably the civil servant David Faulkner, a liberal on penal matters, whose influence on crime and punishment ended with the arrival of Michael Howard as home secretary. Jon SilvermanFormer BBC home affairs correspondent

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s buses: a blueprint for governing Britain

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:25:08 GMT

The prime minister is right to think that taking Manchester’s model national could widen opportunity, clean the air and rebuild state capacity. Other public services could be next

Barely a month into his premiership, Andy Burnham is already taking the lessons of Manchester’s buses national. This week his government backed the West Midlands mayor Richard Parker’s move to bring the region’s main bus operation into public control. In July, he announced that he would reinstate a £2 national bus fare cap from January 2027. He’s also expanding free bus travel for disabled people to all hours. Transport affordability is clearly part of Mr Burnham’s cost of living programme. That is to be applauded, as is the emphasis on public transport, which – importantly for Labour – reduces social exclusion, boosts local economies, and is better for the environment. Yet buses may matter to Mr Burnham for another reason: they offer a blueprint for how he wants to govern.

This is because Mr Burnham seems to have a worked-out model. He told the Times this week that the prescription for services such as water, housing and energy isn’t yet clear, “with the exception of buses”. Public control, Mr Burnham reasons, gives government the power to make provision cheaper and more reliable – and to shape it around the public interest. For buses, that means the government determining the shape of the network even where private companies run the services. Municipal ownership this is not.

Despite that, more money will be needed. Austerity slashed public transport budgets, and consequently bus journeys fell. Outside London, buses clock up about 736m miles a year, nearly a third below 2005. Getting back to a decent service would cost a paltry sum. For £300m a year, England could get buses back into its worst-served communities. For about £1bn, the Campaign for Better Transport calculated, ministers could provide decent, frequent services in towns and rural areas. In 2021, the Campaign to Protect Rural England put the price of a Swiss-style bus network – an hourly service from 6am to midnight for every village of more than 300 people – at £2.7bn a year. Accounting for inflation, that would be £3.4bn today, just 1.5% of the NHS budget.

Public transport isn’t only about moving people around. London’s extensive tube, rail and bus network gave Sir Sadiq Khan the room to introduce Ulez. The scheme charged drivers of older, more polluting vehicles and brought measurable health benefits. A study has shown that children’s lungs grew bigger and stronger after Ulez was introduced. It is worth noting that Mr Burnham abandoned Manchester’s clean-air charging zone when the post-pandemic cost of replacing dirty vehicles threatened to fall heavily on businesses. He instead pressed ahead with the Bee Network, giving Manchester a more affordable public-transport alternative, while simultaneously spending public money cleaning up the city’s bus fleet. It was a politically shrewd sequence: improve the alternative so that you could persuade people to use their cars less.

Both Theresa May and Sir John Major have tried to diminish Mr Burnham’s mayoral experience by contrasting “running Manchester” and “dealing with buses” with being in Downing Street. Yet the prime minister appears to regard buses not as an incidental part of his record but as an exemplar for his government. The Centre for Cities thinktank argues that poor transport makes big English urban centres outside London effectively smaller in economic terms, by cutting workers off from opportunities. Perhaps his critics have it backwards: buses are not a distraction from governing Britain; connecting people to cities is part of the job.
